This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA Serverless is available. For more information, see Amazon MWAA Serverless Regions . To learn more, see Managing connections and variables and Using environment variables in Amazon MWAA Serverless workflows in the Amazon MWAA Serverless User Guide.
title: Amazon MWAA Serverless supports Apache Airflow connections and variables

summary: Amazon MWAA Serverless now supports operators from Apache Airflow provider packages, such as HTTP, Snowflake, or dbt, and custom operators that you write. This gives data engineers the flexibility to integrate with more systems and build specialized workflow tasks without provisioning infrastructure. To get started, add the provider package or your own operator to a code package, upload it to Amazon S3, and reference the operator in your workflow definition when you create or update a workflow. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA Serverless is available. For a list of supported Regions, see Amazon MWAA Serverless Regions . To learn more, see Running custom code with Python, Bash, and custom operators in the Amazon MWAA Serverless User Guide.
title: Amazon MWAA Serverless now supports custom and provider package operators

summary: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) now supports Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) for NVIDIA GPUs and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) network devices when using Amazon EKS Auto Mode and Karpenter. You can now define the device attributes your Kubernetes workloads need with DRA, share GPU devices across Pods, and allocate topology-aligned GPU and EFA devices while Amazon EKS Auto Mode and Karpenter dynamically scale Amazon EC2 instances based on workload demand. With DRA, you define ResourceClaim or ResourceClaimTemplate objects that describe what GPU or EFA devices can be allocated to workloads, by model, architecture, or other attributes. When running distributed training or inference, you can define PCIe-aligned GPU and EFA devices for optimal performance. Workloads then request those DRA objects in their configuration, and Karpenter automatically launches the lowest-cost instances that match. When using Amazon EKS Auto Mode, the NVIDIA DRA driver and EFA DRA driver (DRANET) are built-in, and you simply define your DRA objects and use them in your workloads. Amazon EKS Auto Mode automatically prevents workloads using DRA and workloads using device plugins for the same device type from running on the same nodes to mitigate the risk of silent device oversubscription during migrations. DRA support for Amazon EKS Auto Mode and Karpenter is available in all AWS Regions, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. DRA support is available for all Kubernet
title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode and Karpenter now support Dynamic Resource Allocation

summary: You can now attach Amazon S3 Access Points to your Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems in 4 additional AWS Regions, and to your Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems in 20 additional AWS Regions. With this capability, your file data in Amazon FSx is accessible for use with the broad range of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and analytics services and applications that work with S3, while your data continues to reside on your FSx file system. An S3 Access Point for Amazon FSx is an S3 endpoint that gives S3-based applications and services access to the data on your FSx file system through the Amazon S3 API, without copying or moving that data. For example, you can connect generative AI applications and agents to your file data with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases so they deliver relevant, contextual responses. Users can query the same data in place with Amazon Athena or transform it with AWS Glue, and you can share files with partners over SFTP, FTPS, and FTP using AWS Transfer Family. You can also access your files from serverless compute such as Amazon ECS and AWS Fargate, or from your own S3-based applications. Amazon S3 Access Points for FSx for ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS are now available in additional AWS Regions across North America, South America, Europe, Asia Pacific, and Africa. For the full list of AWS Regions supported for each file system, see the FSx for ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS user guides. Get started by creating and attaching S3 Access Points using
title: Amazon S3 Access Points for Amazon FSx are now available in additional AWS Regions

summary: AWS Nitro Sandboxes are now available as lightweight VMs managed by the Nitro Hypervisor. You can use Nitro Sandboxes for an Amazon EKS pod, or Amazon ECS task, or lightweight Virtual Machines (VMs), including AI agents running inside them, in their own hardware-isolated virtual machine powered by the AWS Nitro System . Each workload gets the isolation boundary of a Nitro isolated virtual machine. This allows you to safely run untrusted, multi-tenant, or regulated workloads within the resources of a single instance. Nitro Sandboxes run on your EC2 instances with near-native EC2 performance and inherits Nitro-hypervisor isolation. You can also validate your workloads through cryptographic attestation, so that secrets are released only to Nitro Sandboxes that have proven their integrity. With Nitro Sandboxes, you can safely execute LLM-generated code in an isolated environment of its own all while improving utilization and lowering compute costs by securely sharing a single EC2 instance across multiple agentic workloads. You can easily enable EKS pods or ECS tasks to run on Nitro Sandboxes and each pod or task gets its own isolated environment. Enabling Nitro Sandboxes in EKS or ECS is a one-line change and each pod or task gets its own VM, with your workloads remaining fully native (Pod Identity, VPC CNI, EBS/EFS/S3 storage, and CloudWatch all work out of the box). If you want full control, run Nitro Sandboxes directly on EC2 with your own AMI, orchestration, and with virtual
title: Introducing AWS Nitro Sandboxes on Amazon EKS, ECS and EC2 for hardware isolated pods, tasks and VMs

summary: Claude Fable 5.2 is now available on AWS and brings Anthropic's most capable generally available model for technical work to all customers. Fable 5.2 sets a new standard on the hardest projects in coding, math, and science, and Anthropic recommends it for fields like software engineering, scientific research, and finance, where judgment, iteration, and accuracy are critical. Claude Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model as Claude Fable 5.2 with its full cyber and bio capabilities retained for cybersecurity and biology research, is available through Anthropic’s verification programs. Claude Fable 5.2 can work for hours and up to days unattended, driving autonomous work and taking on bigger, more challenging projects. It takes on large, loosely defined engineering problems across multiple repositories and monorepos, tests its own work as it goes, and is more willing to question inherited conclusions, so it finds root causes previous Claude models miss. In Anthropic’s testing, it coordinated hundreds of subagents as a lead agent and flagged results that don't reproduce. Beyond coding, it develops new analytical methods for scientific research and brings frontier reasoning to quantitative finance. Anthropic has designated Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 as covered models, which require data retention for safety monitoring. Until Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is available, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention. Visit the Amazon Bedrock abuse detection page to lear
title: Claude Fable 5.2 is now available on AWS

summary: Amazon Athena now offers system tables which automatically capture your usage data and make it available for observability, usage analysis, and audit use cases. When you enable system tables, usage data is available within minutes of query completion across your workgroups and stored as service-managed, read-only Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables with configurable retention. You can query it directly with Athena, while AWS manages the tables for you, including schema definition, partitioning, compaction, and snapshot maintenance, removing all operational burden. Athena provides usage data through APIs like GetQueryExecution, CloudWatch metrics, and CloudTrail logs. With this launch, usage data is also available as iceberg tables that you can search, filter, aggregate, and join directly without building or maintaining custom pipelines. Platform teams can query the query_executions table to build cost allocation dashboards that show data scanned by workgroup, by user, or by table using simple SQL statements, and without custom ETL. Additionally, the AWS Agent Toolkit provides skills for querying system tables to surface usage patterns and optimization recommendations. Because the data is stored in the open Apache Iceberg format, you can also query it with DuckDB , Amazon Redshift, Amazon EMR or any other Iceberg-compatible engine. Athena system tables are available in all AWS Regions where Athena and Amazon S3 Tables are available. To get started, enable system tables from the
title: Amazon Athena introduces system tables for observability, auditing, and usage analytics

summary: Amazon DocumentDB Serverless now provides up to 35% higher throughput with the launch of platform version 4. Platform versions represent improvements in performance, scaling capabilities, or features, and are automatically managed at the cluster level. All new serverless clusters launch on the latest platform version available in your AWS Region. You can upgrade existing clusters on platform version 3 to platform version 4 by applying the serverless-platform-version-update pending maintenance action. This gives you control over when to apply the update, either immediately or during your next scheduled maintenance window. After you upgrade to a newer platform version, you can't downgrade to a previous version. You can view the platform version of a cluster in the AWS Management Console or through the ServerlessV2PlatformVersion field of the DescribeDBClusters API. For more information, see Amazon DocumentDB serverless scaling capacity and Checking and upgrading the platform version of a serverless cluster .
title: Amazon DocumentDB Serverless now provides up to 35% higher throughput

summary: Today, AWS is introducing an open-source solution with a local web UI that helps customers turn data lake records into graphs for analysis with Amazon Neptune Analytics. By projecting selected records and relationships, customers can investigate connections across tables and run graph algorithms without building their own ETL pipelines. For example, a customer could project accounts and transactions into a graph to explore how accounts are connected or identify communities that may warrant investigation. Doing this today often means writing queries to prepare node and relationship data, creating a Neptune Analytics graph, and managing the import. Customers may also need to build a selective projection so they do not load an entire dataset for a narrower question. The new UI brings those steps into single workflow. To run graph analytics over iceberg tables, customers select an Athena catalog and database, define a property graph using SQL/PGQ, and preview rows before import. The solution runs the projection queries through Athena, stages the selected data in Amazon S3, and imports it into Neptune Analytics. The UI helps customers manage the resulting graph. They can open the loaded graph in Graph Explorer to query and visualize relationships. [1] The UI runs locally and it is available in all regions where Amazon Neptune Analytics is available. To get started, see the setup instructions .
title: Introducing an open-source UI for graph analytics over data lakes with Amazon Neptune Analytics

summary: Amazon Connect Customer now provides evaluation form templates so managers don't have to build forms from scratch, reducing the time to deploy automated evaluations of human and AI agent performance. These templates cover typical customer interaction scenarios: customer service, inbound sales, and self-service. Each template assesses human and AI agent behaviors. For example, the customer service template includes questions such as "Did the agent show empathy toward the customer's issue?" Templates also include questions that assess business outcomes such as customer satisfaction and attrition risk, so managers can see how agent behaviors relate to outcomes. Managers can use the templates as-is or customize them before deploying. This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, visit our documentation and our webpage . For Amazon Connect Customer pricing, visit our pricing page.
title: Amazon Connect Customer launches evaluation form templates

summary: Amazon Bedrock, the platform for building generative AI applications and agents at production scale, now offers Claude Mythos 5.2 to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Mythos 5.2 is Anthropic's most advanced AI model to date for use cases across cybersecurity, software coding, and complex reasoning tasks. The model can identify sophisticated security vulnerabilities in software and demonstrate exploitability. It can also comprehend large codebases and deliver actionable findings with less manual guidance than previous AI models. This enables security teams to accelerate defensive cybersecurity work, find and fix security vulnerabilities in the world's most critical software, and address them before threats emerge. Claude Mythos 5.2 is the first of Anthropic's AI models with powerful cybersecurity capabilities to be available in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions through Amazon Bedrock . Access is limited to allow-listed organizations; to get started, visit Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program .
title: Amazon Bedrock now offers Claude Mythos 5.2 to Eligible Customers in AWS GovCloud (US)

summary: AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) now lets your workloads use their AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity in one partition to get temporary credentials for an IAM role in a different partition, without storing long-term credentials, which can help improve your security posture. Partitions are groups of AWS Regions, such as the commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and each partition has an independent instance of IAM, creating a hard boundary between them. Previously, organizations that run workloads across partitions commonly relied on long-term credentials, such as IAM user access keys, that don't expire automatically. With this launch, your workload requests a short-lived token from AWS STS in its own partition and exchanges it for temporary AWS credentials in the other partition, using the existing GetWebIdentityToken and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity APIs. You control which identities can access each role, apply governance across your organization, and audit token use in AWS CloudTrail in both partitions. This launch helps with scenarios such as consolidated security and compliance reporting, and centralized operations tooling. If your organization already operates a public key infrastructure (PKI), IAM Roles Anywhere is another option for cross-partition access. Cross-partition federation is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) Regi
title: AWS STS now supports cross-partition federation for AWS identities

summary: AWS Sign-In now supports OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), enabling applications to exchange third-party OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens for short-lived, AWS service-scoped OAuth access tokens. This allows customers to securely integrate third-party applications with supported AWS services without sharing AWS credentials, while maintaining access controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). This capability is available for supported AWS services that use AWS Sign-In OAuth , enabling customers to use existing identity providers to securely access AWS services without managing additional credentials. To learn more , see the AWS Sign-In User Guide , AWS MCP Server User Guide and the AWS Glue launch announcement .
title: AWS Sign-In now supports OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange

summary: Today, AWS announces a new bi-directional, zero-copy integration between AWS Analytics services and Workday Data Cloud. Instead of building and maintaining ETL pipelines to replicate data between systems, joint customers can now query across their AWS and Workday datasets in place, without moving or copying data, while retaining existing security controls in both environments. From AWS, you can use Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon Athena to query Workday data through Workday Live Data Query or federate to Apache Iceberg tables in Workday Data Cloud through catalog federation. Configure a connection in SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Glue, or AWS Lake Formation consoles and begin querying immediately. Access is governed by AWS and Workday permissions. From Workday, you can register your AWS Glue Data Catalog Iceberg REST endpoint as an external catalog in Workday Analytics and query your AWS Iceberg tables directly. Common use cases include joining workforce data with business data for talent analytics, workforce planning, and machine learning. This integration is available in all AWS commercial regions where AWS Glue is available. To learn more, see the AWS Glue User Guide , the Workday Data Cloud integration with AWS on Workday Data Cloud , and the AWS Big Data Blog post .
title: AWS Analytics services now support Workday Data Cloud integration

summary: Amazon Route 53 Profiles now lets you associate more than one Profile with a VPC. Previously, a VPC could have only one Profile, so teams that managed Route 53 configurations separately (for example, security teams managing DNS Firewall rule groups while cloud infrastructure and network admin teams manage private hosted zones and Resolver forwarding rules) all had to share a single Profile and associate their private hosted zones, Resolver rules, and DNS Firewall rule groups with it. With this launch, you can now associate multiple Profiles with the same VPC and set a priority for every Profile. Route 53 evaluates a VPC's Profiles in priority order, starting with the lowest number, so you can keep shared Route 53 configurations in one Profile and team-specific configurations in another without merging them, while assigning them the right priority. Combined with the granular IAM permissions launched in March 2026, multiple Profiles per VPC improves security posture by letting each team own and manage its own Profile with least-privilege permissions. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where Route 53 Profiles is available. Each Profile-VPC association is billed at standard Route 53 Profiles pricing. For details, see Amazon Route 53 pricing . To learn more, see Route 53 Profiles in the Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide.
title: Amazon Route 53 Profiles now supports multiple Profiles per VPC

summary: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) now supports DuckDB operators. DuckDB is an embedded analytical database that lets customers perform data quality checks, summaries, and transformations on data from sources DuckDB supports, including Amazon S3. Native support is available for DuckDB on Amazon MWAA Provisioned environments running Apache Airflow 3.3.1. DuckDB comes preinstalled and preconfigured for AWS connections in the latest MWAA Airflow 3.3.1 update. After updating their MWAA environment to Airflow 3.3.1 and adding execution role access to their data stores, customers can start writing tasks with DuckDBExecuteQueryOperator with no additional setup. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA is available. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To learn more, see Using DuckDB with Amazon MWAA in the Amazon MWAA User Guide.
title: Amazon MWAA now supports DuckDB operators

summary: Amazon Quick, the AI workspace built only for work, is now AWS Quick, a name that reflects the enterprise security and governance built into Quick from the start as an AWS service. The new name now appears across the Quick website, the web, desktop, and mobile apps, and AWS documentation. Existing customers don't need to take any action, and Quick works the same way it did before. Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence capability in Quick, is now AWS Quick Sight. Quick Sight customers can keep using their dashboards, datasets, and analyses just as they do today, with no changes to their data, settings, or pricing. With Quick, teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already use, regardless of vendor. Quick understands your role, your team, and how your work connects, and anyone can build agents, apps, and automations in plain language that become shared assets for the whole team. Quick is HIPAA eligible and holds compliance certifications including FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data stays in your environment and never trains someone else's models. AWS Quick is available in many AWS Regions. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To learn more, see AWS Quick .
title: Amazon Quick is now AWS Quick

summary: AWS Glue now supports 100 new native connectors that simplify access to data in popular SaaS and REST API-based applications. Previously, bringing data from SaaS applications into AWS required writing custom code. Now, teams can create a connection once in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and reuse it across ETL jobs with the same permissions model they already use for AWS Glue. The new connectors span generative AI, finance, payments, marketing, product analytics, human resources, engineering, IT operations, and collaboration tools. AI teams can bring usage and cost data from model providers such as Anthropic to track generative AI adoption and spend. Finance teams can consolidate transactions from applications such as Adyen, Square, and Xero for faster reporting. Product and marketing teams can combine billing, usage, and campaign data from tools such as Chargebee, Amplitude, and Klaviyo to understand customer lifetime value. HR teams can unify workforce data from systems such as BambooHR and Gusto for headcount planning. Engineering teams can join incident and deployment data from tools such as PagerDuty, Sentry, Jenkins, and Vercel to track reliability. You can load the integrated data into Amazon S3 or Amazon Redshift for analytics and reporting. The 100 new AWS Glue connectors are available in all AWS Commercial Regions on Glue versions 5.0 and above. To learn more, see the complete list of available connectors and learn about connecting to individual connectors in the AWS Glu
title: AWS Glue adds 100 new native connectors for popular SaaS applications

summary: Amazon CloudWatch Logs now supports account-level retention policies, so you can use a single policy to set how long log data is kept across all or subset of log groups in an AWS account. Account-level policies allow platform and security teams to bring each log group in line with their retention standards. With today's launch, you can create policies that cover all log groups in the account or apply to a specific set of log groups with names that start with a prefix, such as /aws/lambda. You can additionally choose whether it applies to existing log groups or only new ones. When more than one policy matches a log group, the longest retention period applies. For example, a central platform team can set a 90-day baseline for the account and a 1-year policy for log groups that start with /security to meet audit requirements, without tracking individual log group names. Account-level retention policies are available in all commercial AWS Regions except Middle East (Bahrain), and Middle East (UAE) at no additional cost . You can create and manage up to 20 policies per account and region using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, and AWS SDKs. Learn more in the CloudWatch Logs documentation , and the API reference .
title: Amazon CloudWatch Logs announces account-level retention policies

summary: Today, AWS announces the general availability of the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which lets you search the web with a single API call. Web Search on AgentCore has been available as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway. The new InvokeWebSearch API gives applications, custom agent loops, and data pipelines search results with no resources to create. The API returns ranked results from the Amazon-operated web index behind Web Search on AgentCore. Each result includes a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You can filter each request by domain and publication time, for example to find recent product announcements or check a claim against trusted domains. You call the API with the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and authorize calls with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). You can call it from your virtual private cloud (VPC) through AWS PrivateLink and log requests as AWS CloudTrail data events. Web Search API queries are billed at $7 per 1,000 queries, the same rate as Web Search through AgentCore Gateway, with no gateway charges. The Web Search API is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To learn more, see Search the web with the InvokeWebSearch API in the AgentCore Developer Guide, the Web Search page, and AgentCore pricing .
title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers a Web Search API

summary: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports clone-based upgrades, which let you validate a new OpenSearch version alongside your current one and cut over to it only when you're satisfied. If you find a problem, you can cancel before you cut over or roll back afterward. With clone-based upgrades, you can move to new versions with more confidence. When you start a clone-based upgrade, OpenSearch Service copies the data from your existing cluster (the primary cluster) to a second cluster running the new version (the cloned cluster). While the primary cluster keeps serving your workload, you can run the same search queries on both clusters and compare their performance using Amazon CloudWatch metrics. After you finish validating, you can cut over to the cloned cluster. If you keep the previous version for a retention period you choose, you can roll back to it at any time during that period. You can start and manage a clone-based upgrade from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, or the OpenSearch Service APIs. Clone-based upgrades are available for domains running OpenSearch 1.1 or later, or Elasticsearch 7.10, in AWS Commercial Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is offered, except Asia Pacific (New Zealand), Asia Pacific (Taipei), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Mexico (Central). For a complete list of Regions, see the AWS Region Table . To learn more, see Upgrading Amazon OpenSearch Service domains in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide. To get started, visit the Amaz
title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now lets you validate and roll back version upgrades

summary: Amazon CloudWatch alarms that use Prometheus Query Language (PromQL) can now trigger Amazon EC2 and Application Auto Scaling step and simple scaling policies. You can scale your EC2 Auto Scaling groups on CloudWatch OpenTelemetry metrics using the same kind of PromQL queries you use for dashboards and alerting. In this release, PromQL alarms also support EC2 Auto Scaling simple and step scaling policies. Target tracking is not currently a supported policy type for PromQL alarms. Teams moving to OpenTelemetry can scale capacity on the same metrics as the rest of their monitoring, instead of keeping separate classic metric alarms for scaling. For step scaling, how far the value is past the threshold in your PromQL query decides which step applies. The query must return a single series and compare it to a threshold. You can add EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling actions in the CloudWatch console when you create or edit an alarm, or with the PutMetricAlarm API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. You can also use the PutMetricAlarm API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch PromQL alarms are available. Standard CloudWatch alarm pricing applies. To get started, see Using PromQL in alarms and Alarm actions in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.
title: CloudWatch PromQL alarms now support EC2 and Application Auto Scaling

summary: AWS Partner Central now offers a new business planning experience in the AWS Console. AWS Partners can initiate plans for growing their AWS business or collaborate on plans initiated by AWS teams. Partners can collaborate with AWS partner development, technology, marketing, and specialist teams to define plan narratives, goals, and initiatives. AI-assisted plan readiness scores help partners identify areas to improve, while real-time tracking shows progress against goals. Partners can also add attachments and export plans to prepare for business reviews. Partners can use application programming interfaces (APIs) and software development kits (SDKs) to integrate business planning into their workflows. Programmatic notifications are also available. Business planning is available to AWS Partners who are actively engaged with AWS Partner management teams. AWS Partner Central is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and choose Business Plan.
title: AWS Partner Central now provides an improved business planning experience

summary: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) 8.0.3 adds hybrid post-quantum key exchange for TLS, wildcard indexes, the $unionWith aggregation stage, and new change stream events. Post-quantum TLS protects data in transit from traffic that is recorded today and decrypted later with a quantum computer. The new MongoDB APIs let you move more MongoDB workloads to Amazon DocumentDB without changing application code. What's new in 8.0.3: Post-quantum TLS: TLS 1.3 connections use hybrid key exchange based on the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) when the client supports it. Other clients keep using classical key exchange. Two new Amazon CloudWatch metrics, TLSHandshakesClassical and TLSHandshakesPostQuantum, count the handshakes of each type. Wildcard indexes: index every field, or every field under a path, to query documents with dynamic schemas. Aggregation: $unionWith combines results from multiple collections in one pipeline. $lookup and $graphLookup work in views, and correlated $lookup sub-pipelines accept $unionWith and $facet. Change streams: dropIndex() and dropIndexes() now emit dropIndexes events. Compression metrics: collStats and stats() report per-collection input bytes, output bytes, and compression ratio. Amazon DocumentDB 8.0.3 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon DocumentDB is offered. To learn more, see the Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide .
title: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) now supports post-quantum TLS, wildcard indexes, and $unionWith in version 8.0.3

summary: Amazon S3 Tables now support server access logging, providing you detailed records of the requests made to your table buckets. You can now track table operations, namespace management, and data access to support security audits, access analysis, and cost attribution. Log delivery is available at no additional cost, and you pay only for the storage of the log files. When you enable server access logging on a table bucket, S3 delivers logs for requests to all tables and namespaces in that bucket to a general purpose bucket in the same account and Region. Each record captures the requester, operation, table name, namespace, response status, and request timing, using the same space-delimited format as S3 server access logs for general purpose buckets. This lets you reuse your existing log analysis workflows to query S3 Table logs with any query engine of your choice such as Amazon Athena and DuckDB. Server access logging for S3 Tables is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are available. You can enable it using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables overview page and S3 Tables server access logging in the Amazon S3 User Guide.
title: Amazon S3 Tables now support S3 server access logging

summary: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports vector, full-text, and hybrid search, along with aggregations. Applications searching live data often face a hard trade-off between latency and recall, along with delays before updates become searchable. With search on ElastiCache Serverless, applications can search data with latency as low as microseconds at up to 99% recall for vector search, while serving billions of queries per day. Updates are searchable in as little as microseconds, as soon as writes complete. Search on ElastiCache Serverless is ideal for latency-sensitive applications with unpredictable traffic and for teams that want to get started with search quickly. You can combine search types in a single query, tune recall as needed, and analyze results with server-side aggregations. Developers can give every agent, session, or task its own datastore for memory and context retrieval, so agents can experiment, fail, and retry without touching production or each other. Each datastore is ready in seconds, reachable over a public endpoint with no network setup, and billed only for what it uses, with zero infrastructure to manage. Applications can also power product discovery, recommendation systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Search is available on ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey in all commercial AWS Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud Region on ElastiCache version 9 for Valkey. Valkey is the most permissive o
title: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless now supports vector, full-text and hybrid searches plus aggregations

summary: Today, AWS announces next-generation firewall (NGFW) policy for AWS Network Firewall, a new policy model that provides security teams with a simpler policy structure and increased rule capacity. AWS Network Firewall is a managed network security service that protects your Amazon VPCs with access control and threat detection. The new policy model strengthens your security posture by layering firewall and IPS protections instead of combining them, which also makes policies easier to manage. You author firewall rules that enforce deny-by-default access control, such as allowing traffic only to approved domains. For IPS rules, you can use managed rule groups from AWS or AWS Marketplace partners, which update automatically as new threats emerge. You can also create your own custom IPS rule groups. Firewall and IPS rules each have their own capacity, so you no longer trade one off against the other. For rules you don't share across policies, you can create embedded rule groups that draw capacity on demand without pre-allocation. With NGFW policy, all rules are stateful and evaluate with full connection context, for consistent, predictable traffic handling. Your existing policies continue to operate without changes, and IPS rules remain backward compatible. NGFW policy is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. For a full list of supported regions, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page . To learn more, see the AWS Network Fi
title: AWS Network Firewall launches next-generation firewall policy

summary: Today, AWS Marketplace announces that free trials of usage-based software as a service (SaaS) products can now convert automatically to paid subscriptions. When a free trial ends, the buyer's subscription continues at the seller's usage-based pricing, so buyers pay only for what they use after the trial. This helps sellers turn more trial users into paying customers. Buyers get a simple way to evaluate software before they buy, with no new subscription and no interruption in access. Sellers can offer a free trial of 7 to 90 days that converts to a paid subscription at the price they set. For example, a data team can try an analytics product for 30 days and, if it meets their needs, keep using it after the trial ends. Buyers see the trial length, conversion date, and pricing before they subscribe. They receive reminder emails before the trial converts and can cancel at any time before conversion at no charge. Sellers can create a free trial in AWS Partner Central, or update an existing free trial offer to convert automatically. This capability is available for public offers in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace is available. To learn more, see the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide and the AWS Marketplace Buyer Guide .
title: AWS Marketplace SaaS free trials now convert automatically to paid subscriptions

summary: Amazon GameLift Servers now offers Game Session Placement Insights, delivering detailed, per-placement diagnostic logs for game session queue routing. Amazon GameLift Servers routes game session placement requests through queues that evaluate multiple fleet locations based on latency and cost factors. This feature is designed for game developers and engineers who need greater transparency into how their game session queues operate. Previously, developers had limited visibility into why placements succeeded, failed, or timed out, making queue optimization difficult. Game Session Placement Insights captures which fleet locations were evaluated, the player latency and cost factors that influenced routing decisions, and the final placement outcome for every placement. This enables teams to identify patterns such as consistently slow placements, repeated failures, or sessions landing in unexpected locations, and to tune their queues to improve the overall player experience. You can enable this feature per queue and deliver logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, and Amazon Data Firehose. Game Session Placement Insights is available in all supported Amazon GameLift Servers regions. To learn more about Game Session Placement Insights and how to get started, visit the Amazon GameLift Servers documentation .
title: Amazon GameLift Servers now supports Game Session Placement Insights

summary: Eligible customers can now access OpenAI’s specialized cybersecurity models Daybreak Red: GPT-5.6 Cyber and Daybreak Blue: GPT-5.6 Sol through the bedrock-runtime endpoint on Amazon Bedrock. Daybreak Blue is the starting point for most security teams across defensive workflows, including vulnerability discovery, detection engineering, and incident response. Daybreak Red is designed for advanced, authorized tasks such as vulnerability research, exploit reproduction, and mitigation development. For these tasks, a lower refusal threshold, matched by stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls, improves the speed and depth of an investigation. Your inference data is not used for model training, and neither model requires you to opt in to sharing your data with OpenAI. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, the models are available through US and Global cross-Region inference (CRIS) profiles. Access to the models requires enrollment in Daybreak access from OpenAI. To enroll, contact OpenAI or reach out to your AWS account team for guidance on eligibility. Once approved, work with your account team to request access on AWS. For regional availability through the bedrock-mantle endpoint and more information, view the documentation.
title: Amazon Bedrock adds bedrock-runtime endpoint support for Daybreak models

summary: Amazon S3 Access Grants can now discover and list all your grants across multiple AWS accounts with a single API call, eliminating the need to query each account separately. A single ListCallerAccessGrants call returns grants from your own S3 Access Grants instance and every instance shared with you, giving you a complete view of the S3 data you can access. By setting the new InstanceScope parameter to ALL in your ListCallerAccessGrants request, S3 Access Grants queries every instance shared with you through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) and returns all the grants in one combined response, each identifying the account that owns it. Additionally, when you request credentials with GetDataAccess for an S3 path and set InstanceScope to ALL , S3 Access Grants locates the owning account for you, routes the request to its instance, and returns credentials for the matching grant. This capability is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Access Grants is available, at no additional cost. You can use the AWS SDK, API, or CLI to list and access grants across accounts. To learn more, visit the S3 Access Grants overview page and the S3 documentation .
title: Amazon S3 Access Grants now support listing grants across multiple AWS accounts

summary: Starting today, Amazon RDS for MySQL 26.10 is available in the Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment , allowing you to evaluate the pre-release of MySQL 26.10 on Amazon RDS for MySQL. MySQL 26.10 includes bug fixes, security patches, and some improvements to READ COMMITTED workload performance and purge lag warnings in the error log. On busy READ COMMITTED workloads, NUMA systems performance could be impacted as each read view that closed required a global mutex. Read-view objects can now be reused which eliminates the global mutex on closure. The error log now reports warnings when the history-list length (HLL) crosses innodb_max_purge_lag and when purge lag begins delaying DML, so you can detect purge backlogs before they affect performance. To learn more, please refer to the MySQL 26.10 release notes . Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment database instances are retained for a maximum period of 60 days and are automatically deleted after the retention period. Amazon RDS database snapshots that are created in the Preview Environment can only be used to create or restore database instances within the Preview Environment. Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment database instances are priced as per the pricing in the US East (Ohio) Region.
title: Amazon RDS for MySQL 26.10 is now available in Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment

summary: Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) for PostgreSQL announces Amazon RDS Extended Support minor versions 13.23-rds.20260819, 12.22-rds.20260820 and 11.22-rds.20260822. Amazon RDS Extended Support provides up to three additional years of fixes for critical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) and bugs beyond a major version's end of standard support date, giving you more time to upgrade to a new major version. You can upgrade your database using Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments , in-place upgrade, or restore from a snapshot. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL User Guide . Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale PostgreSQL deployments in the cloud. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).
title: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL announces Extended Support minor versions 13.23-rds.20260819, 12.22-rds.20260820 and 11.22-rds.20260822

summary: Amazon OpenSearch Service now offers managed cross-Region disaster recovery, so you can meet strict availability and business continuity requirements for mission-critical search, AI, and analytics workloads without building or maintaining replication yourself. After you create domains in two Regions, you can pair them with a single API call or a few steps in the AWS Management Console. Managed disaster recovery delivers a recovery point objective (RPO) of under one minute and a recovery time objective (RTO) of under 20 minutes. The secondary domain stays continuously in sync with the primary. For planned events such as maintenance or Region rotation, a switchover swaps the two domains' roles with zero data loss. If your primary domain becomes unavailable, a failover promotes the secondary, with data loss limited to the replication lag. After a failover, you restore protection by pairing the new primary with a secondary domain. You can monitor replication health and lag with Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Managed disaster recovery requires OpenSearch 3.7 or later and supports domains in the same AWS account, including domains encrypted with customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys. Domains that use UltraWarm storage or OpenSearch Optimized instances (OR1 or OR2) aren't supported. If you're on an earlier version, clone-based upgrades let you test OpenSearch 3.7 against your workload, cut over when you're ready, and roll back if needed. There's no additional charge
title: Amazon OpenSearch Service announces managed cross-Region disaster recovery

G7 instances deliver up to 4.6x AI inference performance and up to 2.1 graphics performance compared to G6 instances. G7 instances also deliver faster performance for GPU-accelerated data analytics workloads. Customers can use G7 instances for deploying AI models for language translation, video and image analysis, speech recognition and recommender systems. They also accelerate graphics workloads such as creating and rendering real-time, cinematic-quality graphics and game streaming. Additionally, G7 instances support video transcoding, spatial computing, and data analytics workloads. G7 instances feature up to 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with 32 GB of memory per GPU and custom Intel Xeon 6 processors. They support up to 192 virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and up to 700 Gbps of Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking bandwidth. They also support up to 768 GiB of system memory, and up to 7.6 TB of local NVMe SSD storage. You can use G7 instances for Amazon EC2 in the following AWS Regions: US West (Oregon), US East (N. Virginia, Ohio) , Europe (London, Spain, Frankfurt, Stockholm) , Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Sydney) and South America (Sao Paulo). You can purchase G7 instances as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or as part of Savings Plans. To ge
title: Amazon EC2 G7 instances now available in additional regions

summary: Custom billing views now support AWS Billing Conductor and AWS Billing Transfer views as source views. These are the views AWS maintains per billing group and per billing transfer relationship. You can combine them into a single custom billing view, apply filters, and use that view in Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and the Billing and Cost Management console. There are three source view types. Billing group views contain the cost of each Billing Conductor billing group, which you can combine for chargeback and showback across business units. Billing transfer views contain the cost transferred to you for each end customer, and transfer showback views contain the cost that end customer sees. Aggregating each type gives you your total transferred cost and the total bill your end customers see. Your access does not change: you can use an AWS-managed view as a source only where you can already access it. Once created, you can share a custom billing view using AWS Resource Access Manager with accounts inside or outside your organization, so your finance team or a downstream seller works with the data in their own account. Whether you are an AWS Partner reselling AWS services or an organization using billing groups for pro forma billing, you get one consolidated view instead of one per customer or group. title: AWS Billing and Cost Management now supports AWS Billing Conductor and AWS Billing Transfer views as source views for custom billing views

summary: The AWS Quick desktop app for macOS and Windows and the Quick mobile app for iOS and Android are now available in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. This launch builds on the recent availability of Quick in Singapore . The desktop app works with your local files and connects to your calendar, email, and business apps. The mobile app lets you chat with Quick, review your activity feed, and open dashboards. Your conversations, context, and agents stay in sync across web, desktop, and mobile, so you can start an agent on your desktop, check on it from your phone, and let it keep running after you close your computer. To get started, download the desktop app from the AWS Quick download page or the mobile app from the Apple App Store or Google Play . To learn more, see AWS Quick on mobile in the AWS Quick User Guide and the AWS Quick product page .
title: AWS Quick apps are now available in Asia Pacific (Singapore)

summary: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports security groups for Pods, letting you apply dedicated Amazon EC2 security group rules to individual Pods. Different workloads on the same node can carry different security groups, giving your Pods network-level segmentation without creating separate node pools for each application. Security groups for Pods extends your existing AWS network controls to the Pod level, so your Pods can reach resources such as Amazon RDS and Amazon ElastiCache databases that authorize connections by security group under the same rules the rest of your VPC uses. You define which Pods receive which security groups with a SecurityGroupPolicy resource, and Pods not matched by a policy keep using their node’s security groups. Security groups for Pods is included as part of EKS Auto Mode at no additional charge and is available on clusters running Kubernetes version 1.36 or later, in all AWS Regions where EKS Auto Mode is supported. To learn more, see Security groups for Pods in the Amazon EKS User Guide and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode product page.
title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports security groups for Pods

summary: AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports the x86 CPU architecture, so you can run your existing x86 applications, tools, and software dependencies without recompiling or porting them. When you create a MicroVM image, you can now choose between x86 and Arm (AWS Graviton) to give each user or job an isolated MicroVM on the architecture your workload uses. Lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for running user or AI-generated code, in applications such as AI coding assistants, CI/CD runners, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners. Today’s launch enables you to run x86-based workloads on Lambda MicroVMs as-is. For workloads that run on Arm, you can continue using AWS Graviton processors which is the default CPU architecture option. To start building x86 workloads on Lambda MicroVMs, choose the x86 architecture when you create a MicroVM image from your Dockerfile, then launch MicroVMs from that image. You can use MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS . Support for the x86 CPU architecture is available in all AWS Regions where Lambda MicroVMs is available, except Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Europe (Spain). To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide . For information o
title: AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports the x86 CPU architecture

summary: Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) now supports higher limits for email identities, tenants, and configuration sets. You can view your current usage against each limit and request increases in the AWS Service Quotas console. A single account can now keep pace with your growth, so you no longer need to split email workloads across several accounts to stay within per-account limits. Customers running multi-tenant workloads often create a separate email identity, tenant, or configuration set for each customer, brand, or AI agent they serve. As you add more customers, brands, and AI agents, these resources can multiply quickly, and higher limits let all of these workloads grow in one account. To help you manage larger accounts, you can now also search these resources by name or status. Higher limits for email identities, tenants, and configuration sets are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SES is available. To learn more, see Service quotas in Amazon SES in the Amazon SES Developer Guide and the Amazon SES product page.
title: Amazon SES now supports higher limits for email identities, tenants, and configuration sets

summary: AWS Emulator is now available for building and testing AWS applications locally. Starting today, you can use AWS Emulator to build and test AWS applications on your computer or in your continuous integration (CI) environment. Your existing AWS SDK and CLI calls go to AWS Emulator and come back in milliseconds, so you and your coding agents can find and fix errors locally, with no deployments or AWS account required. You create and manage resources with the same AWS SDK and AWS CLI calls you use with AWS, signed with credentials the emulator provides. For the operations it supports, AWS Emulator returns the same result as AWS for valid calls and the same errors for invalid ones. Operations it doesn’t yet support return 501 Not Implemented. AWS Emulator keeps the state of your resources in memory until you stop it. Each copy you start gets its own port, keys and in-memory state, so agents, test suites, and CI jobs never see each other’s resources. For example, a coding agent can create an Amazon DynamoDB table, test against it offline, and fix its code before it deploys. Services in AWS Emulator are generated from the API models AWS publishes, the same models behind the AWS SDKs. When AWS adds a service or API, it shows up in AWS Emulator, and its behavior is filled in and verified release by release. To see how its responses compare to AWS, review the AWS Emulator fidelity report . AWS Emulator doesn’t depend on an AWS Region. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pa
title: AWS Emulator is now available for building and testing AWS applications locally

summary: Amazon Cognito now supports session management for user pools, giving you visibility into and control over the sessions your users establish when they sign in to your applications. Single sign-on (SSO) sessions are created when a user signs in through managed login and let them access other app clients without re-authenticating. Token sessions are created when a user signs in to an app client and receives tokens. Session management lets you list a user's active SSO and token sessions across all devices and app clients and revoke any of them on demand. You can also now configure how long each app client reuses an SSO session before requiring re-authentication, instead of the previous fixed one-hour duration. Each session includes details such as session type, app client ID, device type, last activity time and location, and initial sign-in time, so you can build your own end-user or admin session experiences. You can revoke an individual session, optionally with its linked sessions, or use global sign-out to end all sessions associated with one user. You can also set a maximum number of active token sessions per user. Session management is available for user pools in the Essentials or Plus feature plans in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. You can manage sessions using the AWS Management Console, API, AWS Command Line Interface, and AWS Software Development Kits, and configure settings with AWS CloudFormation. Visit the Developer Guide and API Reference for det
title: Amazon Cognito now supports user pool session management

summary: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) now offers a larger 24 GB etcd database, up from 16 GB, for 4XL and 8XL Provisioned Control Plane clusters. etcd is the key-value store in the Kubernetes control plane that holds your cluster state, so its size limits how many Kubernetes objects your cluster can store. With 50% more capacity, you can run bigger clusters with more pods, jobs, events, and custom resources. The larger database gives more headroom to workloads that create and update many Kubernetes objects, such as large-scale AI/ML training and inference, batch processing, and CI/CD pipelines. When the etcd database fills up, you can’t add or change objects in your cluster, so the extra headroom helps keep these workloads running as they scale. To get the larger database, choose the 4XL or 8XL tier of Provisioned Control Plane on a cluster running EKS version 1.34 or later. Existing clusters on the 4XL and 8XL tiers running these versions get the larger database automatically, with no action required. The 24 GB etcd database is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Provisioned Control Plane is available. To learn more, see the Amazon EKS Provisioned Control Plane user guide .
title: Amazon EKS Provisioned Control Plane now offers a 24 GB etcd database on 4XL and 8XL tiers

summary: AWS Cloud WAN now supports VPC Flow Logs, giving you central visibility into IP traffic across your global network. Flow Logs capture detailed information for each flow, so you can understand how traffic moves across your core network without leaving your AWS Cloud WAN account. Until now, network administrators had to stitch together VPC Flow Logs from many VPCs, accounts, and Regions to see traffic across their global network. They often depended on other teams for access to those logs. Cloud WAN Flow Logs give core network owners one consolidated view of traffic between VPCs, Regions, and on-premises networks connected over AWS Direct Connect, AWS Site-to-Site VPN, or SD-WAN. You can use this data to troubleshoot connectivity and performance problems, plan capacity from historical bandwidth trends, find unusual traffic patterns, and keep records for security and compliance. Flow log records include IP addresses, ports, protocol, traffic volume, and packet-loss counters, along with Cloud WAN metadata such as segment, Region, service insertion hops and attachment details. You can turn on Flow Logs for an entire core network, a single core network edge, or individual attachments. You can publish them to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or Amazon Data Firehose. Cloud WAN adds no charge for Flow Logs. Standard charges apply for each destination. Cloud WAN Flow Logs are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Cloud WAN is available. You can get st
title: AWS Cloud WAN now supports Flow Logs

Network Security Manager is a comprehensive network security management solution designed to simplify security policy deployment and enforcement at scale. California); US West (Oregon); Asia Pacific (Mumbai); Asia Pacific (Hong Kong); Asia Pacific (Taipei); Asia Pacific (Seoul); Asia Pacific (Osaka); Asia Pacific (Hyderabad); Asia Pacific (Singapore); Asia Pacific (Sydney); Asia Pacific (Melbourne); Asia Pacific (Malaysia); Asia Pacific (New Zealand); Asia Pacific (Thailand); Asia Pacific (Johor); Asia Pacific (Tokyo); Canada (Central); Canada West (Calgary); Mexico (Central); Europe (Frankfurt); Europe (Zurich); Europe (Stockholm); Europe (Ireland); Europe (Milan); Europe (Spain); Europe (London); Europe (Paris); Israel (Tel Aviv); South America (São Paulo), Africa (Cape Town). title: AWS Network Security Manager now available in AWS European Sovereign Cloud and Additional New Regions

summary: DeepSeek's DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash models are now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, expanding the portfolio of foundation models available to AWS customers. These three open-weight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, released under the MIT license, deliver frontier-class performance across reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads while activating only a fraction of their total parameters per token, enabling high efficiency at scale. These models address different AI challenges with specialized capabilities: DeepSeek-V4-Pro is designed for complex reasoning and high-quality text generation at flagship scale. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash provides next-generation agentic efficiency with native multimodal support. title: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash models now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

These two models are part of the Ornith 1.0 family of open-source, self-scaffolding agentic coding models released under the MIT license, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open-source models of comparable size on coding benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-Bench, NL2Repo, and OpenClaw. title: Ornith-1.0-9B and Ornith-1.0-35B models now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

The new runtime restores each session from a snapshot of your initialized agent, scales compute and memory with the work, and scales idle agents to zero. Every session still runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker microVM. Your agents can run heavy work like compiling a large codebase, driving a browser, or loading a local model inside the session. Sessions scale to 8 vCPU and 32 GB of memory and support container images up to 10 GB. On a 2 GB image, sessions start in under 2 seconds at P75, down from 29.7 seconds on the previous generation. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Se
title: The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default

summary: EC2 Image Builder now integrates with the AWS DevOps Agent directly in the Image Builder console, enabling you to troubleshoot failed image pipelines and create resources directly from the console chat panel. You can diagnose up to 50 failed pipelines at once and ask follow-up questions in the same conversation. You can also choose to create resources by describing what you want, and the agent populates the console with values the service has already validated. With this integration, diagnosing a failed pipeline no longer requires manually inspecting build logs, cross-referencing error codes, or iterating through configuration fixes, saving you significant time and expertise. The agent reads build logs, workflow steps, components, and network configuration, then provides the root cause and the steps to fix it. For resource creation, the agent verifies the configuration before populating the console for you to review and submit. If you troubleshoot or build with your own AI agents, the new EC2 Image Builder skill in the AWS Agent Toolkit provides you the same troubleshooting and creation capabilities. This feature is available in all commercial regions. To get started, open the EC2 Image Builder console and use the DevOps Agent from the console panel. For more information, see the EC2 Image Builder documentation and for pricing refer DevOps agent Pricing page .
title: EC2 Image Builder console now integrates with the DevOps Agent for troubleshooting and resource creation

summary: Amazon MWAA Serverless now supports DuckDB operators, enabling you to analyze and transform data with high-performance in-memory analytics directly in your workflows. You can query data in Amazon S3 or run analytics locally, without manual credential configuration. DuckDB operators are also supported in SageMaker Unified Studio visual workflows. To get started in MWAA Serverless, add a DuckDB task to your workflow definition. A pre-created default connection automatically uses your workflow's execution role credentials for S3 access, so you can start analyzing data immediately. In SageMaker Unified Studio, add DuckDB operators from the task panel to your visual workflow canvas. DuckDB operators are available in all Regions where Amazon MWAA Serverless is available. To learn more, see Using DuckDB in Amazon MWAA Serverless workflows and Using serverless visual workflows .
title: Amazon MWAA Serverless supports DuckDB operators

summary: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports M8id and R8id instances. These instances are powered by custom Intel Xeon 6 processors, available only on AWS, and include local NVMe SSD storage. They scale up to 384 vCPUs, 3 TiB of memory, and 22.8 TB of local NVMe SSD storage. That's 4x the vCPUs and memory and more than 6x the local storage of M5d and R5d instances. When you create or modify a DB instance to use M8id or R8id, RDS for SQL Server automatically places the tempdb data and log files on the local NVMe instance store. This gives tempdb lower read and write latency than Amazon EBS storage. Your database data and log files stay on Amazon EBS. Because snapshots don't include tempdb files on the instance store, your snapshots are smaller and use less of your free backup storage. To learn more, see Instance store support for the tempdb database on Amazon RDS for SQL Server . To use the new M8id and R8id instances, you can modify your existing RDS database instance or create a new RDS database instance from the RDS Management Console, or using the AWS SDK or CLI. M8id and R8id instances are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Stockholm), Europe (Spain), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Malaysia). For pricing details, see Amazon RDS for SQL Server Pric
title: Amazon RDS for SQL Server now supports M8id and R8id instances

summary: AWS Glue introduces automatic version upgrades, a capability that keeps your Apache Spark jobs current on the latest AWS Glue runtime without manual coordination. Staying current on supported runtimes gives your jobs the latest security patches, performance improvements, and support for evolving table formats such as Apache Iceberg. Auto upgrades include multiple levels of validations including assessing jobs for compatibility with the upgraded runtime, obtaining your consent before executing jobs on a newer version, and validating upgraded job runs against each job's established output profile, so your jobs upgrade with the right guardrails in place. By setting a job's version to "Auto", upgrades that once required weeks of planning and execution now happen automatically. Platform teams can standardize runtime versions across large fleets without chasing individual job owners, and business units without a central upgrade team can keep their jobs current hands-free. Each job is validated against its established output schema, data volume, latency, and format before it upgrades, so you can advance with confidence. Jobs that need code changes keep running safely on their current version, and AWS Glue provides an upgrade analysis with specific fixes you can apply directly or with the Apache Spark upgrade agent. Auto upgrades for AWS Glue are available in all AWS Commercial Regions. To get started, select "Auto" as the AWS Glue version when creating or updating an Apache Spark jo
title: AWS Glue announces automatic version upgrades for Apache Spark jobs

summary: AWS Cloud WAN now supports BGP communities on Direct Connect attachments, enabling advanced routing controls for enterprise hybrid networks. Previously, Cloud WAN Routing Policy evaluated BGP communities only on Site-to-Site VPN and Connect attachments. Now, customers can tag routes with routing intent on-premises, apply filtering and path preference rules inside Cloud WAN, and propagate communities back to their on-premises routers over Direct Connect. With this capability, enterprises can simplify hybrid network orchestration by signaling routing policies dynamically from on-premises environments. Customers can match community tags to filter production versus disaster recovery traffic, prioritize preferred paths, or restrict regional propagation. This eliminates the need for VPN overlay workarounds and manual policy replication, reducing operational complexity and misconfiguration risk. BGP community support on AWS Cloud WAN Direct Connect attachments is available in all AWS Regions where both AWS Direct Connect and AWS Cloud WAN are available. For the complete list of available Regions, see the Cloud WAN Routing Policies documentation .
title: AWS Cloud WAN now supports BGP communities on Direct Connect attachments for routing policy

summary: Amazon FSx for Lustre is reducing the minimum provisioned throughput capacity and metadata IOPS on Intelligent-Tiering file systems by 75%, allowing you to use Intelligent-Tiering even more cost-effectively for high-performance computing (HPC) and machine learning workloads that start with small datasets and grow over time. The FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering storage class delivers the lowest-cost and only fully elastic Lustre file storage in the cloud. It is optimized for workloads that mix hot and cold data and do not require consistent SSD-level performance. A file system's throughput capacity determines the read and write speeds supported by its underlying file servers, and its level of metadata IOPS determines how many files and directories you can create, read, and delete per second. Today’s launch reduces the minimum throughput capacity on an Intelligent-Tiering file system from 4,000 to 1,000 MBps and the minimum metadata performance from 6,000 to 1,500 IOPS. The lower throughput capacity and metadata IOPS levels are available on new FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering file systems in all AWS Regions where the Intelligent-Tiering storage class is available. To learn more, see Performance characteristics of Intelligent-Tiering storage class in the Amazon FSx for Lustre User Guide.
title: Amazon FSx for Lustre lowers the entry cost of Intelligent-Tiering file systems by 75%

summary: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink now supports enhanced snapshots, a capability that lets you capture, export, and restore application state across Apache Flink applications and AWS Regions, so you can run blue/green deployments, easily migrate self-managed workloads to Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink without losing state, and keep backup in a secondary Region for cross-Region recovery. To deploy an application update without pausing processing for blue/green deployments, create an enhanced snapshot from an application and use it to start a second application. To migrate a self-managed workload, import its Apache Flink savepoint into Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink as an enhanced snapshot. For cross-Region recovery, export an enhanced snapshot to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and replicate the exported state to a bucket in a secondary Region. Enhanced snapshots are available today for applications on Apache Flink 1.20 and later in all AWS Regions where Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink is available except European Sovereign Cloud (Germany). You pay for enhanced snapshot storage per GB-month as durable application backups. To learn more and get started, see enhanced snapshots in the Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Developer Guide. You can also use Agent Toolkit for AWS with Kiro, Claude Code, or Cursor for guidance on building and operating Flink applications with enhanced snapshots.
title: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink introduces enhanced snapshots

summary: Amazon Route 53 Domains now lets you restore an expired or recently deleted domain yourself, using the Amazon Route 53 console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Previously, restoring a domain required a request to AWS Support. Now you can recover a domain lost to a missed renewal, an expired payment method, or an accidental deletion, and restore the website, email, and applications that depend on it. To restore a domain, you enter the domain name, review the restoration price, accept the charge, and submit the request. Route 53 works with the top-level domain (TLD) registry to reactivate the registration and return the domain to your AWS account. Most TLD registries support restoration, and each registry sets how long after expiration or deletion a domain can still be restored. Restoring a domain typically costs more than registering or renewing one. To learn more, see Restoring an expired or deleted domain in the Route 53 Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page . For a complete list of supported TLDs, see the Route 53 TLD list . For pricing, visit the Route 53 pricing page .
title: Amazon Route 53 Domains now supports self-service restore for expired and deleted domains

summary: Today, AWS Backup announces support for resource modifiers when restoring Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) backups. Resource modifiers let you transform Kubernetes resources during a restore, so you can adapt a restored cluster to its target environment. When you restore an EKS backup that has been copied across accounts or across AWS Regions, the restored cluster can carry references tied to the source environment, such as IAM roles, database endpoints, and Amazon ECR registry URIs. Previously, you had to locate and update these references manually after every restore, which was time consuming and error prone. With resource modifiers, you can define transformation rules once via a YAML file, and AWS Backup applies them automatically as part of the restore, improving the reliability of your cross-account and cross-Region disaster recovery workflows. AWS Backup support for resource modifiers for Amazon EKS backups is available in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see the AWS Backup Documentation and read the launch blog .
title: AWS Backup now supports resource modifiers for Amazon EKS restores

summary: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault now supports Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive. Logically air-gapped vaults are a type of AWS Backup vault that allows secure sharing of backups across accounts and AWS Organizations, supporting direct restore to reduce recovery time from a data loss event. You can now archive Amazon EBS backups held in a logically air-gapped vault to Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive, a low-cost tier for snapshots you rarely access. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default, and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys. This helps you meet long-term retention and compliance requirements at lower storage cost. You can get started using the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. In a backup plan rule that runs monthly or less often, specify a logically air-gapped vault as the primary backup destination or copy destination. Then enable Archive Amazon EBS snapshots in the backup rule lifecycle or copy lifecycle and set the time in warm storage before the backup transitions. This support is available in all AWS Regions where both logically air-gapped vault and Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive are available. For more information and detailed regional availability, visit the AWS Backup documentation . To learn more about logically air-gapped vaults, visit the product documentation and pricing page .
title: AWS Backup adds logically air-gapped vault support for Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive

summary: Today, AWS Quick is announcing the general availability of structured data connector restrictions through custom permissions. This capability gives administrators granular control over which types of data sources users can create, update, or share, helping organizations enforce data governance requirements while enabling self-service analytics. With this feature, administrators can configure custom permissions profiles in Enterprise edition through the Quick UI, APIs, or AWS Command Line Interface. For example, an organization can allow users to create Amazon Redshift data sources while restricting the creation of file-upload data sources. Administrators can also prevent users from sharing data sources for a particular connector. Create, update, and share restrictions can be configured independently, providing more precise controls than restrictions that apply to all data source types. This feature is now available in all supported AWS Quick Regions listed here . To learn more, check our documentation here .
title: AWS Quick enhances granular governance with the ability to restrict structured data sources

summary: Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) now supports sending push notifications in the Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Europe (Zurich), and AWS GovCloud (US-East) Regions. Amazon SNS is a fully managed pub/sub service that provides message delivery to multiple endpoints, including AWS Lambda, Amazon SQS, Amazon Data Firehose, HTTP, SMS (via AWS End User Messaging), push notifications, and email. With this launch, customers in these four additional Regions can use Amazon SNS to send push notifications to the following supported push notification services: Amazon Device Messaging (ADM), Apple Push Notification Service (APNs), Baidu Cloud Push (Baidu), Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), and Windows Push Notification Services (WNS). For the full list of Regions from which you can send push notifications, see Supported Regions and Countries in the Amazon SNS Developer Guide. For more information, see the Amazon SNS push notifications documentation .
title: Amazon SNS now supports push notifications in four additional AWS Regions

summary: Amazon Connect Customer now lets agents merge and link related cases in the agent workspace, so they can resolve customer issues faster and respond consistently. When a customer contacts a business about the same issue more than once, or on different channels, the history can end up split across several cases. Agents can merge those cases into one case with a single, consolidated history. For example, an agent can merge the chat and email cases a customer opened about a delayed shipment. Agents can also link related cases, such as cases from different customers affected by the same issue, so they can coordinate one consistent response for every affected customer. Cases is available in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documentation .
title: Amazon Connect Customer supports merging and linking related cases in the agent workspace

summary: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) now supports fine-grained access control, giving administrators precise control over who can access which workflows and resources in an Apache Airflow environment. Fine-grained access control is delivered through two new capabilities: IAM Identity Center integration and multi-team environments. With IAM Identity Center integration, users sign in to the Apache Airflow UI with their corporate identity provider.
