Authorization is evaluated per request using IAM policies attached to IAM Identity Center Permission Sets, with condition keys that scope access by resource type (DAGs, connections, variables, pools, and more), action, and specific resource ID. With multi-team environments, several teams can share a single MWAA environment. Each team gets its own DAG folder in Amazon S3, and users see only shared DAGs plus their own teams' DAGs based on IAM Identity Center group membership. Teams reduce cost through shared infrastructure and simplify management by configuring environment settings once. Multi-team environments are based on the Apache Airflow multi-team feature, which is currently in preview. These features are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA is available. To learn more, visit the IAM Identity Center integration documentation and the multi-team environments documentation .
title: Amazon MWAA now supports fine-grained access control with IAM Identity Center and multi-team environments

summary: AWS Graviton5-based R9g database instances are now generally available for Amazon Aurora with PostgreSQL compatibility and MySQL compatibility, and for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB. Graviton5-based R9g instances provide up to a 30% performance improvement and up to a 22% price-performance improvement for on-demand pricing over Graviton4-based instances of equivalent sizes on Amazon Aurora, depending on database engine, version, and workload. Built on the AWS Nitro System, R9g instances are available in nine sizes, from large to 48xlarge. They deliver up to 192 vCPUs, an 8:1 ratio of memory to vCPU, up to 100 Gbps of networking bandwidth, and up to 72 Gbps of bandwidth to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). You can get started using the R9g database instances through the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI). The instances are available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Frankfurt) regions. For the specific engine versions that support these instance classes, see the Aurora and RDS documentation. For pricing, see Amazon Aurora pricing and Amazon RDS pricing .
title: Amazon Aurora and RDS now support Graviton5-based R9g database instances

summary: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693). Amazon Cognito helps you add sign-up, sign-in, and access control to your web applications, mobile applications, and AI agents. With token exchange, a service or AI agent acting on a user's behalf can exchange the user's token for a new token scoped to a specific downstream service. Previously, a service that called another service on a user's behalf had to forward the user's original token or build and maintain its own token minting logic. With token exchange, you can issue a new token that has a narrower scope than the original token, is bound to a single audience, and comes without a refresh token. When you include an actor token, Cognito adds an act claim that identifies the intermediary, so downstream services can tell a request that an agent made on a user's behalf from one the user made directly. For example, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server can exchange a user's token for a narrowly scoped token to call a backend API, with the act claim recording the MCP server as the actor. You can exchange tokens through the token endpoint or with the new GetDerivedToken API . Token exchange is available on the Essentials and Plus feature plans in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see exchanging tokens for downstream services in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.
title: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange

summary: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) Schema Conversion now supports offline source conversion for Oracle Database. You can convert Oracle schemas and code without direct connectivity to your source databases. You can extract metadata using standard database commands in your own environment, then upload it to DMS Schema Conversion for processing. This removes the need for security reviews, firewall changes, and VPN setup that delay migration projects, and delivers the same conversion results as the connected approach. Offline Source suits organizations whose security policies restrict external tool access to production Oracle databases. Database administrators can generate human-readable metadata files within their existing environment. Security teams can review the commands and output before upload, simplifying approval. By removing the connectivity requirement, Offline Source turns weeks of security reviews into a simple command-and-upload workflow. Offline Source supports all DMS Schema Conversion targets at no additional conversion charge. For regional availability, see the Supported AWS Regions page. To get started, see Using Offline Source in the DMS Schema Conversion documentation. To learn how to run offline assessment and conversion with AI agents, read the launch blog post .
title: AWS DMS Schema Conversion expands offline source conversion to Oracle

summary: Amazon CloudWatch now offers accelerated compute insights, a capability that provides monitoring and observability for self-hosted AI inference workloads running in Amazon EKS clusters. Previously, platform and AI teams lacked fleet-level visibility into their accelerators, whether workloads were running efficiently, and what was causing performance issues. Accelerated compute insights collects telemetry from across the inference stack to help teams identify idle accelerators, optimize workloads to reduce costs, and troubleshoot common inference issues such as high time to first token. Getting started is as simple as enabling the Amazon CloudWatch Observability add-on for Amazon EKS, which discovers every NVIDIA GPU in the cluster automatically. Curated views in the CloudWatch console let you monitor from the fleet level down to an individual workload or accelerator. Teams can see which workloads are idle, which are underutilized, and the estimated cost per token for each inference workload. The feature is also available on CloudWatch Omni, where it includes an agentic experience that makes answering questions about inference workloads easy. There is no additional charge for accelerated compute insights. Standard CloudWatch pricing applies to the telemetry you collect from your AI workloads. For more information about the AWS Regions where Accelerated Compute Insights is available, see the AWS Region table . To get started, see Accelerated Compute Insights .
title: Announcing Accelerated Compute Insights for Amazon CloudWatch

summary: Cases in Amazon Connect Customer now lets agents and supervisors assign, comment on, and update the status of up to 100 cases at once, so teams spend less time on repetitive case updates. When one issue affects many customers, such as a shipping delay or a service outage, teams no longer need to update each case one at a time. Agents and supervisors with the appropriate permissions can select the related cases and change the assignee, add a comment, or close them in a single action. Developers can also use batch APIs to make the same updates programmatically. Cases is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documentation .
title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports batch actions on up to 100 cases at once

summary: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now reduces downtime for automatic minor version upgrades, as well as minor version upgrades and operating system updates scheduled for your maintenance window. Shorter maintenance makes it easier to stay current on the latest Oracle minor versions and operating system updates with less disruption to your applications. If you turned on automatic minor version upgrade, your DB instances benefit automatically. To apply these upgrades and updates, RDS has to set up new resources as part of the maintenance. Previously, RDS set up these resources after the maintenance started, which made your downtime longer. Now, RDS prepares them up to 30 minutes before your maintenance window, while your DB instance keeps serving your workload. When the maintenance window opens, your DB instance is offline for less time because resources required for the maintenance are already prepared. This applies to both Enterprise Edition and Standard Edition 2 DB instances. The preparation never blocks or delays your own operations, and your DB instance stays available while RDS prepares. If a change that you make conflicts with the preparation, RDS rolls back the staged resources, and your change goes ahead. If the preparation can't finish, RDS still applies the maintenance in your window, without the preparation. New RDS events tell you when the preparation starts, when it finishes, and when it can't finish. RDS for Oracle will continue to intro
title: Amazon RDS for Oracle reduces downtime for automatic minor version upgrades and scheduled maintenance

summary: A new model is now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Grok 4.7 is SpaceXSI's most capable model for coding and knowledge work. It's built to stay focused through hard tasks that run for hours, and it checks its work before moving on. Compared with Grok 4.6, it plans and recovers from errors more reliably in repo-scale coding work. Grok 4.7 is available with experimental support and a 500K context window. Requests up to 200K tokens use a 2.7x credit multiplier, and requests over 200K tokens are billed at 5.4x. Kiro administrators control which models are available to their users, so organizations can align model access with their internal policies. Ensure your IDE or CLI is updated to the latest version, then restart it to access the new model from the model selector. For more details, visit the GovCloud documentation , the monitoring and tracking guide , or contact your AWS account team. To learn more about Kiro, visit the Kiro product page .
title: Grok 4.7 now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)

summary: The next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports intelligent ingestion for time series collections. You can bring logs and event data from Amazon S3 into a time series collection without operating an ingestion pipeline. With intelligent ingestion, you can now complete the setup and get data ingested with a few clicks in the AWS Management Console or with a single API call. Intelligent ingestion detects the data type, parses each record, and indexes it into your collection. It works with observability logs in JSON, NDJSON, and JSON arrays. Use an ingestion job for one-time loads, use an ingestion stream to keep the collection up to date as new objects arrive in S3, or backfill and then stream. Source buckets can be in the same AWS account as the collection or in a different one. Capacity scales with your workload up to the collection's configured limit, and you pay only for active processing. Once ingested, your data gets everything time series collections already provide. The collection absorbs ingest spikes automatically and keeps recent data in the hot tier for fast queries. Older data moves to the lower-cost warm tier based on the retention you set. Because tiering and retention are based on time, each document must include a valid timestamp field, and documents with a missing or invalid timestamp are rejected. Alerting and anomaly detection run directly on the ingested logs and events. Together, these make it simpler to put large S3 log archives to work fo
title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless supports intelligent ingestion for time series collection

summary: Amazon Route 53 now supports record set protection, which helps DNS administrators prevent accidental changes to critical DNS records in their hosted zones. This feature allows you to protect records such as those at the zone apex, MX records, and production endpoints directly in the hosted zone. Any change to a protected record is blocked until the protection is removed by an authorized user. Previously, to lock specific records, you had to write record-level conditions into the IAM policies of every user and role that could change your hosted zones. When those policies blocked a change, the caller had no indication of whether the record was protected or why. Now you can protect records by name and type directly in the hosted zone. A single protection covers all records with that name and type, including records with different set identifiers; weighted, latency, and other routing policy records are protected together. You can also create a protection proactively before the record exists, preventing records from being created for that name and type. Each protection can include an optional comment of up to 256 characters, allowing you to indicate the reason for the protection. You can manage protections using the Route 53 console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs through the CreateResourceRecordSetProtections, DeleteResourceRecordSetProtections, and ListResourceRecordSetProtections API actions. To control who can remove protections, restrict the DeleteResourceRecordSetProtections permissi
title: Amazon Route 53 now supports record set protection

summary: Amazon MWAA Serverless provides the native Apache Airflow UI for your workflows. You can browse workflows, inspect workflow runs and task instances, read task logs, view a workflow's source and versions, and start a workflow run. The UI uses the permissions of the IAM identity that opens it and shows only what that identity can read, so read-only access is possible. AWS CloudTrail records the calls the UI makes under your identity. You can open the Airflow UI from the Amazon MWAA console, the AWS CLI, or the API. Teams already familiar with Airflow can use the interface they know to work with their workflows. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA Serverless is available. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To get started, see Access the Airflow UI . Apache Airflow is a trademark of the Apache Software Foundation .
title: Apache Airflow UI available in Amazon MWAA Serverless

summary: AWS Batch now supports additional Kubernetes security context settings in Amazon EKS job definitions, including Linux capabilities, seccomp profiles, and pod-level settings. For EKS clusters that enforce the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards restricted profile, you can now run AWS Batch jobs with only the privileges and system calls they require. To get started, use the RegisterJobDefinition API to set capabilities and seccompProfile in a container's securityContext , or set securityContext in podProperties to define pod-wide settings such as fsGroup . Container-level settings override pod-level defaults. You can configure these settings through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. The additional security context settings for AWS Batch on Amazon EKS are now supported in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see the Amazon EKS properties section in the AWS Batch User Guide .
title: AWS Batch on Amazon EKS adds Linux capabilities, seccomp, and pod-level settings

summary: AWS Marketplace sellers can now submit Value Added Tax (VAT) credit notes for refunded deemed supply transactions through a self-service experience in AWS Partner Central. Previously, VAT was disbursed to sellers for eligible transactions, and when a buyer was later refunded, sellers had to contact AWS to submit the corresponding credit note. This launch simplifies post-refund VAT documentation for sellers. Sellers can view eligible refund line items in the VAT on deemed supply section, select the refunds covered by a credit note, upload a PDF or the applicable electronic invoice format, and track the submission status. Sellers can consolidate multiple eligible refunds into a single credit note where applicable and review the associated financial adjustment in the Seller Insights reporting. These capabilities are available for eligible AWS Marketplace transactions, including Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO) transactions, in supported EU member states, Norway, and the United Kingdom. Country-specific invoicing and electronic-invoicing requirements continue to apply. To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and go to Settings → Tax information → VAT on deemed supply. To learn more, visit the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide or Deemed Supply FAQs .
title: AWS Marketplace now supports VAT credit notes for deemed supply refunds

summary: AWS Systems Manager Cloud Connector now extends simplified multicloud onboarding support to Google Cloud, making it easy to connect your existing Google Cloud VMs to Systems Manager for centralized management alongside AWS, on-premises, and Azure resources without manual agent installation. Previously, managing virtual machines across multiple cloud providers often required coordinating and setting up configurations separately in each environment. With Cloud Connector for Google Cloud, you can automatically deploy the SSM Agent to Google Cloud VMs at scale. Once connected, Google Cloud VMs appear alongside EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and other multicloud resources in a unified view, enabling you to use Session Manager, Automation runbooks, Run Command, State Manager, Patch Manager, and Inventory across AWS, on-premises, Azure, and Google Cloud from a single workflow. This simplifies operations for teams managing infrastructure across multiple clouds, enabling them to standardize management practices and reduce operational complexity. Cloud Connector for Google Cloud is available in Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong, Hyderabad, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, Mumbai, New Zealand, Osaka, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Taipei, Thailand, Tokyo), Canada (Central, Calgary), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain, Stockholm, Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Mexico (Central), South America (Sao Paulo), US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), and US West (N. California, Or
title: AWS Systems Manager simplifies onboarding of Google Cloud VMs for centralized management

summary: AWS Secrets Manager now supports cross-account replication, enabling you to maintain a synchronized copy of a primary secret in a secondary AWS account for cross-account access, backup, and disaster recovery. Cross-account replication extends the existing multi-Region replication capability across account boundaries. With cross-account replication, platform or security teams can own and rotate a secret centrally, and each consuming account gets a local, always-current copy without any shared KMS keys or cross-account secret policies. The replica secret is a full, independent resource, encrypted with a customer managed KMS key owned by the replica account. Secrets Manager updates it automatically whenever the primary secret's value changes, including rotations. You can keep a live copy of critical secrets in a dedicated recovery or failover account, isolated from ransomware or a compromised primary account. If needed, the replica can be promoted to a standalone secret. Cross-account replication is available in all AWS Regions where Secrets Manager is available. For a list of regions where Secrets Manager is available, see the AWS Region table . To learn more, see Replicate secrets across AWS accounts in the Secrets Manager User Guide and the AssociateCrossAccountReplica API reference . For pricing details, see AWS Secrets Manager pricing .
title: AWS Secrets Manager now supports cross-account replication

summary: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports AWS Organizations declarative policies. You can use them to enable Security Hub CSPM across all accounts and Regions in your organization and to define which security standards and controls are enabled. Policies can apply broadly to every account and Region, or target specific account and Region combinations. Declarative policies help keep each account's configuration aligned with its attached policy, which helps prevent configuration drift. You can also apply them automatically to new accounts, so each account starts with a baseline configuration as soon as it's created. Declarative policies are now the recommended way to manage Security Hub CSPM across an organization. They align with how other security services, such as Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, and AWS Security Hub allow customers to manage configuration of the service. They also provide more flexibility, such as configuring Region-specific settings. You can continue to use central configuration until you're ready to migrate. When you are, use the migration process in the Security Hub CSPM console. It converts your existing central configuration policies into declarative policies and applies them to the appropriate accounts and regions. Declarative policies for Security Hub CSPM are available in all commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and China Regions. To get started, see Migrating central configuration policies . To learn more, see Declarative policies in the AWS Security Hub CSPM
title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports centralized configuration with AWS Organizations declarative policies

summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs for both inbound JWT authorization and outbound OAuth credential providers. This update enables developers to configure AgentCore with OAuth 2.0 authorization servers that do not use OpenID Connect (OIDC). Previously, AgentCore Identity accepted only OIDC discovery URLs. Authorization servers that implement OAuth 2.0 without OIDC publish their metadata at a different well-known path and could not be used with AgentCore. With this launch, you can use either OIDC or OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs when you configure a JWT authorizer or a custom OAuth credential provider on AgentCore. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is available, at no additional cost. To learn more, see Configure inbound JWT authorizer and Add OAuth client using custom provider in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide .
title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports OAuth 2.0 discovery URLs

summary: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports layout customization, a new capability that gives domain administrators control over which tools and left navigation items project members see based on their designation. Organizations with data engineering, analytics, and machine learning teams on a single platform can configure a layout within each designation definition, and that layout applies across every project in the domain without per-project configuration. Previously, all project members saw the same interface regardless of their role, creating confusion and potential governance issues. With layout customization, administrators define a layout as part of a designation that specifies which left navigation items are visible for project members assigned to that designation. When a project member opens a project, SageMaker Unified Studio resolves the member's designation and renders only the tools included in their designation's layout. For example, a SQL analyst designation can be configured to show only the Query Editor, while an ML engineer designation shows notebooks, training jobs, and model endpoints. Navigation items are configurable across categories including Data Analytics, artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), Generative AI, and IDEs. If a project member navigates directly to a hidden page, they see an access-denied page. For members with multiple designations, visible tools are the union of all their designations' layouts. New navigation items adde
title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports layout customization for designations

summary: Aurora PostgreSQL now supports express configuration in AWS CloudFormation for infrastructure as code deployment. This launch enables you to automate the infrastructure deployment of your Aurora clusters through CloudFormation templates while benefiting from the speed of express configuration. Aurora PostgreSQL clusters created with express configuration allow you to create and query an Aurora serverless database in seconds. The new withExpressConfiguration createOnly property on the AWS::RDS::DBCluster resource creates both the cluster and its primary database instance from one property declaration. You don't need to model or manage the instance separately in your CloudFormation template. This simplifies your templates and makes it easier to manage Aurora clusters with express configuration through infrastructure as code. The CloudFormation support is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is offered. To learn more, see the Aurora User Guide and the AWS::RDS::DBCluster resource reference in the AWS CloudFormation documentation .
title: Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration now supported in CloudFormation

summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances are now available in six additional AWS Regions: US West (N. California), Canada (Central), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Seoul). Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. By expanding to these AWS Regions, more teams can use runtime instance capabilities such as GPU-accelerated, memory-optimized, or compute-optimized instance types, and long-running agent sessions of up to 14 days. You can run your agents closer to your users to reduce invocation latency, and keep agent instances, storage volumes, and session data in the Region that your data residency requirements call for. With this expansion, you can use runtime instances in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). You are charged for managing the provisioned compute, in addition to your Amazon EC2 costs. To get started, see the following resources: Supported AWS Regions in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide AgentCore pricing Runtime instances and capacity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
title: AgentCore runtime instances are now available in six more AWS Regions

summary: AWS WAF advanced rate-based rules are now available in the Asia Pacific (Thailand), Mexico (Central), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. Customers in these Regions can now aggregate requests using custom keys and choose a 1 or 2 minute evaluation window in addition to the existing 5 and 10 minute options, the same capabilities already available in other AWS Regions. A rate-based rule counts requests and applies an action, such as Block or CAPTCHA, when the request rate exceeds a limit you set. Previously, rate-based rules in these Regions could aggregate requests only by IP address and used a 5 or 10 minute evaluation window. Now you can aggregate by request components such as HTTP headers, cookies, query strings, URI paths, HTTP methods, and label namespaces, and combine up to five of them into a composite key. For example, you can limit login attempts per IP address and User-Agent pair, or per session cookie, which helps against attacks spread across many IP addresses. A shorter evaluation window detects request floods sooner, and a longer window catches slower, sustained attacks. You can configure these options in the AWS WAF console, the AWS CLI and SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation. There is no additional charge for these capabilities, and standard AWS WAF pricing applies. Advanced rate-based rules are now available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS WAF is available and in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Using rate-based rule s
title: AWS WAF advanced rate-based rules are now available in AWS GovCloud (US), Thailand, and Mexico

summary: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault now supports Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) DB instances. Logically air-gapped vaults are a type of AWS Backup vault that stores immutable, isolated backups, which are locked by default with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode. Secure sharing across accounts and AWS Organizations enables direct restore, reducing recovery time from a data loss event. You can now protect your Amazon RDS DB instances in logically air-gapped vaults. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default, and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys. This helps reduce the risk of downtime, ensure business continuity, and meet compliance requirements. To get started, use the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. Assign your RDS DB instances to a backup plan and specify a logically air-gapped vault in the same AWS Region as the copy destination. Share the vault for recovery or restore testing with other accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), or safeguard vault access during account compromise using Multi-party approval . Once shared, you can initiate direct restore jobs from that account. This support is available in most AWS Regions where both logically air-gapped vault and Amazon RDS are available. For more information and detailed regional availability, visit the AWS Backup documentation . To learn more about logically air-gapped vaults for RD
title: AWS Backup adds logically air-gapped vault support for Amazon RDS

summary: Building AI agents has become essential. Across your organization, teams want agents to handle ERP transactions, work through a claims queue, and operate the same applications your people use every day. But how do you move from experiments to production? Before an agent touches real systems and real data, you need to verify who it acted on behalf of, what it did, and whether it stayed within the limits you set. Without that visibility, the agent stays stuck in testing, and the value is never realized. Earlier this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents , extending the power and security of a cloud work environment to agents, not just people. Today, we're excited to announce new capabilities that make it even easier to operate agents confidently across your enterprise and move them from proof of concept to governed production in fewer steps. You can set up new agents or connect the ones your builders have already built, run them under your own identity providers and policies, and keep a record of everything they do. You don't need to stitch together new tools or build custom monitoring. Setup used to mean configuring the machine by hand. Now, you can just describe what your agent needs to your AI coding assistant such as Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro. Guided by AWS MCP skills, the assistant builds the WorkSpace from defaults you can adjust. If your teams build on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, you can connect an agent directly with your AWS credentials and skip writing an
title: Set up, connect, and govern AI agents faster with Amazon WorkSpaces

summary: Now available in AWS GovCloud (US-West), AWS DevOps Agent is your always-available operations teammate that resolves and proactively prevents incidents, optimizes application reliability and performance, and handles on-demand SRE tasks across AWS, multicloud, and on-prem environments. DevOps Agent investigates incidents and identifies operational improvements as an experienced teammate would: by learning your applications and their relationships, working with your observability tools, runbooks, code repositories, and CI/CD pipelines, and correlating telemetry, code, and deployment data. It autonomously triages incidents and guides teams to rapid resolution, reducing mean time to resolution (MTTR) from hours to minutes, while analyzing patterns across historical incidents to deliver actionable recommendations that prevent future outages. For the full list of AWS Regions where AWS DevOps Agent is available, visit the Regions list. Pricing details are available on the AWS DevOps Agent pricing page . AWS Support customers receive monthly DevOps Agent credits based on the prior month's AWS Support charge: 100% for Unified Operations, 75% for Enterprise Support, or 30% for Business Support+. For many customers, this significantly reduces or eliminates DevOps Agent costs. For details, visit the support compare page . To learn more, read the launch blog and see getting started .
title: AWS DevOps Agent is now available in AWS GovCloud (US-West)

summary: Amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, automatic write-conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg tables. You can run multi-step, concurrent transformation pipelines directly on Iceberg tables and audit the results, with the transaction semantics you expect from a data warehouse. This helps anyone writing to Iceberg tables at production scale. Batch jobs get all-or-nothing commits across multiple steps. Streaming and scheduled jobs can write to the same tables at the same time. Analysts, auditors, and AI agents can query a table as it existed at any point in time. With multi-statement transactions, you group several statements in a single BEGIN…COMMIT statement and publish them as one atomic Iceberg snapshot. This means a multi-step load such as a MERGE followed by a DELETE, can be commited together as one atomic operation, are never queryable in a half-applied state, and roll back cleanly if there's a failure. Automatic conflict resolution lets concurrent writes, such as streaming inserts alongside scheduled deletes, write to the same table and commit together when their changes don't overlap, instead of failing and retrying. Time travel lets you query a table as it existed at a past point in time with AS OF TIMESTAMP. You can use it to reproduce reports, audit changes, or recover from a bad write without keeping extra copies. These capabilities are available in all AWS commercial Regions for Amazon Redshift’s provisioned RG or serverless clu
title: Amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg

summary: AWS IAM Identity Center now gives you the option to require workforce users to re-authenticate with your external identity provider (IdP) each time their user interactive session expires. By default, when a user's session expires, IAM Identity Center renews it through the user's existing IdP session, and the user isn't prompted to sign in again. For organizations with strict security or compliance requirements that mandate explicit user verification at regular intervals, this automatic renewal may not meet policy requirements. When you set user re-authentication to Required and a user's user interactive session expires, IAM Identity Center prompts the user to re-authenticate with your external IdP. This helps you enforce stronger sign-in controls for regulated workloads. IAM Identity Center implements this by adding the SAML 2.0 ForceAuthn attribute to the SAML request sent to your IdP. You can configure user re-authentication for any IAM Identity Center instance (organization or account) that's connected to an external IdP as its identity source. The setting applies only to service provider initiated sign-ins, where users sign in through your AWS access portal URL. Changes to the user re-authentication setting are logged in AWS CloudTrail, so you can audit when it was turned on or off. User re-authentication is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available at no additional cost. To learn more, see Require user re-authentication in the AWS IAM Identity C
title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports ForceAuthn in SAML requests

summary: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports KV cache-aware routing for real-time inference endpoints, enabling you to reduce time to first token for LLM workloads with long or repeated prompts. Serving engines such as vLLM store the computed key-value (KV) cache for repeated prompt starts such as shared system prompts, documents, and conversation history, to skip repeated work. Across several instances, a request that lands where the cache is missing recomputes it. Under high load, instances also evict cached blocks to free GPU memory, including shared prompts and earlier conversation turns. KV cache-aware routing sends each request to the instance that holds the longest matching part of its prompt in cache. The vLLM container reports the cache blocks it stores and evicts, and SageMaker routes with that live view. If the lookup is slow or finds no match, the endpoint falls back to load-aware routing, so the request is still served. Prefix-aware routing suits stable shared prompts, short prompts, or moderate load. KV cache-aware routing suits long prompts, high load, and limited GPU memory. Customers can now enable this feature by setting `RoutingStrategy` to `KV_AWARE` on a production variant and adding one environment variable so the container reports cache events. Customer can invoke the endpoint with the same APIs and OpenAI-compatible payloads. It supports single-model endpoints and inference components, including LoRA adapters, on GPU instances. It requires the AWS vLLM Deep Learni
title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports KV cache-aware routing for real-time inference endpoints

summary: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) now supports Networking Flexible Cost Allocation (FCA), which splits shared networking costs by the resources that actually drive them, so you can see what each team or application used. Until now, AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR), including CUR 2.0 in AWS Data Exports, showed networking usage as a single item, and most customers split it across teams with custom scripts and manual estimates. FCA splits this line item by the resources that generated it. It supports NAT gateway data processing and data transfer, including traffic to the internet, and in-Region Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and VPC peering data transfer. Today, when several teams share a resource such as a NAT gateway, the account that owns it pays the full cost and can't see which team or application drove it. To work around this, some customers built custom scripts to analyze VPC Flow Logs, which takes ongoing engineering effort. Others used fixed-percentage splits, which overcharge some teams and undercharge others. FCA breaks down usage based on traffic sources, helping you accurately track financial metrics based on applications and teams. To get started, attach a cost allocation policy to a NAT gateway, VPC peering connection, or Amazon EC2 instance, then select Networking flexible cost allocation under split cost allocation data in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Allocated line items appear in your CUR within 24 hours. FCA changes only how costs
title: AWS announces Networking Flexible Cost Allocation for Amazon VPC

summary: AWS Secrets Manager now supports managed external secrets for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks. Long-lived credentials that are not rotated increase the risk of unauthorized access if exposed. Rotating a third-party credential requires coordinated updates to the external service and every application that uses it. You set a rotation schedule from the AWS Management Console or API. Secrets Manager rotates the credential and stores the current value without a custom rotation Lambda function. Secrets Manager offers self-rotation and administrator-assisted rotation for Auth0 credentials. With self-rotation, the target application replaces its own secret. With administrator-assisted rotation, a separate Auth0 application with Management API permissions replaces the target application's secret. For Okta, Secrets Manager offers administrator-assisted rotation with a separate administrator JSON Web Token (JWT) key and validates the replacement before deactivating the old secret. For Palo Alto Networks, Secrets Manager offers self-rotation, in which the current API key authorizes its replacement. Applications that already retrieve credentials from Secrets Manager receive the rotated value without a code change or deployment. These integrations join existing managed external secrets support for BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, Databricks, Datadog, GitLab, Jenkins, MongoDB Atlas, Netskope, Paddle, Salesforce, Snowflake, SonarQube, and Twilio. Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alt
title: AWS Secrets Manager adds managed external secrets support for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks

summary: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports interface VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink and network access controls, enabling you to keep IAM Identity Center traffic private and restrict which networks can reach your IAM Identity Center services. Previously, IAM Identity Center rejected traffic arriving through VPC endpoints, requiring all sign-in and API traffic to use public endpoints. With this launch, you can create interface VPC endpoints for AWS access portal and service APIs to route traffic over the AWS private network. IAM Identity Center sign-in traffic flows through the AWS Sign-in VPC endpoint. You can attach VPC endpoint policies to each endpoint to scope which AWS organizations, accounts and resources are reachable through your private connection. Network access controls add a second layer of enforcement at the IAM Identity Center instance level. When enabled, you can require that all access arrive through a VPC endpoint, allow specific IP address ranges or VPCs as trusted sources, and exclude individual applications from enforcement to accommodate services that connect from outside your VPC. SCIM provisioning traffic from your external identity provider can be independently restricted to known IP address ranges. Network access controls are configured through the IAM Identity Center API and are disabled by default. This capability is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions at no additional cost. To learn more, see Interface VPC
title: IAM Identity Center now supports VPC endpoints and network access controls

summary: AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities in the MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage APIs. Previously, AWS Marketplace sellers reported usage to both APIs in whole numbers, and now they can report usage with up to six decimal places. Sellers can price and meter in the units that match how customers consume their product, for example reporting 1.5 terabytes (TB) of storage instead of 1 or 2 TB. To report decimal quantities, sellers use the new UsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter in MeterUsage and QuantityAsDecimal parameter in BatchMeterUsage, and existing integrations that report whole numbers continue to work without changes. Usage allocations, which split reported usage into buckets by tags, also support decimal quantities with the new AllocatedUsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter. This new feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace Metering Service is available. To learn more, see MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage in the AWS Marketplace API Reference.
title: AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities

summary: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and users. You can now let trusted parties define the access they need through reusable managed permissions in RAM, while keeping full control of your keys and key policies. To share a key, create a resource share by selecting the keys to share, choosing a managed permission, and specifying the principals. You can use AWS managed permissions for common scenarios, or customer managed permissions (CMPs) authored by you or by trusted parties such as SaaS providers and central security teams. Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain. The trusted parties who need access to your keys can publish the policy once as a CMP, without the need for you to modify the key policies by hand. You simply fill in the values that scope it to your environment and attach it to the resource share. Your existing key policy is untouched, so you are always in control of your key as your environment grows. When a new policy version is available via an updated CMP, you decide when to apply it to your resource shares. This enhancement is built on new AWS RAM capabilities that are available for every resource type RAM supports. CMPs now support multiple policy statements and additional IAM conditi
title: AWS KMS now supports key sharing with AWS Resource Access Manager

summary: Amazon Connect Customer agent assist now supports interactive components, including cards, carousels, buttons, and input fields. The AI agent analyzes conversation context in real time, recommends actions, retrieves information, and executes tasks on behalf of contact center agents using MCP tools in Connect Customer or third-party services. Interactive responses let agents review information, provide details, select options, and confirm actions without manually typing a separate request for each action. The AI agent can also recommend step-by-step guides, cases, customer profiles, and third-party applications that agents can open with one click. For example, when a customer calls to dispute a charge, the AI agent can dynamically generate an interactive list of the customer’s recent transactions. The agent can select the disputed transaction, provide or confirm the required details, and approve the action. The AI agent can then use a connected tool to create the dispute request and display confirmation in the agent workspace. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer agent assist is available. To learn more and get started, see Agent Assist in the Amazon Connect Administrator Guide.
title: Amazon Connect Customer agent assist now supports interactive responses

summary: Today, AWS announces the public preview of medical coding in Amazon Connect Health , a HIPAA-eligible AI service that works alongside healthcare teams across patient engagement and point-of-care workflows. Medical coding uses existing clinical documentation to suggest ICD-10-CM and CPT codes, including E&M levels and modifiers, for a provider or coder to review and approve before submission. You can integrate medical coding into your EHR or billing application through the Amazon Connect Health SDK, or use it with Amazon Connect Health ambient documentation. Each code links to the evidence that supports it and carries a confidence score, so reviewers can confirm a code before a claim goes out. In this public preview, you can choose to upload your organization's previously coded encounters, and the service builds a coding reference set specific to your organization. The corrections coders make feed that reference set and improve future coding suggestions. Medical coding is available in public preview in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) AWS Regions. To learn more, see medical coding in the Amazon Connect Health user guide.
title: Amazon Connect Health medical coding is now available in public preview

summary: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with full-text search within a single query. By combining semantic meaning and exact term matching into a single ranked list of results, hybrid search captures both intent and precise terms for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agent memory, and search applications. This can deliver more relevant ranked results than either method alone. Hybrid search works with the same S3 Vectors APIs and maintains subsecond latency for infrequent queries and latency around 100 milliseconds or less for frequent queries. S3 Vectors is designed to provide the same elasticity, durability, and availability as Amazon S3, and it reduces the total costs of storing and querying vectors by up to 90% compared to alternative vector solutions. With hybrid search, customers can now store the data that they want to make full-text searchable alongside the vectors. Customers write data with the PutVectors API as they do today and include the searchable text as another metadata field. S3 Vectors then automatically indexes that field for full-text search with BM25 relevance scoring. By default, S3 Vectors uses a language-agnostic text analyzer to index this data which works across most languages, and customers can optionally select a language-specific analyzer for more accurate language-aware matching. To perform a hybrid query, customers send their query text strings alongside their query vector in a single QueryVectors c
title: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search combining vector and full text for more relevant search results

summary: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) now supports associating additional AWS Key Management Service (KMS) keys with EBS snapshots. This new capability enables you to share and copy encrypted snapshots across accounts without first re-encrypting them, simplifying your disaster recovery and backup workflows. Customers use EBS snapshots as durable, point-in-time backups of EBS volumes. By associating an additional customer-managed KMS key (CMK) with a snapshot encrypted with an AWS managed key (AMK), for example, you enable cross-account sharing for that snapshot without re-encrypting its data. This feature accelerates your disaster recovery workflows and enhances operational efficiency for enterprise backup administrators and disaster recovery teams. Support for associating additional KMS keys with Amazon EBS snapshots is available in all AWS commercial, China, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) Regions, plus AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts. You can access this capability through the AWS Console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), and AWS SDKs. To learn more, see the Amazon EBS documentation .
title: Amazon EBS now supports associating additional KMS keys with snapshots

summary: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports replicating image deletions and tag removals to your replication destinations. Previously, ECR replication copied images to destination regions and accounts but did not replicate deletions, requiring you to manage deletions separately in each location. With replication of deletes, your destination repositories stay consistent with the source automatically. Teams running multi-region or multi-account architectures no longer need to script or manually track image cleanup across every destination. When you delete an image or remove a tag in your source registry, whether directly or through a lifecycle policy, ECR propagates that deletion to each destination in the replication rule. Replicated deletions emit EventBridge events and are recorded in CloudTrail, so you have the same visibility into deletions as you do for image pushes. Replication of deletes is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is available, at no additional cost. To get started, update your replication configuration in the Amazon ECR console or AWS CLI. For more information, see the Amazon ECR User Guide .
title: Amazon ECR now replicates image deletions across regions and accounts

summary: AWS Network Firewall attached to AWS Transit Gateway now allows you to use context-aware rules in your firewall policy. Network Firewall is a managed firewall and intrusion prevention service that inspects and filters traffic across your virtual private clouds (VPCs). With context-aware rules, you write rules that reference context from VPC resources instead of IP addresses. This makes it easier to apply consistent security controls as your organization grows. Existing rules automatically cover new workloads, so you don't need to update rules manually. Context-aware rules match traffic using VPCs, subnets, security groups, and Transit Gateway attachment identifiers, collectively known as context identifiers. You can reference context identifiers in a rule's source for any protocol, and in its destination for TCP-based protocols such as HTTP, TLS, and SSH. Flow and alert logs include context identifiers, so you can investigate activity based on context. Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. For a full list of supported Regions, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page . To learn more, see the AWS Network Firewall product page and documentation .
title: AWS Network Firewall now supports context-aware rules with AWS Transit Gateway-attached firewalls

summary: Amazon S3 Storage Lens now provides storage metrics for each S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tier. You can see object counts and storage bytes in every tier across your buckets. This helps you track how your data moves between tiers, estimate storage costs, and measure your savings. S3 Storage Lens gives you visibility across your organization into storage usage and activity to help you optimize costs and performance. Access tier metrics appear in your S3 Storage Lens dashboards and metrics exports alongside your existing metrics. S3 Storage Lens also now publishes prefix metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management, so you can allocate shared bucket costs to teams and applications with split cost allocation data for S3. To get started, enable access tier metrics in your S3 Storage Lens advanced tier configuration. Access tier metrics are available in all AWS Regions, except the AWS China Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, visit the S3 Storage Lens documentation . For pricing, visit the S3 pricing page .
title: Amazon S3 Storage Lens now tracks S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers

summary: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) introduces resource optimization for EKS Auto Mode, a new capability that rightsizes the CPU and memory requests of running Pods based on their actual usage. CPU and memory requests are often set at deploy time and rarely revisited, and Auto Mode provisions EC2 instances to fit them. Rightsizing lets Auto Mode run the same Deployments and StatefulSets on fewer or smaller instances, without hand tuning and at no additional charge. Turn on resource optimization by creating a ClusterResourceOptimizationPolicy in your EKS cluster, review its recommendations in the default Recommend mode, and switch to Apply mode when you're ready to resize running Pods in place, without recreating them. For example, a platform team running Java services under Argo CD can rightsize every application namespace without editing templates or creating GitOps drift, while resource optimization keeps memory above each Java heap and raises memory after an out-of-memory kill. It doesn't change the CPU or memory that a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or KEDA scales on, and you can exclude workloads that the Vertical Pod Autoscaler already manages. You can use resource optimization on EKS Auto Mode clusters running Kubernetes 1.36 or later in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Seoul), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see Rightsize workloads with resource optimi
title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now rightsizes Pods to reduce compute costs (Preview)

summary: Amazon Web Services announces the preview of Infoblox Threat Defense on Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall . Security administrators can now apply Infoblox threat intelligence directly in DNS Firewall rules to preemptively protect applications in their Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) from cyber threats, by subscribing to the Infoblox product listing on AWS Marketplace from the Route 53 DNS Firewall console. With this launch, you can add Infoblox managed rules to your DNS Firewall rule groups to filter and block queries to malicious and high-risk domains at the DNS layer. Infoblox continuously updates its threat intelligence feeds to preemptively protect cloud workloads from phishing, malware, ransomware and other advanced attacks. You can apply these protections to DNS queries from your VPCs and to hybrid traffic forwarded through Route 53 Resolver endpoints, so security teams keep consistent DNS policies across AWS and on-premises environments and add a layer of protection on top of AWS managed domain lists. Infoblox Threat Defense on Route 53 DNS Firewall is available in preview in all AWS commercial Regions where Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is available. DNS Firewall Advanced customers can add Infoblox rules to existing rule groups at no additional DNS Firewall charge, and the Infoblox subscription in AWS Marketplace is free during preview. To get started, see the Route 53 DNS Firewall documentation . To view Route 53 pricing, visit the Route 53 pricing page . T
title: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now supports Infoblox Threat Defense (Preview)

summary: Today, AWS announces that AWS Security Hub now monitors Google Cloud Platform (GCP) resources, extending risk analytics, cloud security posture management, vulnerability management, and security response management across both clouds. Many AWS customers running workloads in AWS and GCP have had to operate separate security tools for each environment, making it difficult to prioritize risks holistically or respond consistently. Security Hub now provides a single, unified experience to detect and respond to risks across your AWS and GCP environments in addition to existing support for monitoring Microsoft Azure environments. Security Hub automatically discovers GCP resources, including GCP Virtual Machines (VMs), GCP Google Artifact Registry (GAR) container images, GCP Cloud Run functions, and GCP identities, and evaluates them for misconfigurations, internet exposure, and software vulnerabilities. You receive posture checks against security standards including the CIS Benchmarks™ for Google Cloud Platform Foundations, unified resource inventory, risk and exposure analysis, and automated response through existing EventBridge integrations. AWS and GCP findings appear in the same prioritized view with the same finding formats and automation workflows, so security teams can operate from one console rather than switching between tools. Security Hub includes an independent 30-day free trial to monitor GCP resources that begins once you create your integration with Google Cloud Platf
title: AWS Security Hub extends unified security management to Google Cloud Platform

summary: You can now allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to its prefixes in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Many organizations store data for multiple teams, applications, or tenants in one bucket under different prefixes such as "marketing/" and "finance/". Previously, splitting that bucket's bill by prefix required custom pipelines and your own pricing logic. With this new capability, S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management. Billing and Cost Management then allocates the bucket's storage and Tier 1 and Tier 2 request costs to the deepest matching prefix in the range of prefix levels you choose. Each prefix line item carries its full prefix path as AWS-generated cost allocation tags, so you can total costs by top-level prefix, team, or application, and reconcile it back to the bucket. You can use this data for chargeback and showback, and to see which prefixes drive your S3 spend. To get started, enable AWS Billing and Cost Management publishing in your S3 Storage Lens advanced tier configuration, then enable split cost allocation data for S3 in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. This feature is available in all AWS Regions, except the AWS China Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, at no additional charge beyond S3 Storage Lens advanced tier pricing. To learn more, visit the AWS Cost and Usage Reports product page, Understanding split cost allocation data
title: AWS Split Cost Allocation Data now supports Amazon S3

summary: AWS now enables agentic coding harnesses to open the new AWS sign-up experience for developers who don't have an AWS account yet. Previously, developers working in agentic coding environments like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor had to manually navigate to aws.amazon.com , sign up for an AWS account and configure credentials before deploying workloads, interrupting the developer's experience. Now, developers can go from an idea to deploying a running application by the browser automatically opening, completing sign up and returning short-lived credentials to the harness. When developers sign up for AWS from their coding agent, they start with the new AWS experience. Their first project comes set up with a home Region, IAM role manager, and short-term credentials that refresh automatically, so the agent can start deploying right away. To try the new experience, install the AWS plugin or configure the AWS Agent Toolkit in your agentic coding harness. To learn more, see the AWS Agent Toolkit documentation or the AWS Account Documentation .
title: AWS announces agentic account creation for agentic coding harnesses

summary: Starting today, you can allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to the prefixes in that bucket in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Organizations often store data for many teams, applications, or tenants in one bucket under different prefixes, such as `marketing/` and `finance/`. Until now, attributing that bucket's bill to each prefix required custom pipelines built on S3 Inventory or Storage Lens reports and your own pricing logic. With Split Cost Allocation Data for Amazon S3, Amazon S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management, which allocates the bucket's storage and Tier 1 and Tier 2 request costs to the deepest matching prefix in the range of prefix levels you choose. Each prefix line item carries its full prefix path as AWS-generated cost allocation tags, so you can total cost by top-level prefix, team, or application, and reconcile it back to the bucket. You can use this data for chargeback, showback, and to see which prefixes drive your S3 spend. To get started, enable AWS Billing and Cost Management publishing in an S3 Storage Lens advanced tier dashboard configuration, then enable split cost allocation data for Amazon S3 in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Prefix cost data appears in your CUR after the next daily Storage Lens metrics are published. Split Cost Allocation Data for Amazon S3 is available in all AWS commercial Regions where S3 Storage Le
title: AWS Split Cost Allocation Data now supports Amazon S3

summary: AWS now supports credit splitting and transfers, enabling customers to divide any AWS credit into multiple smaller credits and transfer them to other linked accounts within their payer account. Previously, AWS applied credits starting with the owning account, then shared any excess with other accounts based on their usage, making it difficult for customers with large credits to direct precise amounts to specific teams or business units. FinOps teams can now split credits by dollar amounts, percentages, or even splits, and transfer each portion to the team that earned it. Credit splitting and transfers eliminate hours of monthly manual chargeback work for FinOps teams and provide predictable credit budgets per team or business unit. Each split credit inherits the same expiration date and service eligibility as the original, and split credits retain sharing settings by default so unused balances flow to other eligible accounts. Accounts receive first-priority consumption for transferred credits. Credit splitting and transfers compose naturally with existing credit features, including credit-level sharing and credit pausing. After a split, customers have full control over each resulting credit. For example, customers can split and share one credit across all intended accounts so multiple teams benefit, while restricting another split credit to a single account. They can also pause a credit earmarked for a future project, then resume it when needed. You can split any credit type
title: AWS launches credit splitting and transfers

summary: AWS Billing and Cost Management now gives customers symmetric, granular control over how credits, Reserved Instances, and Savings Plans are shared across their organization. Organizations with grant funding, regulatory obligations, or multi-entity structures can now automate benefit allocation that previously required manual chargeback reconciliation. With these new capabilities, customers can set default sharing preferences that automatically apply to all cost-saving benefits, and override those defaults for individual benefits when business requirements demand it. Customers configure Credit Group Sharing through the Billing Preferences page to set a single default that every new credit inherits automatically, ending the cycle of per-credit manual configuration. For Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, customers configure sharing preferences at the individual commitment level through the Savings Plans or Reserved Instances inventory pages, whether purchased at a linked account or at the payer level. All sharing configurations use Cost Categories, the same grouping construct customers already use in Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and the Cost and Usage Report. These capabilities are available starting November 17, 2026, in all AWS Regions through the AWS Billing and Cost Management Console and public APIs. There is no additional charge. To learn more, visit the for documentations for Credit Group Sharing and Savings Plan and Reserved Instances Level Sharing .
title: AWS announces consistent sharing controls for credits, Savings Plans, and Reserved Instances

summary: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) introduces Access Troubleshooter , a new capability that gives you visibility into the full authorization context behind access denied errors so you can resolve them without trial-and-error. Previously, developers relied on the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the denying policy to debug a denial, with no visibility into the authorization context or other policies evaluated in the request that could contribute to the denial. This made troubleshooting access issues time-consuming and inefficient. Starting today, access denied error messages for supported services and APIs will include a unique identifier that you can use to retrieve details of the authorization performed by the service. You gain visibility into what policies were evaluated for each request, the authorization context of those requests, and the results of the evaluation. This enables you to identify the root cause of authorization issues quickly, streamlining your access management workflows and reducing time spent debugging permission problems. To learn more about Access Troubleshooter and how it can help you resolve access denied errors efficiently, see the User Guide on troubleshooting access denied error messages .
title: AWS IAM announces Access Troubleshooter to debug access denied errors

summary: Amazon API Gateway now offers a native JWT authorizer for REST APIs, a new authorizer type that validates JSON Web Tokens directly in the gateway. Until now, validating tokens from an OpenID Connect or OAuth 2.0 identity provider other than Amazon Cognito required a Lambda authorizer. You now configure token validation instead of writing and operating code for it. You can define one or more issuers, the audiences accepted for each, the signing algorithms you permit, and any additional claims a token may present. API Gateway verifies each token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and claims on every request. You can attach one authorizer to many methods and require different scopes on each. This fits machine-to-machine APIs, mobile and web backends, and multi-tenant APIs that accept tokens from several identity providers. The JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see Amazon API Gateway documentation and AWS blog post .
title: Amazon API Gateway REST APIs now support JWT authorizers

summary: AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a new capability called Multipath Resilience. Multipath Resilience makes it easier to improve the resilience of mission-critical applications that send traffic across Regions, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming. The AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths. When a path fails, such as during a fiber cut, the network's automatic sub-second rerouting moves traffic to a healthy path. In the rare event that such mechanisms do not resolve the issue in a timely manner, such as when there's a partial degradation, it might take minutes for connectivity to be reestablished. Some applications, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming, can't tolerate single-digit seconds interruptions, let alone minutes of unavailability. Until now, customers running these applications relied on workarounds, including modifying their applications and operating systems to split a single connection into multiple connections, or replicating data into every Region to avoid cross-Region calls. These workarounds add complexity and don't always work, because applications can't control which network paths their traffic takes. Now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for
title: Amazon VPC, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN now offer a 99.999% availability SLA for cross-Region traffic

summary: When a WorkSpace is slow or won't connect, the IT administrator trying to help has traditionally had to dig through Amazon CloudWatch metrics, logs, and configuration data across multiple tools to find out why. And in the meantime, the user on the other end can't get their work done. In April this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor, an AI-powered agent that helps IT administrators diagnose and fix WorkSpaces performance, connectivity and provisioning issues and get users back to work faster. With Advisor, administrators can investigate a WorkSpace from the console and, in minutes, see the likely root cause and recommended actions they can take right away. Since then, we've continued to invest in Advisor so your team can spend less time chasing down issues one by one, and more time on the projects your business is counting on you to deliver. Today, we're excited to announce the preview of proactive troubleshooting in WorkSpaces Advisor, which moves your team from reacting to individual tickets to staying ahead of issues across your whole environment. Advisor can identify issues across your WorkSpaces, explain the likely cause of each one and recommend a fix. You don't need to start an investigation, wait for a user to report a problem, or set alarm thresholds first. If the same problem affects many WorkSpaces, Advisor will show it as a single issue with the likely cause and a recommended fix. Your team fixes the root cause once instead of chasing the same symptom one
title: Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor now helps you find issues before your users notice them (Public Preview)

summary: Amazon WorkSpaces provides a new Windows client experience for Amazon WorkSpaces Personal. The new client experience includes an updated interface, a simplified connection flow, easier-to-find settings, and the new WorkSpaces Advisor proactive troubleshooting (Public Preview) that suggests actions you can take to resolve common issue WorkSpaces Advisor proactive troubleshooting (Public Preview) is an intelligent new capability that monitors key metrics from your device, network, and the WorkSpace itself, and provides you with actionable recommendations if there are issues with registration, sign-in, or the connection in general. The new client experience also includes an improved full screen experience, a welcome tour to help orient you, and for WorkSpaces that are admin-enabled, a self-service option to enable nested virtualization. The new client experience is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Personal is available. To learn more, visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Windows client documentation or download the Amazon WorkSpaces client .
title: Amazon WorkSpaces provides a new Windows client experience

summary: AWS announces the general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud with Microsoft Azure. Customers have been adopting multicloud strategies while migrating more applications to the cloud. They do so for many reasons including interoperability requirements, the freedom to choose technology that best suits their needs, and the ability to build and deploy applications on any environment with greater ease and speed. Previously, when interconnecting workloads across multiple cloud providers (CSPs), customers had to go the route of a ‘do-it-yourself’ multicloud approach, leading to complexities of building and managing global multi-layered networks at scale. AWS Interconnect - multicloud is the first purpose-built product of its kind and a new way of how clouds connect and talk to each other, allowing customers to quickly provision resilient, scalable private connections to other cloud providers. In August, Microsoft Azure launched support for AWS Interconnect in public preview and became the latest CSP to adopt the open specification that powers the service. With today’s GA launch, AWS customers can now rely on the same consistent, simple experience to interconnect their workloads on Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Interconnect - multicloud is available with Microsoft Azure in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia), ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), and eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Regions. You can create an Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Com
title: AWS announces general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud connectivity with Microsoft Azure

summary: Today, AWS announces the general availability of OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on Amazon Bedrock. GPT-6.2 Astra brings frontier-level reasoning and judgment to your most ambitious work, including complex business problems, demanding research, and advanced coding and agentic workflows. Astra also includes an Ultrafast mode for latency-sensitive applications that need fast responses. GPT-6.2 Sol is designed for recurring coding, agentic, and professional workflows with clear outcomes, where speed and cost per task matter. Use GPT-6.2 Astra for challenging work that calls for expert judgment and a finished deliverable, such as reconciling competing inputs, investigating complex codebases, reasoning across text and images, and creating professional artifacts. Select ultrafast mode for Astra for interactive coding assistants, real-time agents, and customer-facing applications where latency shapes the customer experience. Use GPT-6.2 Sol for recurring, high-volume work with verifiable outcomes, such as implementing and debugging software, analyzing documents and data, and automating multistep workflows. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.
title: OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra, and GPT-6.2 Sol are now generally available on Amazon Bedrock

summary: Amazon Aurora DSQL now records statistics for each SQL statement your cluster runs and publishes them as Amazon CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics. You can view them in Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights. For each statement, you see how often it runs, how long it takes, the rows it scans, returns, or changes, and the DPUs it uses. Statement statistics measure every successful statement rather than sampling activity. Use them to find the statements that take the most time, run most often, or cost the most. In Database Insights, choose a statement under Top SQL to see its normalized SQL text and per-call charts. You can also query the metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch. Turn on statement statistics for each cluster in the Aurora DSQL console or the API when you create or update the cluster. Statement statistics are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. Standard CloudWatch metrics and Logs charges apply, with no additional Aurora DSQL charge. To learn more, see monitoring SQL statements with statement statistics in the Aurora DSQL User Guide and CloudWatch pricing .
title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now offers SQL statement statistics in Database Insights

summary: AWS Config now offers managed conformance packs. AWS builds and maintains these packs for specific compliance and governance frameworks. When you deploy one, you choose a framework, and AWS Config evaluates your resources against it. AWS keeps the pack up to date as things change. When new AWS Config managed rules map to the framework's controls, or when the framework itself is revised, AWS updates your deployed pack automatically. Because AWS maintains a consistent pack definition in every supported Region, you can deploy the same framework across Regions without building or maintaining Region-specific rule sets. With managed conformance packs you no longer have to track framework changes or update rules yourself. Previously, to evaluate resources against a framework such as PCI DSS or SOC 2, you started from a sample conformance pack template, customized it for your environment, and then updated it yourself whenever new rules became available or the framework changed. Managed conformance packs remove that work, so your coverage stays current without manual template changes. Each pack includes the managed rules available in the Region where you deploy it and adds new rules as they become available there, so you don't need a separate template for each Region. You can set rule parameters to fit your environment. Compliance results and compliance scores appear in the AWS Config console alongside your other rules and conformance packs. Managed conformance packs cover frameworks
title: AWS Config announces managed conformance packs

summary: Amazon API Gateway now offers a native JWT authorizer for REST APIs, a new authorizer type that validates JSON Web Tokens directly in the gateway. Until now, validating tokens from an OpenID Connect or OAuth 2.0 identity provider other than Amazon Cognito required a Lambda authorizer.
