You now configure token validation instead of writing and operating code for it. You can define one or more issuers, the audiences accepted for each, the signing algorithms you permit, and any additional claims a token may present. API Gateway verifies each token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and claims on every request. You can attach one authorizer to many methods and require different scopes on each. This fits machine-to-machine APIs, mobile and web backends, and multi-tenant APIs that accept tokens from several identity providers. The JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see Amazon API Gateway documentation and AWS blog post .
title: Amazon API Gateway REST APIs now support JWT authorizers

summary: AWS Security Hub now detects when software with a known vulnerability is actively running on your Amazon EC2 instances. Exposure findings now include a new trait, *The EC2 instance is running software with a known vulnerability*. These findings get a higher severity rating than findings for the same vulnerability where the software isn't running. This helps your security team focus on the vulnerabilities that pose the greatest risk, without investing time and resources to investigate if the software is actually in use. Security teams managing thousands of instances can now prioritize patching based on actual runtime risk. Security Hub correlates data from Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring and Amazon Inspector VM Scanner to detect running vulnerable software. It then combines this with other signals to generate exposure findings for EC2 resources that may be at risk, so you can prioritize response and remediation. This capability is available at no additional cost with the AWS Security Hub Essentials plan in all AWS Regions where Security Hub is available . To learn more, see the AWS Security Hub User Guide , the exposure definition in Remediating exposures for EC2 , the AWS Security Hub product page , the GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring User Guide , and the Amazon Inspector VM Scanner User Guide . For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List .
title: AWS Security Hub now detects when vulnerable software is running on Amazon EC2 instances

summary: AWS Security Hub Network Scanning now scans Amazon RDS DB instances to identify those that are reachable from the internet. Network Scanning automatically discovers existing and new RDS DB instances in your accounts and scans each instance that has Public Access configured. For each reachable port associated with a DB instance, Security Hub creates a finding with details about the instance and the reachable port. RDS scanning gives you more visibility into which resources in your environment are reachable from the internet. You can then investigate and update their access settings as needed. RDS scanning is turned on automatically for all customers who already have Network Scanning enabled. Network Scanning probes your resources from the internet to detect reachability, beyond what security group rules and route tables suggest. Security Hub Exposures then correlates these findings with other findings and resource configurations to assess broader risk. Existing Security Hub customers can enable Network Scanning in individual accounts and Regions, or across an organization with a configuration policy. For new Security Hub customers, Network Scanning is on by default. Network Scanning is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions that support Security Hub. To learn more, see the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page . For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List .
title: AWS Security Hub Network Scanning now supports scanning Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database instances

summary: AWS Lambda durable functions now lets you pause a running durable execution and resume it later without losing its progress. When you resume an execution, it continues from its last checkpoint on the same function version. By default, time spent paused doesn't count toward the execution timeout. You can also now delete a completed execution's data before its retention period ends. With Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. With this launch, when a downstream service is degraded or a model provider's rate limit is reached, you can pause affected executions while you resolve the issue instead of letting the retries run out. You can also delete an execution's history, checkpoint data, and input and output payloads after it succeeds, fails, stops, or times out. For example, you can delete an execution whose input contains personal data, or clean up failed executions that a bug left behind. You can pause, resume, and delete executions using the Lambda console, the AWS CLI, or the AWS SDKs in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more, see Managing durable executions in the AWS Lambda Developer Guide, or visit the AWS Lambda durable functions product page. If you build with an AI coding assistant such as Kiro, the Agent Toolkit for AWS gives it skills and guidance for building on AWS.
title: AWS Lambda durable functions now supports pausing and deleting executions

summary: Amazon Route 53 Global Resolver now supports anycast DNS resolution for private connections managed through your AWS Cloud WAN configuration. This enables organizations with hybrid networks to resolve DNS queries to public and private domains over existing AWS Direct Connect or AWS VPN connections, with automatic multi-region failover for high availability. Previously, customers had to either deploy and manage separate Resolver endpoints in each AWS Region and customer location, with no automatic failover between AWS Regions, or use Global Resolver with internet-reachable anycast IPs, making it hard for clients without internet access or those restricted by compliance requirements to take advantage of Global Resolver's anycast DNS resolution. With this launch, customers with clients configured with private connectivity over your Cloud WAN network get all the benefits of Global Resolver: automatic regional failover for higher availability, centralized DNS filtering with Route 53 DNS Firewall to prevent DNS-based data exfiltration, and simplified query resolution of both public internet domains and private domains (hosted on Route 53). You can get started by enabling Global Resolver, for two or more AWS Regions, and associating it with your Cloud WAN network configuration. You can select one or more privately routable IP addresses (IPv4, IPv6) that do not conflict with addresses already in use in your Cloud WAN and define DNS Views to specify which private hosted zones and DNS
title: Amazon Route 53 Global Resolver is now available over AWS Cloud WAN for hybrid networks

summary: AWS Cost Optimization Hub now lets you stop idle Amazon EC2 instances directly from your recommendations. Cost Optimization Hub consolidates and prioritizes cost optimization recommendations across your AWS accounts and Regions, including idle resources. Previously, stopping an idle instance required you to leave Cost Optimization Hub and identify the specific instance in the Amazon EC2 console. Now you can stop it from the Savings opportunities page in Cost Optimization Hub. When you choose Stop next to an idle instance recommendation, a confirmation shows the instance, its account and Region, what the instance loses when it stops, such as instance store data and data in memory, and what continues to bill, such as EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses. Stopping does not terminate the instance or delete its EBS volumes, and you can start it again from the EC2 console. Stop needs no separate setup and uses your existing permissions. To receive idle resource recommendations, turn on Cost Optimization Hub and AWS Compute Optimizer. This feature is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To get started, open Cost Optimization Hub in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console and go to Savings opportunities. To learn more, see the Cost Optimization Hub product page and user guide .
title: Cost Optimization Hub now supports stopping idle Amazon EC2 instances

summary: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now automatically generates domain allow-lists from your VPCs' observed DNS query traffic, helping you enforce least-privilege DNS access and reduce the risk of DNS-based data exfiltration. Previously, implementing a least-privilege model required security teams to manually analyze DNS query logs to identify the domains their VPCs depend on before deploying allow-list rules. This created operational overhead and delayed enforcement of a deny-by-default (walled-garden) posture. With automated allow-list generation, DNS Firewall analyzes DNS query traffic using a lookback window configurable from 1 hour to 7 days to create an allow-list of observed domains. It then continuously monitors DNS queries and flags newly observed domains, so you can review them before adding them to the allow-list. You can deploy the rule across multiple VPCs and accounts using AWS Firewall Manager or Route 53 Profiles. This capability is available at no additional cost to DNS Firewall Advanced customers, in all AWS Regions where Route 53 DNS Firewall is supported, except in AWS GovCloud (US) and Amazon Web Services China Regions. To get started, use the Route 53 DNS Firewall console, AWS CLI, or API. To learn more, visit the Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall product page and the Route 53 DNS Firewall Developer Guide .
title: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now supports automated allow-list generation

summary: The open source AWS Workload Credentials Provider can now export AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates to applications running in containers on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), including AWS Fargate, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and Docker on Amazon EC2. You can now automate certificate deployment and renewal for containerized TLS workloads the same way you do on EC2 instances, on both Linux and Windows. The provider runs as a sidecar in your ECS task or EKS pod. It exports each certificate and private key to a shared volume and writes the renewed files when ACM rotates the certificate. For TLS servers that don't reload certificate files on their own, such as NGINX, Apache, HAProxy, or IIS, a companion watcher in the TLS container runs your reload command after each renewal. The watcher needs no AWS credentials. TLS servers that reload automatically, such as Envoy, Traefik, and Caddy, need only the shared volume. Access is controlled through IAM: the sidecar assumes a per-workload role that is allowed to export only that workload's certificates. To get started, download the provider and watcher binaries for Linux (x86_64 and Arm64) or Windows, and follow the setup steps and ECS and EKS examples in the AWS Workload Credentials Provider README on GitHub. The provider is available at no additional charge, and standard ACM charges apply to exported certificates. To learn more, see the AWS Certificate Manager documentation .
title: AWS Workload Credentials Provider adds container support for ACM certificates

summary: Amazon Connect Customer message templates, which personalize each message with details about its recipient, now support case fields from Cases and calculated attributes from Customer Profiles, such as a customer's most frequent contact channel. Companies that send updates about a claim, an order, or an application need each message to reflect that customer's record. Template authors can insert case fields, including custom fields that administrators define, and Connect Customer fills in the current value for each recipient every time it sends a message that uses the template. A claims manager at an insurance company can build one email template that pulls each claim's reference number and status from its case, so every policyholder receives an update about their own claim. A retailer can add a custom calculated attribute, such as each customer's total orders in the past year, to a loyalty email so every customer sees their own count. Developers can pass these values when they render a template with the RenderMessageTemplate API. You can use case and calculated attributes in message templates in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). To learn more, see Add personalized content to message templates in the Amazon Connect Customer Administrator Guide.
title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports case and calculated template variables

summary: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod introduces cluster operations, giving you visibility into every scaling and on-demand deep health check request from submission to completion. When a request runs into errors, the SageMaker AI console shows an alert that links directly to that request's error events. With continuous provisioning, HyperPod brings capacity online in the background as it becomes available, retries failed nodes automatically, and lets you run multiple scaling requests at the same time. Cluster operations show you when each request finishes and which request caused the activity on your cluster. When a scale-up falls short of its target, you can go directly to the failure reason. Each scaling or on-demand deep health check request creates a cluster operation that tracks the request from submission to completion, including whether it is still in progress and what it changed on each instance group. Events that HyperPod records while working on the request are linked to its operation. For example, if a scale-up of your training instance group doesn't reach its target, you can open the operation and see only the events for that request, without sorting through unrelated cluster activity. If you or an autoscaler such as Karpenter send several requests to the same instance group, for example during a burst of inference traffic, each operation shows whether it completed or was replaced by a newer request. That way you can tell which request actually changed your cluster. After yo
title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports cluster operations for tracking scaling and on-demand Deep Health Check requests

summary: AWS Transit Gateway now supports context sharing with security services, such as attached firewalls, allowing you to use Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), VPC subnets, VPC security groups, and transit gateway attachments in firewall policies alongside IP addresses. Until now, attached firewalls segmented traffic by IP address, which is hard to plan and maintain, or by resource tags, which firewalls periodically synchronize with IP addresses and can miss new workloads in between. With this feature, you can enforce segmentation based on how workloads and attachments are defined in AWS. Transit Gateway embeds resource context in the traffic it sends to your firewall, which can enforce the right policy from the first packet. For example, you can apply threat protection to traffic between web-tier and database-tier security groups, block development VPCs from reaching production VPCs, apply a common inspection policy to traffic entering AWS through AWS Direct Connect and AWS Site-to-Site VPN attachments, or apply policies to short-lived AWS Lambda functions as soon as they send traffic, all without updating rules as IP addresses change. AWS Network Firewall and Palo Alto Networks Software Firewalls support policies using resource context alongside IP-based rules. To get started, create a context store in AWS Network Manager and associate your transit gateways. The context store monitors resources connected to those transit gateways and shares their context with firewalls. Cont
title: AWS Transit Gateway now shares resource context with firewalls for segmentation policies

summary: With AWS Elemental MediaConnect , you now have more protocol support and routing control for your live video workflows. First, MediaConnect now supports more protocols, including RTMP, RTMPS, and eRTMP, across both flows and router . RTMP is widely used by live streaming encoders and software such as OBS. With this support, you can now bring RTMP sources into MediaConnect and deliver to RTMP endpoints, such as social and live streaming platforms. Second, the service adds three new routing capabilities: - PID remapping on MediaConnect router reassigns transport stream PIDs inline, without transcoding. - Clean switch aligns input transitions on video boundaries for a more seamless switching experience. - SRT merge input mode bonds redundant SRT streams of the same content, reconstructing a clean feed when one path degrades to add resilience for lossy or long-haul contribution. These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where MediaConnect Router is available. To learn more, see the AWS Elemental MediaConnect documentation .
title: AWS Elemental MediaConnect expands routing control and protocol support

summary: Today, AWS WAF announces a simplified console experience for Bot Control at the targeted inspection level. A single setting, Targeted bot control, turns on targeted protection for your Amazon CloudFront distributions with the configuration AWS recommends. It comes with two additions to the Bot Control managed rule group: bot confidence levels, which summarize the targeted detections on each request as High, Medium, or Low, and a LATEST version that keeps you on the newest detections automatically. Together, they help you protect your applications against sophisticated and AI-powered bots without writing label match rules or changing application code. The targeted inspection level uses machine learning and client-side signals to detect evasive bots. Previously, acting on those signals meant integrating the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into every page, learning dozens of labels, and writing label match rules to combine them. Now, the rule group combines the detections into one confidence level per request, with one rule per level, and the Targeted bot control setting adds the rule group, applies the recommended action for each level, sets the version to LATEST, and turns on automatic SDK integration so CloudFront adds the SDK to your pages. You can change any action or start in Count. The Targeted bot control setting is available today for protection packs (web ACLs) used with Amazon CloudFront. Bot confidence levels and the LATEST version are available in all AWS Regions where AWS W
title: AWS WAF announces simplified onboarding for Bot Control targeted protection

summary: AWS Transit Gateway now supports network function attachments of type Gateway Load Balancer, simplifying the deployment and management of network security across your AWS network. With a network function attachment, you can connect your transit gateway to a Gateway Load Balancer VPC endpoint service that fronts firewalls and other security appliances without complex VPC configurations. Transit Gateway creates and manages the Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in the Availability Zones you choose, removing the need to create dedicated endpoint subnets and route tables. The endpoint service can be in another AWS account. Network function attachments also support context sharing with security services. Transit Gateway adds resource context to traffic sent to your firewall, including the transit gateway attachment, VPC, subnet, and security groups. Your firewall can use this context alongside IP addresses to enforce segmentation policies. This capability is available in all commercial AWS Regions where both AWS Transit Gateway and Gateway Load Balancer are available, except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). It is also available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. To get started, see Network function attachments in the AWS Transit Gateway Guide and visit the AWS Transit Gateway product page .
title: AWS Transit Gateway supports native integration with Gateway Load Balancer

summary: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports queues, a simpler and more cost-effective way to process a stream. Because queues track the delivery state of each record, your consumer instances receive records instead of leasing shards, acknowledge each record when processing is complete, and scale beyond the number of shards. Kinesis Data Streams consumers can reduce the cost of processing data by up to 43% by using queues instead of the Kinesis Client Library. You no longer run a DynamoDB table or custom metrics, and you use compute more efficiently. Queues in Kinesis Data Streams are powered by Amazon SQS. Built on that foundation, a queue delivers records at least once, redelivers records your consumers do not acknowledge, and provides built-in dead-letter handling for records that keep failing. Each queue publishes its own CloudWatch metrics, so you can scale consumer instances on records waiting to be received and alarm on records that repeatedly fail. Use queues for applications that process each record independently, such as log processing, order fulfillment, and notifications. Use a stream consumer when processing one record depends on the records before it, such as live analytics, personalization, and anomaly detection. You ingest data once and let each application consume records through a queue or directly from the stream, with no change to your producers or existing stream consumers. For point-to-point messaging between application components, start with Amazon SQS. Ch
title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams announces queues to simplify and reduce costs of real-time processing

summary: Amazon S3 adds post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS) key exchange support to S3 Vectors and AWS PrivateLink for Amazon S3 interface endpoints. This extends the post-quantum cryptography support already available on regional S3, S3 Tables, and S3 Express One Zone endpoints. S3 Vectors endpoints and PrivateLink interface endpoints now support Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), one of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. PQ-TLS key exchange is available to all clients configured to use the ML-KEM key exchange algorithm. S3 Vectors and PrivateLink endpoints automatically negotiate the strongest key exchange that your client software supports, so clients that support ML-KEM receive the benefits of PQ-TLS key exchange without any changes to your applications or endpoint configuration. PQ-TLS key exchange for S3 Vectors and AWS PrivateLink for S3 is supported at no additional cost in all AWS Regions. To learn more about PQ-TLS support in S3, visit the Amazon S3 User Guide .
title: Amazon S3 adds post-quantum TLS key exchange support to additional S3 endpoints

summary: Amazon S3 now records the TLS key exchange algorithm in AWS CloudTrail for S3 requests, so you can see which requests and clients use post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS). With this visibility, you can measure the share of your S3 traffic that is protected with post-quantum cryptography, and identify the applications, SDK versions, and IAM principals that still connect with classical key exchange and need to be upgraded. The new keyExchange value in the tlsDetails field of CloudTrail management and data events shows the key exchange negotiated on each TLS connection, such as the hybrid post-quantum algorithm X25519MLKEM768 or a traditional algorithm such as x25519. For example, you can query your CloudTrail logs to find the user agents of S3 requests that did not use ML-KEM, then prioritize those clients for your post-quantum migration. The keyExchange value is recorded for requests to general purpose buckets, directory buckets, table buckets, and vector buckets, including requests made through AWS PrivateLink. Key exchange details for S3 requests are available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. Standard AWS CloudTrail pricing applies for S3 data events. To learn more, visit post-quantum TLS in the Amazon S3 User Guide and the CloudTrail record contents reference .
title: Amazon S3 now provides post-quantum TLS visibility in AWS CloudTrail

summary: On Nov 17, 2026, Amazon announced critical security patch update (CSPU) for Amazon Corretto Long-Term Support (LTS) and Feature Release (FR) versions of OpenJDK. Corretto 27.0.1.1.4, 25.0.5.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 17.0.21.1.2, 11.0.33.1.1, and 8u514 are now available for download . Amazon Corretto is a no-cost, multi-platform, production-ready distribution of OpenJDK. Visit Corretto home page to download Corretto 27, Corretto 25, Corretto 21, Corretto 17, Corretto 11, or Corretto 8. You can also get the updates on your Linux system by configuring a Corretto Apt, Yum, or Apk repo . Feedback is welcomed !
title: Amazon Corretto November 2026 Critical Security Patch Updates

summary: AWS Graviton4-based M8g instances are now generally available for Standard Brokers in Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). Compared to Standard Brokers on M7g, M8g delivers up to 35% lower P99 produce latency and 30% faster catch-up for consumers that fall behind. Standard Brokers on M8g are available today across all AWS regions where MSK Standard Brokers and M8g instances are available. For pricing, refer to the Amazon MSK pricing page . To get started, use the AWS Management Console or API to create a new cluster with Standard Brokers on M8g or start an in-place migration of an existing cluster from Standard Brokers on M7g to M8g. To learn more, see the Amazon MSK Developer Guide .
title: Amazon MSK Standard Brokers now support Graviton4-based M8g instances

summary: AWS Graviton4-based M8g instances are now generally available for Express Brokers in Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). Compared to Express Brokers on M7g, M8g delivers 15% lower compute costs, up to 45% lower P99 produce latency, and 2x faster catch-up for consumers that fall behind. Additionally, customers no longer pay the broker-side cost when moving data across Availability Zones between clients and brokers, reducing total cross-AZ data transfer costs by 50%. Together, lower data transfer and broker-hour charges result in up to 30% cost savings compared to Express Brokers on M7g. MSK Express Brokers are designed to deliver up to 3x more throughput per broker, scale up to 20x faster, and reduce recovery time by 90% compared to Standard Brokers running Apache Kafka. Express Brokers on M8g further improve on M7g with better economics and performance along with existing Express capabilities. Customers running Apache Kafka on external clusters, including on-premises, self-managed on AWS, or other cloud providers, can use Amazon MSK Replicator to seamlessly migrate to Express Brokers on M8g and immediately benefit from the improved price and performance. Existing Express customers can upgrade from M7g to M8g through in-place migration while client applications keep producing and consuming without interruption. Express Brokers on M8g are available today across all AWS regions where MSK Express Brokers and M8g instances are available. For pricing, refer to t
title: Amazon MSK Express Brokers now support Graviton4-based M8g instances

summary: Today, we are announcing that Amazon Elastic VMware Service (Amazon EVS) now supports the r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) bare metal instance types for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.x deployments. EC2 r7i instances are memory optimized, with custom 4th Generation Intel Xeon Scalable (Sapphire Rapids) processors, and designed to be used with external storage. With these instances possessing no local NVMe disks, Amazon EVS now supports VCF external principal storage with solutions such as Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP. With this launch, you can use the Amazon EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO) within the Solutions for EVS GitHub repository to fully automate the end-to-end deployment and configuration of your VCF 9.x environment on EVS. With this release, you now have more options for running VMware-based Virtual Machines (VM) in your Amazon VPC - while keeping the same tools, skills, and operational processes, and full control of your architecture, configuration, and lifecycle of your environment. We are also launching a new Amazon EVS Agent Skill, which gives your AI Agents context to help you plan, deploy, and operate your Amazon EVS environments - from answering questions and recommending designs to generating blueprints and driving deployments with EDO. To get started, point the AI agent of your choice to the EVS Agent Skill file in the latest release of the EVS GitHub repository . This release is available in all regions where Amazon EVS
title: Amazon EVS launches support for r7i.metal instances, external principal storage, and an Agent Skill

summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers 5,000 free web search queries per month through the Web Search Tool in AgentCore gateway and the Web Search API. AgentCore helps developers build, deploy, and operate highly effective agents securely at scale. Developers can now build and test agents with web search capabilities at no cost for their first 5,000 queries each month. The free allowance applies automatically, with no setup required. It is shared across supported AWS Regions and by all accounts in an organization, and resets each month. Additional queries are billed at standard rates without interrupting your agents. Free web search queries are available in all AWS Regions that support the Web Search Tool and Web Search API: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see AgentCore pricing , Web Search Tool in the AgentCore Developer Guide , and the AgentCore product page .
title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers free monthly web search queries

summary: Amazon OpenSearch UI has expanded to the AWS Africa (Cape Town) Region, bringing availability to 25 AWS Regions. OpenSearch UI provides a single endpoint to query, visualize, and analyze data across Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running OpenSearch version 1.3 or later and OpenSearch Serverless collections, including Classic and NextGen. One OpenSearch UI application can connect to multiple domains and collections. Workspaces organize dashboards, saved queries, and other content, with purpose-built experiences for observability, security analytics, and search. The Discover interface supports multiple data sources and query languages, including Piped Processing Language (PPL) and SQL. It also includes a data selector, query autocomplete, and an updated design. OpenSearch UI runs separately from your domains and collections, giving you access to the latest UI capabilities without requiring cluster upgrades. To get started, create an OpenSearch UI application using the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. OpenSearch UI is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the domains and collections it connects to. For the complete list of supported Regions, see OpenSearch UI endpoints and quotas . To learn more, see Using OpenSearch UI in Amazon OpenSearch Service in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.
title: Amazon OpenSearch UI is now available in the Africa (Cape Town) Region

summary: Today, AWS announces the general availability of DynamoDB caching with Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey, a serverless alternative to Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) that delivers sub-millisecond read latency for frequently accessed DynamoDB data. Previously, if you needed faster reads than the single-digit millisecond latency of DynamoDB, you had to provision and scale DAX nodes or run your own cache and keep it in sync with DynamoDB. Now you can access DynamoDB table data from a write-through cache that updates as data changes and scales automatically to meet changing workload demands, with no clusters or nodes to manage. DynamoDB caching requires no application logic changes and minimal configuration. You choose which DynamoDB tables and APIs to cache and how long to retain cached data. Your application's IAM credentials are used to access DynamoDB, so existing access control policies are automatically applied. DynamoDB caching is available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. DynamoDB caching is offered at no additional cost, so you pay only for the ElastiCache Serverless and DynamoDB resources your applications use. To get started, see the ElastiCache Developer Guide .
title: Amazon DynamoDB caching is now available with Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey

summary: AWS Lambda now supports scale to and from zero for Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). Lambda automatically scales execution environments for your function to zero during idle periods and scales them back up when requests arrive, without requiring you to provision minimum capacity. This makes LMI cost-effective for intermittent workloads such as asynchronous processing, development, and test environments. Lambda Managed Instances lets you run Lambda functions on your Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With Lambda Managed Instances, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing advantages, without managing infrastructure. Previously, customers needed to keep a minimum number of execution environments running even when there was no traffic. With this launch, Lambda scales execution environments for your function to zero after a period with no activity, and provisions them again when requests arrive. This improves cost efficiency for workloads with periods of no traffic. This feature is available today in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To get started, set MinExecutionEnvironments to zero for your function using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, or AWS CDK. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda pricing .
title: AWS Lambda now supports scale to and from zero for Lambda Managed Instances

summary: Building high-quality training datasets has traditionally required weeks of manual labeling and data cleaning. Amazon SageMaker now offers AI data preparation capabilities that help data scientists and ML engineers build high-quality training and evaluation datasets for both text-based model customization and traditional ML. Teams can generate synthetic examples grounded in their own documents, auto-label records at scale with confidence scores, incorporate expert feedback through human review, evaluate data quality, and transform data for their chosen training or evaluation technique. Synthetic data generation creates training, evaluation, and test data from a specification grounded in your documents. Auto-labeling labels data at scale with built-in task types including classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, plus custom tasks. Rows below your confidence threshold go to a human review queue in the Label Studio Community Edition in SageMaker AI Studio. Data quality evaluation finds duplicates and surfaces issues such as tone and insufficient diversity with both quality metrics and rules. Data transformation cleans and reshapes data for your training or evaluation technique, using operators such as dedupe, filter, and format conversion. Teams can start with just a few examples, production traces, or existing data in Amazon S3 , Amazon Athena , or AWS Glue Data Catalog . Developers access these capabilities dir
title: Amazon SageMaker now supports AI data preparation capabilities to build high-quality datasets for model development

summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now keeps a full session summary for every session. It's a single record that gives a snapshot of what happened in the conversation. Summary chunks cover the conversation in more detail, while the full session summary captures the overall picture of where the session stands. AgentCore Memory updates it as new events arrive, so it always reflects the session so far. This works well for developers who want a quick recap rather than a play-by-play. Full session summaries come with the summary strategy and need no extra setup. Every memory that has a summary strategy gets them automatically, including existing sessions. Each summary is stored as a long-term memory record next to the session's summary chunks. You retrieve it with the Memory operations you already use, and you can filter by record type to return only full session summaries. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is available. To get started, see the Summary strategy documentation .
title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now provides full session summaries

summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now lets you keep short-term memory events for up to 10 years, up from one year. Developers can now use short-term memory as a long-lived record of agent conversations and interactions. This helps when that history needs to stay available for a long time, such as for compliance and audit, for users who come back after months away, or for agents that need to look back at past sessions. You set retention on the memory resource, and it's applied to each event when the event is created, so existing events keep their original retention. Standard short-term memory storage charges apply for as long as you keep the data. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is available. To get started, see the AgentCore Memory documentation .
title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now supports short-term memory retention of up to 10 years

summary: AWS Elemental Inference now lets you customize how it analyzes your live video in two ways. You can create functions that ask custom questions of the video using multi-modal foundational models in Amazon Bedrock, or add contextual metadata decisions using labels and questions you define. Both run on the same pipeline as built-in features such as vertical video creation and smart subtitles, and return results through the GetMetadata API, with no separate pipeline to build. Use contextual metadata decisions when the answer you need fits labels and yes/no questions. You define yes/no questions, such as whether a scene is a weather report, or "pick-one" categories, such as genre. For each scene, contextual metadata returns a decision and a confidence score for every label and question, alongside the standard Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), and mood fields, so your workflows can act when confidence meets a threshold you set. No model selection or prompt writing is required. Use functions for open-ended answers, custom response formats, or analysis contextual metadata doesn't cover, such as sponsor logo exposure. A function specifies an Amazon Bedrock model and JSONata expressions that shape the request and response. You attach it to a feed and choose how frequently it runs. Contextual-metadata decisions configuration is included in the contextual metadata price. Functions are available at no additional charge on feeds with at lea
title: Customize AWS Elemental Inference with custom models, prompts, and decisions

summary: Today, AWS Security Hub adds installed software and resource usage as signals for resource criticality, which indicates how important a resource is to your business. Security Hub uses criticality to rank exposure findings, so that central security teams can prioritize the exposures that affect their most important resources. Security Hub already infers criticality from resource tags and names, but inconsistently tagged resources often have an Unknown criticality, which makes their exposures harder to prioritize. With installed software and resource usage as additional signals, more of your resources receive a meaningful criticality with no tagging or configuration required. For example, an EC2 instance that runs a database engine and serves steady traffic receives a higher criticality than an instance that runs only monitoring agents and sits idle. These signals are included with the Security Hub Essentials plan at no additional cost and require no new enablement. To learn more, see Resources in Security Hub in the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page . For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table .
title: AWS Security Hub now infers resource criticality from installed software and usage

summary: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports global authentication tokens for private registries. Previously, you needed to request a separate authentication token in each AWS Region where you push or pull container images. Now, you can request a single token from the AWS Sign-In CreateBearerToken API and use it across all ECR private registries in the same AWS partition. Teams that run proxy services to route container pulls across Regions, a common pattern for optimizing latency or availability, previously had to request, refresh, and coordinate a separate token for every Region behind the proxy. With global tokens, the proxy manages one token for all Regions in the AWS partition. Global tokens are valid for 12 hours by default, but can be configured to be as low as 5 minutes. These tokens work with the Docker CLI, and the Amazon ECR Docker Credential Helper. Existing regional authentication tokens continue to work as before. Global authentication tokens are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is supported. To learn more, see Private registry authentication in the Amazon ECR User Guide .
title: Amazon ECR now supports global authentication tokens for private registries

summary: AWS Partners can now expedite Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) deals, from qualification to incentive payout, with an end-to-end agentic workflow in AWS Transform. Partners can manage the full MAP lifecycle without leaving AWS Transform, including deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, migration planning and execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. Previously, Partners had to switch between separate systems for opportunity discovery, assessments, deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. This fragmentation, along with manual handoffs between steps, led to longer qualification cycles. Now, with the agentic MAP experience in AWS Transform, Partners connect their AWS Partner Central account and invite customers into the same engagement. Partners start by scoping customer environments with the built-in agentic discovery tool, or by importing data from RVTools or AWS-validated ISV tools listed in AWS Marketplace. AWS Transform then combines this discovery data with opportunity details from APN Customer Engagements (ACE) to automatically qualify Partner-initiated opportunities in a guided flow, so Partners get eligibility decisions sooner and close deals faster. As the migration progresses, MAP resource tags are applied automatically, and Partner cash and customer credits are disbursed based on actual usage data. Throughout, customers get shared, real-time visibility into migrat
title: AWS Transform now accelerates migration deals for Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) benefits

summary: Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8gn instances, powered by the latest-generation AWS Graviton4 processors, are available in the AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region. The C8gn instances provide up to 30% better compute performance than Graviton3-based Amazon EC2 C7gn instances. Amazon EC2 C8gn instances feature the latest 6th generation AWS Nitro Cards, and offer up to 600 Gbps network bandwidth, the highest network bandwidth among network optimized EC2 instances. Take advantage of the enhanced networking capabilities of C8gn to scale performance and throughput, while optimizing the cost of running network-intensive workloads such as network virtual appliances, data analytics, CPU-based artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) inference. For increased scalability, C8gn instances offer instance sizes up to 48xlarge, up to 384 GiB of memory, and up to 120 Gbps of bandwidth to Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS). C8gn instances support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on the 16xlarge, 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes, which enables lower latency and improved cluster performance for workloads deployed on tightly coupled clusters. C8gn instances are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon, N.California), Europe (Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London, Spain, Zurich, Milan, Paris), Asia Pacific (Singapore, Malaysia, Sydney, Thailand, Mumbai, Seoul, Melbourne, Jakarta, Hyderabad, Tokyo,
title: Amazon EC2 C8gn instances are now available in AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region

summary: Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8ine instances are available in the AWS Europe (Ireland) region. C8ine instances are powered by custom sixth generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors, available only on AWS. These instances feature the latest sixth generation AWS Nitro cards, delivering up to 43% higher performance compared to previous generation C6in instances. C8ine instances offer up to 2.5 times higher packet performance per vCPU versus prior generation network optimized instances, providing up to 2x higher network throughput for traffic going through Internet gateways compared to existing C6in network optimized instances. C8ine instances are designed for security and network virtual appliances, including virtual firewalls, load balancers, and Telco 5G UPF workloads. Amazon EC2 C8ine instances are available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland, Frankfurt) regions. C8ine instances are available via Savings Plans, On-Demand, and Spot instances. For more information, visit the Amazon EC2 C8i instance pages.
title: Amazon EC2 C8ine instances are now available in AWS Europe (Ireland) region

summary: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available with new features across Amazon EMR on EC2, Amazon EMR on EKS, and Amazon EMR Serverless. This release upgrades Apache Spark to 4.1.3, Apache Iceberg to 1.11.0, and Delta Lake to 4.2.0, and it is designated a Long Term Support (LTS) release. This release makes it easier to run secure, governed analytics at scale — you can now write to the same Delta Lake table on Amazon S3 from multiple clusters concurrently, refresh Iceberg materialized views incrementally, and propagate end-user identity from Spark jobs and interactive sessions all the way to AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 so access is authorized and audited as the original user. Amazon EMR 8.2 expands governance and performance across all three deployment options. New features include concurrent Delta Lake writes using Amazon S3 conditional writes (no DynamoDB log store required), and Lake Formation fine-grained access control (FGAC) now covers materialized views, governed user-defined functions, more Iceberg operations, and a broader set of Spark SQL features. The release also adds OpenLineage-based lineage capture to the AWS Glue Data Catalog and trusted identity propagation for steps and sessions. With EMR 8.2, data engineers can now precompute each pipeline stage as an Iceberg materialized view in SQL. Each materialized view refreshes only the changes instead of recomputing the entire source table across projections, inner joins, filters and SUM, COUNT aggregations. Specific to EMR on
title: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available

summary: Amazon EMR Serverless now offers the Apache Spark optimization agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations in seconds. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and plain-language reasoning behind each suggestion. The agent can analyze a single run or compare it against a known-good baseline to pinpoint what changed. You access it from the EMR Serverless console or through the SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server. The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen intent and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. The configurations the engine targets are the settings most commonly tuned across millions of Spark jobs running on AWS. When cost and performance trade off, the recommendation improves the metric you asked for while keeping degradation of the other within defined limits. The engine also evaluates a best practices checklist covering platform-level improvements such as upgrading to a newer Spark version or using Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the surface it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configura
title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless

summary: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so users can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets. Administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in. These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications. To get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. New stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stac
title: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications adds support for smart card redirection

summary: AWS Transform now supports AWS Outposts as a migration target. You can migrate workloads onto your Outposts from on-premises environments, another Outpost, or a different Availability Zone or Region. AWS Transform is a collaborative enterprise IT transformation service powered by agentic AI that accelerates cloud migration, application modernization, and continuous tech debt reduction. Run your migration with AI agents in AWS Transform for migrations, or use AWS Transform MGN , the rehost engine within AWS Transform, directly from its console. If you run workloads on Outposts for low latency, local data processing, or data residency, migrating them has meant manual effort or legacy tooling, often with a detour through the Region and an AMI copy. Now you choose subnets on the Outpost for your migration, and AWS Transform continuously replicates your source servers at the block level, directly from your source environment to the Outpost. You launch test instances before cutover and cut over with minimal downtime. Migration to Outposts is available in all AWS Transform for migrations target Regions and AWS Transform MGN Regions and requires Amazon EBS on the Outpost. If your Outpost has Amazon S3 on Outposts, you can keep snapshots on the Outpost for data residency or store them in the parent Region. Without it, snapshots are stored in the parent Region. To get started, see the AWS Transform documentation or visit the AWS Transform product page .
title: AWS Transform now supports migration to AWS Outposts

summary: AWS Transform now migrates F5 BIG-IP load balancer configurations to Elastic Load Balancing as part of network migration. Applications cut over with Application Load Balancers (ALB) and Network Load Balancers (NLB) already in place allowing you to adopt cloud-native load balancing during migration rather than after it. Moving to ALB and NLB has typically been a separate post-migration project because of time and cost. Teams rebuilt each F5 BIG-IP virtual server by hand, a slow and error-prone process that could break when traffic moved. AWS Transform compresses that timeline and enables the F5 to Elastic Load Balancing transition during migration, allowing you to run your cloud migration with network, load balancing, and compute moving as a coordinated unit. You can migrate F5 BIG-IP load balancers in every AWS Transform for migrations target Region . To get started, see the AWS Transform documentation , or visit the AWS Transform product page .
title: AWS Transform now provides F5 BIG-IP load balancer migration

summary: AWS Transform for migrations now includes Well-Architected reviews of target networks as it migrates and modernizes infrastructure to AWS. These recommendations, provided by the AWS Well-Architected Agent in public preview, are based on the latest best practices across security, reliability, and cost optimization pillars, and are applied directly to your target network, so you don't have to update the infrastructure after deployment on AWS. While migrating networks, design gaps typically surface after deployment, making fixes costly, requiring separate review and update cycles. For teams migrating large on-premises networks, this capability catches improvement opportunities early in the planning stage. AWS Well-Architected Agent provides recommendations, such as re-addressing spoke VPCs using non-RFC1918 addresses and governing CIDR allocation, and AWS Transform applies them to the network design. Post-deployment recommendations are documented for you as downloadable artifact from AWS Transform chat, so you can address them in your AWS accounts once your network is live. The capability is available in commercial AWS Regions . Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and included with paid Support plans. To get started, see AWS Transform for migrations. To learn more about AWS Well-Architected Agent, visit the product documentation .
title: AWS Transform now provides Well-Architected Agent reviews

summary: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports ingest pipelines, so you can clean, enrich, and vectorize documents inside your collection as they are indexed, without running separate preprocessing infrastructure. Teams building search, log analytics, and generative AI applications can replace data-prep code in Lambda functions or ETL jobs with transformations that apply consistently to every document, regardless of how it is ingested. You can use ingest pipelines to normalize and clean data with processors such as copy, date, dot_expander, join, lowercase, uppercase, remove, rename, set, and trim. For semantic and AI search, you can chunk long text with text_chunking and generate embeddings at ingest time with text_embedding, text_image_embedding, and sparse_encoding. The ml_inference processor calls any model you have connected and lets you map its input and output fields yourself. You create and manage pipelines with the familiar OpenSearch _ingest/pipeline APIs. You can test a pipeline against sample documents with the _simulate API before sending it live traffic, then apply it as an index's default pipeline or on individual indexing and bulk requests. Pipeline processing uses your collection's indexing OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs) and is billed the same way as other indexing activity. If you use a remote model with an ML processor, the model provider bills inference separately. Ingest pipelines are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is availabl
title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports ingest pipelines

summary: Amazon Cognito now supports authentication context class reference (ACR) and authentication methods reference (AMR), by adding ACR and AMR claims to access, ID, and refresh tokens. Your application can use the authentication level (ACR) to make authorization decisions, such as requiring additional factors for sensitive operations. It can also use completed methods (AMR), such as time-based one-time password (TOTP), for auditing and compliance. Amazon Cognito defines four authentication levels based on the factors a user completes, from password-only (level 1) to a password with a TOTP (level 4). Each token reflects the level achieved during sign-in, so your application can make authorization decisions based on how a user authenticated. If your application requires a stronger level, you can request a target level in your application's sign-in flow or through managed login, and Amazon Cognito issues new tokens once the user completes the required factors. You can also customize ACR level URIs for your user pool. For federated users from an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, Amazon Cognito maps the provider's ACR and AMR values to your levels. ACR and AMR token claims are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is offered. Every user pool includes ACR and AMR token claims, regardless of feature plan. Requesting a target authentication level and configuring custom ACR level URIs are available with the Essentials or Plus feature plan. To get started, configure ACR and AMR u
title: Amazon Cognito now supports authentication level and method token claims

summary: AWS Control Tower now lets you use an existing Amazon S3 bucket in your landing zone to store AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail logs. Previously, AWS Control Tower required you to use the Amazon S3 bucket it creates and manages for log storage. Now, customers who want full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure can consolidate centralized logs in an Amazon S3 bucket they already manage. You can use your own Amazon S3 bucket for both AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail, giving you full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure. You can switch between self-managed and AWS Control Tower managed buckets at any time, and your Amazon S3 buckets are preserved during landing zone updates, resets, and decommissioning. The bucket must be owned by an AWS account in your organization, be located in your AWS Control Tower home Region, and be preconfigured with the bucket policy that AWS Control Tower requires. This feature is supported in landing zone version 4.0 and later and is available in all commercial AWS Regions , the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud where AWS Control Tower is available. To learn more about configuring self-managed Amazon S3 bucket for your AWS Control Tower landing zone, visit the AWS Control Tower documentation .
title: AWS Control Tower now supports existing Amazon S3 bucket for log delivery

summary: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes for Lambda Event Functions (formerly Lambda functions). Customer-managed runtimes are a standalone resource type that fully decouples runtime management from function deployment. Platform teams gain centralized control over the runtime contents, updates, access, and lifecycle, including the ability to push updates to shared components without per-function redeployments. Application teams consume the runtime from their functions in the same way as a Lambda-managed runtime, preserving their familiar developer experience. Many organizations require every function to include approved components, such as SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring tools. Previously, sharing these through Lambda Layers or container images meant redeploying every function to pick up a change. With customer-managed runtimes, platform teams manage these components in a central runtime, packaged as OCI container images in Amazon ECR and compatible with existing Docker and CI/CD tooling. Functions pick up updates automatically as Lambda recycles execution environments, so there's no need to redeploy each function or coordinate rollouts. Updates can be scheduled and staged to match change control policies, with centralized health metrics and rapid rollback. With this launch, the existing custom runtimes feature is renamed "bring your own language." AWS Lambda customer-managed runtimes is now generally available in all commercial AWS Regions. There is n
title: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes, giving platform teams centralized control over runtime contents and updates

summary: Amazon RDS now initializes storage volumes faster when you perform a point-in-time restore (PITR), create a read replica, or convert a Single-AZ instance to Multi-AZ. Each of these operations creates storage volumes from a snapshot, and the data blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3 before you can access them. With fast storage volume initialization, you get a fully performant DB instance in a predictable amount of time. Previously, the initialization rate varied with your workload and with which blocks were accessed. As there was no dedicated bandwidth, so you could see increased I/O latency and had no way to tell when an instance would reach full performance. Now, each database instance is initialized at up to 4 TiB per hour, across every gp3 and io2 storage volume attached to the instance. If concurrent initialization across your account exceeds the available bandwidth, the remaining blocks initialize on a best-effort basis, so initialization is never slower than today. Your DB instance stays available and usable while initialization runs. Fast storage volume initialization is enabled by default and no action is required. To follow progress, use the StorageOperationStatus and StorageOperationPercentProgress fields in the Amazon RDS console, the DescribeDBInstances API, the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. This capability is available at no additional cost for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, RDS for Db2, RDS for Microsoft SQL Server, and RDS
title: Amazon RDS now supports fast storage volume initialization

summary: Starting today, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for MySQL supports MySQL minor version 8.4.13, the latest minor released by community MySQL. We recommend upgrading to the newer minor versions to accept fixes for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in prior versions of MySQL and to benefit from bug fixes, performance improvements, and new functionality added by the MySQL community. Learn more about the enhancements in RDS for MySQL 8.4.13 in the Amazon RDS user guide and MySQL 8.4.13 release notes. You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate upgrades across your instances in phases, validating on lower-priority environments before upgrading your most critical ones. You can perform minor version upgrades in-place or via snapshot restore. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon RDS User Guide . This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for MySQL is available. Amazon RDS for MySQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale MySQL deployments in the cloud. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).
title: Amazon RDS for MySQL supports MySQL minor version 8.4.13

summary: Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery (PITR), so you can restore the user data in a user pool to an earlier time. Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices. Previously, you had to build and maintain your own export and restore process, and restored users received new identifiers and had to reset their passwords. With PITR, you choose a recovery point, preview how many users, groups, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys the recovery will create, update, or delete, and then start or cancel the recovery. Recovered users keep their identifiers, passwords, MFA settings, and passkeys, so they can sign in without resetting their credentials. For example, if a script deletes or modifies users by mistake, you can restore the user data to the moment before it ran. PITR is enabled automatically for user pools on the Essentials and Plus feature plans at no additional charge. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. You can initiate and manage a recovery using the AWS Management Console, the Amazon Cognito API, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. PITR is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Point-in-time recovery in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.
title: Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery

summary: Amazon CloudFront (CF) now supports WebSocket and gRPC traffic to application origins in AWS regions, with mutual TLS authentication between CF and the application origin (origin mTLS). Customers can now use TLS certificates to authenticate requests from CloudFront while setting up WebSocket or gRPC connections to their origins. Origin mTLS protects internet facing applications that need persistent, bidirectional or streaming connections, such as chat platforms, collaborative editing tools or live dashboards from unauthenticated requests. Previously, customers serving WebSocket or gRPC traffic through CloudFront had to use shared secrets or IP allow-lists to identify requests originating from CloudFront. This was operationally complex and did not provide strong authentication. With Origin mTLS, customers can use one TLS based authentication for HTTP, WebSocket and gRPC traffic to an application origin. This works with application origins within AWS such as Application Load Balancer and API Gateway, on-premises origins, and origins hosted outside AWS. There is no additional charge for origin mTLS, and it is available with pay-as-you-go pricing and in the Business and Premium flat-rate pricing plans. To learn more, visit the CloudFront origin mutual TLS documentation .
title: Amazon CloudFront Announces WebSocket and gRPC Support for Origin Mutual TLS

summary: AWS Lambda now supports GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances using EC2 G-series instances . You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads including AI inference, media processing, 3D rendering, scientific computing, and financial simulations on Lambda without managing GPU drivers, frameworks, or scaling. Lambda runs multiple invocations concurrently in each execution environment and scales responsively based on GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency to keep your GPUs busy and reduce costs. GPU-accelerated functions integrate with the same 200+ AWS event sources as other Event Functions, so you can add GPU compute as another step in your serverless application. Running GPU workloads today requires customers to provision hardware, manage driver and framework dependencies, and build custom scaling and capacity management. With this launch, you can go from code to a running GPU workload in minutes. Lambda provides GPU base images preconfigured with frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, and PyTorch. You can run workloads with large artifacts using container images and NVMe ephemeral storage of up to 32 GB each. To reduce startup time, Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading and streaming artifacts directly from Amazon S3. For resilience, you can select G-series instance types from multiple generations in the allowed instance types for your capacity provider. Lambda provisions instances from the newest generation that meets your function requiremen
title: AWS Lambda adds support for GPU instances on Lambda Managed Instances

summary: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo. You can now serve models that are too large for a single instance, and keep token generation fast when prompts are long. You don't have to build or operate distributed serving infrastructure yourself. HyperPod manages Dynamo for you through the Inference Operator add-on. As models grow, two problems limit inference. A large model can need more GPU memory than one instance has. Long prompts also slow token generation, because the prefill and decode stages compete for the same GPUs. Until now, customers had to build and run their own distributed serving stack to work around both. With Dynamo on HyperPod, you can run a single model across multiple nodes. You can also split prefill and decode into separate GPU pools that scale independently, so a long prompt no longer stalls token generation for other requests. KV-aware routing sends each request to a worker that already holds the relevant cached context. This cuts recomputation and raises throughput. HyperPod runs the underlying infrastructure: EFA networking, GPU capacity management, node replacement, endpoint registration, autoscaling, and observability. Your team can spend its time on the models instead. To get started, bring your existing Dynamo manifests if you want full control. You can also use a simplified configuration that HyperPod translates into the underlying infrastructure. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with NVIDIA Dynamo support is available in
title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo for disaggregated and multi-node inference

summary: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion service now supports time series collections in the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as a pipeline destination. You can stream logs, metrics, traces and event data into time series collections with fully managed pipelines. You don't have to run your own collectors or write custom ingestion code. OpenSearch Ingestion delivers data from the sources you already use, including OpenTelemetry, Amazon S3, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK, Amazon DynamoDB, and HTTP endpoints. Before indexing, pipelines can filter, enrich, transform, and route data with built-in processors. For example, you can parse and normalize log fields, mask sensitive data, or split a stream into separate indexes. Pipelines scale automatically with your workload. Time series collections add a lower-cost warm storage tier and built-in alerting and anomaly detection. Together they give you an observability pipeline from collection to analysis with no clusters to manage. To get started, create a pipeline in the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, through the AWS CLI, or with AWS CloudFormation, and choose a time series collection as the sink. OpenSearch Ingestion is billed in Ingestion OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs), separately from your collection. For details, see Amazon OpenSearch Service pricing . This capability is available in all AWS Regions where both Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion and the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless are available . To get s
title: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion Service now supports next-generation time series collections

summary: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density per node on EKS-orchestrated clusters, allowing you to get more out of every instance. This leaves more room for your applications alongside system DaemonSets for monitoring, logging, and security, and helps increase GPU, CPU and memory utilization on nodes, allowing you to run the same work using fewer instances. As you schedule more pods, the Amazon VPC CNI automatically adds network capacity to the node. Autoscaling with Karpenter also supports the higher pod capacity, so new nodes take on more pods as your cluster scales out. Here are a few examples of workloads that benefit from higher pod density: Model inference - Serve more model replicas or more models from each GPU instance, including on smaller types such as ml.g5 and ml.g6. Interactive development - Host more notebooks, IDEs, and data science environments on each node. GPU partitioning - Use all the Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) slices on instances such as ml.p5en.48xlarge, where each slice runs its own pod. Operators and Controllers - Run operators, controllers, and observability agents on CPU nodes alongside your workloads, without crowding them out. This feature is available for HyperPod EKS-orchestrated clusters in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To get started, update your cluster's IAM permissions, cluster software, and Amazon VPC CNI add-on. To learn more, please check the documentation .
title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density on EKS-orchestrated clusters

summary: You can now replicate data in Amazon S3 buckets with fewer replication rules using two new S3 Replication capabilities, exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution. Buckets that many tenants or applications share often need many rules to skip certain data or to match encryption keys in each AWS Region. With these capabilities, customers who manage multi-tenant and shared buckets can replace many replication rules with a single rule. With exclusions, you can replicate an entire bucket while skipping specific prefixes or tagged objects, such as logs or experimental data. With Multi-Region key resolution, S3 Replication encrypts each replica with the matching AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Multi-Region key in the destination Region, so replicas meet the same encryption requirements as their source objects. For example, a bucket that stores data for hundreds of tenants, each with its own Multi-Region key, can replicate with a single rule, including tenants you add later. Exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution are optional and available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions. To get started, use the AWS SDKs, AWS CLI, S3 API, or S3 console. To learn more, visit the S3 Replication product page and Replicating objects within and across Regions in the S3 User Guide.
title: Amazon S3 Replication adds exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution

summary: Deploying and using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) account access manager is now even easier: you can use AWS managed policies to enable and administer it; you can include it in your infrastructure-as-code (IaC) configurations; and its role assignments are integrated in a growing number of third-party identity and entitlement management solutions. Administering workforce access with account access manager requires permissions across several services, including AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS Organizations, AWS KMS, and AWS IAM. Previously, defining administrative access required hand-assembling multi-service IAM policies. The new AWS managed policies enable faster ramp up with broadly scoped job-aligned permissions for: 1/ Full administrator (AWSAccountAccessManagerAdministrator) - used to enable and manage account access manager in the AWS organization management account and to map users/groups to IAM roles; 2/ Entitlement Manager (AWSAccountAccessManagerEntitlementManager) - used to assign and remove user access without the ability to change service configuration; and 3/ ReadOnly (AWSAccountAccessManagerReadOnlyAccess) - used by auditors and compliance reviewers for visibility into user access. Account access manager streamlines assignment of IAM roles to workforce users and groups in IAM Identity Center, bringing together access management flexibility, user awareness, and a single point of federation. You can include account access manager in your IaC configurations
title: AWS IAM account access manager is now even easier to deploy and use

summary: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now offers fully managed distributed KV caching, a new capability that reduces self-hosted large language model (LLM) inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Customers who self-host LLMs pay for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can't hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. GPUs can fetch cached KV state in milliseconds to serve more requests and respond faster. Distributed KV caching runs on cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes in the same Availability Zone as the GPU fleet and connects to GPUs through Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). Distributed KV caching works with open-weight, fine-tuned, and custom models, whether they use full, sparse, hybrid, or other attention designs. You can add distributed KV caching to the inference engines you already use, including vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, through the LMCache connector with a configuration change. You can also use the open-source KVTrace tool to estimate the cost and latency reductions on your own application traffic before deploying anything, at no charge. Distributed KV caching is available today on ElastiCache for Valkey in 13 AWS Regions across the US, Europe, and Asia Pacific. To get started, create a cl
title: Amazon ElastiCache now supports distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLM inference

summary: Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitoring now allows you to monitor the health of the AWS network paths that your workloads take by using performance monitors. Performance monitors provide near real-time visibility into whether the AWS network is healthy for your workloads, without installing any software. Performance monitors report per-path metrics such as latency, a network impact score that shows network health, and traffic volume across all flows in your VPCs. You simply select the VPCs you want to monitor, and metrics are available within minutes. Using telemetry AWS already collects, with no additional services to enable, performance monitors determine the paths your traffic takes, within and across Availability Zones, across AWS Regions, and to AWS services, for TCP, UDP, and ICMP traffic. They then score each path by comparing it with its own recent history and with all other paths AWS measures at the same time. For example, a path that suddenly degrades, or degrades with many other paths during an AWS network event, scores high. Metrics publish to Amazon CloudWatch for dashboards and alarms, and AWS Organizations integration lets you monitor VPCs across accounts and Regions.
