Now, teams can name a target role in the SecretProviderClass, and the provider assumes that role to fetch the secrets. With AssumeRole support, customers managing hundreds of AWS accounts and thousands of services can simplify cross-account secret access. A single trust policy on one target role replaces resource policies on each secret. Secrets encrypted with the AWS managed key (aws/secretsmanager) and SSM parameters become readable across accounts. The target account sees workload-specific session names in CloudTrail events for better attribution. This feature works with both IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) and EKS Pod Identity on initial mount and rotation, and supports failover regions. AssumeRole support is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EKS and the AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider are available. To learn more, see the Assume an IAM role to retrieve secrets with the ASCP documentation.
title: AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider now supports AssumeRole for cross-account secret access

summary: AWS Agent Registry now offers public naming capabilities, making it easy to attach verified domain names to your agents and AI tools. Developers and network admins can perform domain verification checks to prove domain ownership, then associate the verified domain names with their agents to promote them for public visibility beyond their registry and AWS account. Previously, developers had to manually configure how agents discover and connect to one another, which added complexity to building multi-agent systems. With this launch, since the public agent records are anchored to a verified domain identity, you can confirm the source of an agent before connecting to it. Once published, agent records are searchable by any AWS-authenticated user using both semantic and lexical search. This capability is available at no additional charge at this time in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available. To learn more about naming and public discovery, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation .
title: AWS Agent Registry now offers naming and public discovery capabilities

summary: AWS Agent Registry now supports registering WebBotAuth (WBA) bots as a new record type, making it easier to verify legitimate bot traffic through a standardized protocol. Previously, organizations lacked a standardized way to distinguish verified bots from malicious traffic. Now, bots can prove domain ownership through WebBotAuth, and you can integrate this verification with AWS WAF Bot Control to write rules that combine verification status and bot identity. This new capability gives content providers and application developers fine-grained control over which bots can access your resources. You can enhance security and improve traffic management by distinguishing legitimate bots from malicious actors. For example, you can allow WBA verified search engine crawlers while blocking unverified traffic or create custom access policies based on both bot identity and verification status. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation and the AWS WAF Bot Control documentation .
title: AWS Agent Registry now supports WebBotAuth bot registration

summary: AWS Device Farm , a service for testing mobile and web apps, now provides Test Insights for Appium, Espresso, and XCUITest runs across multiple devices. Test Insights helps you and AI agents understand the health of your tests and resolve failures faster by providing a detailed breakdown of your test suite by device and by test. With Test Insights, Device Farm's existing APIs now return enhanced test metadata, failure root cause with stack trace, a video for each test, start and stop times, median and average times spent on each device and test, and test counts by result. With this data in one place, your agents spend less time and fewer tokens looking for the root cause of test failures, and the AWS Device Farm troubleshooting skill uses it to help diagnose failed runs and suggest fixes. Test Insights is available alongside any default and custom test reports you generate, at no additional cost. Test Insights is included in all AWS Regions where Device Farm is available. To get started, see Test Insights in the AWS Device Farm Developer Guide.
title: Announcing Test Insights for AWS Device Farm

summary: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) IP Address Manager (IPAM) policies now support AWS Network Firewall automated internet firewall and AWS Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs. You can centrally configure IPAM policies across AWS accounts and AWS Regions to allocate public IPv4 addresses to these resources from specific IPAM pools, such as Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP) addresses or Amazon-provided contiguous IPv4 blocks. This enables a stronger security posture, simplifies network and security operations, and can reduce public IPv4 costs when you use BYOIP. Many customers allowlist the public IPs of their AWS resources in network access control lists (ACLs) and firewalls. Previously, keeping these resources on allowlisted addresses depended on each application team. With this launch, you can define allocation rules for them alongside existing resource types, so security teams can add IP-based filters with confidence that these resources draw addresses from approved ranges. For Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs, this covers the public IPv4 addresses used for outbound traffic through Lambda Network Connectors. If a pool runs out of addresses, resources fall back to Amazon-provided addresses. You can also share allocated ranges with partners through IPAM integration with AWS prefix lists. The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions, in both the Free Tier and Advanced Tier of VPC IPAM. To learn more, see the IPAM policies documentation page and the IPAM documentation . title: Amazon VPC IPAM policies now support automated internet firewall and AWS Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs

summary: Amazon Route 53 now supports Availability Zone (AZ) affinity routing, which routes DNS queries from your VPCs to resources in the same AZ as the client that sends the query. This helps you keep traffic within the same AZ as the client, reducing latency and improving application performance. Until now, customers who wanted lower latency used other routing policies, such as latency-based or geoproximity routing. With this launch, DNS queries from your clients are answered with resources in the same AZ. This keeps traffic within the AZ and gives your clients faster responses. If there's no record for the client's AZ, Route 53 falls back to a record for a less specific location: the Zone Group, then the AWS Region, and then Global, in the same order. To get started, create AZ-affinity records and choose a location type for each: Availability Zone, Zone Group, Region, or Global. For Availability Zone records, specify the AZ ID, such as use1-az1. You can associate a health check with any AZ-affinity record, whether it's for an AZ, a Zone Group, or a Region. If the endpoint is unhealthy, Route 53 answers with the record for the next location. You can use AZ-affinity routing for records in both public and private hosted zones. The Global record answers queries that don't come from your VPCs, such as queries from the internet. You can create AZ-affinity records with the Route 53 console, API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation. AZ-affinity routing is available in all AWS commer
title: Amazon Route 53 now supports Availability Zone (AZ) affinity routing

summary: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) Custom for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) and General Distribution Release (GDR) updates for Microsoft SQL Server. This release includes support for SQL Server 2019 CU32 + GDR KB5128494 (RDS version 15.00.4500.2.v1) and SQL Server 2022 CU27 + GDR KB5126934 (RDS version 16.00.4305.5.v1). For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5128494 and KB5126934. You can upgrade your Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server instances to apply these recommended updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. To learn more about upgrading your database instances, see Amazon RDS Custom User Guide .
title: Amazon RDS Custom now supports the latest Cumulative Update and GDR updates for Microsoft SQL Server

summary: Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies, giving you fine-grained control over which database objects are audited. You can create custom audit policies and attach them to specific tables, users, groups, roles, and authorities in your RDS for Db2 databases. With object-level audit policies, you can focus on auditing the objects that matter most — for example, a single table that contains sensitive data or a specific user — without generating audit records for your entire database. Object-level audit policies complement the existing database-level audit logging in Amazon RDS for Db2. You can use both at the same time, and they operate independently. Amazon RDS provides stored procedures to create, modify, attach, detach, and drop object-level audit policies. Audit records are uploaded to the same Amazon S3 bucket that you configured for Db2 audit logging. Object-level audit policies for Amazon RDS for Db2 are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is available. To get started see the Amazon RDS User Guide.
title: Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies

summary: ​​Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports four new time zones, America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton, America/Inuvik, and America/Winnipeg, that reflect the updated local time rules for British Columbia, Alberta, the Northwest Territories, and Manitoba in Canada. As of November 1, 2026, these provinces and territories observe permanent daylight saving time and no longer set their clocks back by an hour.​ ​Data stored in UTC is unaffected, but values based on the instance's local time, such as CURRENT TIMESTAMP, CURRENT DATE, default timestamp columns, scheduled jobs, and business-day batch logic, can be affected. With these new time zones, you can keep local time values accurate for workloads operating in these regions. ​​You can select the new time zones when you create a new RDS for Db2 instance. To change the time zone of an existing instance, contact AWS Support, as modifying the time zone of an existing instance is not supported through the AWS CLI, API, or SDK. If your instances serve workloads in these regions, we recommend reviewing them and updating your time zone configuration to avoid incorrect local times in your applications.​ ​The new time zones are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered. To learn more and see the full list of supported time zones, visit the Amazon RDS for Db2 time zone documentation .​
title: Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports new Canadian time zones

summary: ​​Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Db2 now supports renaming databases in place. You can rename a database on your DB instance by calling the new rdsadmin.rename_database stored procedure. Previously, renaming a database required you to back it up and restore it under a new name. With rename, the database keeps its data in place, so it's faster than backing up and restoring the database.​ ​​Database rename simplifies workflows such as replacing a database with a restored copy. For example, after you restore a copy of a database from a backup, you can rename the original database, and then give its name to the restored copy, without changing your application connection strings. Database rename runs as a background task that you can monitor with rdsadmin.get_task_status.​ ​​Database rename is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered. To get started, see the Amazon RDS User Guide .​​
title: ​​​Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports renaming databases​

summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances now support Amazon EC2 G7 instances, powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. G7 instances give agents that do 3D rendering or model inference another GPU option, alongside families such as G6e and G7e. To use G7, add G7 instance types, from g7.2xlarge to g7.48xlarge, to the allowed instance types of your capacity provider. AgentCore installs the NVIDIA drivers on the instance, so standard container images run GPU workloads without bundling drivers. For example, an agent can render 3D scenes or run a vision model on its own GPU, in sessions of up to 14 days . G7 instances on runtime instances are available in select AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), and Asia Pacific (Sydney). You are charged for managing the provisioned compute, in addition to your Amazon EC2 costs. To get started, see the following resources: Use GPU instance types in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide AgentCore pricing
title: AgentCore runtime instances now support Amazon EC2 G7 instances

summary: AWS CloudFormation now supports up to 300,000 stacks in each AWS account and Region by default (previously 2,000), which enables you to add stacks as your workloads grow without requesting a quota increase. CloudFormation manages related AWS resources as a stack that you create, update, and delete as one unit. Teams that deploy a separate stack for each customer, environment, or developer can now scale those patterns within a single account. A higher default quota allows you to keep growing workloads in the accounts where they already run. Previously, accounts that needed more than 2,000 stacks in a Region requested a quota increase through Service Quotas. Now, the default quota covers these workloads without a request. For example, a software provider that deploys one stack for each customer can grow from 2,000 to 300,000 customer stacks in one account and Region. Existing stacks work without changes. The higher quota applies to stacks you create in the CloudFormation console or with the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. To view your stacks per account quota, open the Service Quotas console. For more information, see CloudFormation quotas in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide. The increased quota is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where AWS CloudFormation is supported. For Region availability, see the AWS Region table .
title: AWS CloudFormation increases the default stacks per account quota to 300,000

summary: AWS Lambda now supports creating serverless applications using Python 3.15. Python 3.15 is generally available for Lambda Event Functions and is available in public preview for Lambda Web Functions. This is the first Python runtime for Web Functions, which until now only supported Node.js. With this launch, developers can also build web applications and APIs on Web Functions in Python. Developers can use Python 3.15 as both a managed runtime and a base container image (Event Functions only), and AWS will automatically apply updates to the managed runtime and base image as they become available. Python 3.15 is the latest release of Python. With this release, you can use the latest Python 3.15 features in Lambda, such as explicit lazy imports that can reduce function startup time, the new frozendict and sentinel built-in types, and an improved JIT compiler. You can use Python 3.15 with Powertools for AWS Lambda (Python) , a developer toolkit to implement serverless best practices and increase developer velocity. You can also use the full range of AWS deployment tools, including the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM), AWS CDK, and AWS CloudFormation to deploy and manage serverless applications written in Python 3.15. The Python 3.15 runtime is available in all Regions where Event Functions and Web Functions are available. For more information about Python 3.15 in Lambda, refer to the Event Function and Web Function documentation. For more informa
title: AWS Lambda adds support for Python 3.15

summary: Amazon S3 now supports at least 11,000 GET/HEAD requests per second, up from 5,500, for general purpose buckets. With this higher request rate, you can retrieve data faster for read-intensive workloads such as machine learning training, data analytics, and data transfers. To maximize throughput, distribute your requests across multiple prefixes so that S3 can scale each one independently. This increase applies automatically to your existing read requests in all AWS Regions, with no changes required to your applications and at no additional charge beyond standard S3 request pricing. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 user guide and the S3 product page .
title: Amazon S3 increases the read request rate for general purpose buckets by up to 2x

summary: AWS Lambda now supports creating serverless applications using Node.js 26, for both Lambda Web Functions and Lambda Event Functions. Developers can use Node.js 26 as both a managed runtime and a base container image (Event Functions only). AWS will automatically apply updates to the managed runtime and base image as they become available. Node.js 26 is the latest long-term support release of Node.js and is expected to be supported for security and bug fixes until April 2029. With this release, you can use the latest Node.js 26 features in Lambda, such as the Temporal API for easier date, time, and time zone handling, and enhancements to the Fetch API. You can use Node.js 26 with Powertools for AWS Lambda (TypeScript) , a developer toolkit to implement serverless best practices and increase developer velocity. You can also use the full range of AWS deployment tools, including the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM), AWS CDK, and AWS CloudFormation to deploy and manage serverless applications written in Node.js 26. The Node.js 26 runtime is available in all Regions where Web Functions and Event Functions are available. For more information about Node.js 26 in Lambda, refer to the Web Function and Event Function documentation. For more information about AWS Lambda, visit our product page .
title: AWS Lambda adds support for Node.js 26

summary: AWS Lambda MicroVMs is now available in 7 additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Canada (Central), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), South America (São Paulo), and US West (N. California). With this launch, you can use Lambda MicroVMs in a total of 21 AWS Regions. Lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume speeds, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code. The service enables secure, stateful, and responsive code execution for applications including AI coding assistants, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners. With today's launch, developers can run Lambda MicroVMs closer to their end-users in 7 additional Regions, helping meet latency and data residency requirements. To get started, create a MicroVM image from your Dockerfile, then launch MicroVMs from that image. Give each user or job their own MicroVM with a dedicated HTTPS URL that supports popular connectivity protocols such as HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSockets. You can use MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred Agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS . To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide . For information on pricing, see Lambda MicroVMs pricing . Visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page for the latest region availability.
title: AWS Lambda MicroVMs is now available in 7 additional AWS regions

summary: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region, along with Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus collector. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed, Prometheus-compatible monitoring service, that helps you monitor and alert on operational metrics at scale. Customers in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can now run Prometheus-compatible monitoring workloads in-region, which lowers latency for local workloads and keeps metric data within the region. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus collector is a fully managed, agentless collector. It discovers and collects Prometheus metrics from your container workloads, so you do not need to run collection agents yourself. The collector sends metrics to an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus workspace, where you query and analyze them. A workspace is a logical space for storing and querying Prometheus metrics. For the full list of regions where Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is available, see the AWS Regional Services List . For pricing, see the Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus pricing page . To learn more, see the Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus user guide and the product page.
title: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region

summary: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus now supports up to 2 billion active metric time series and up to 300,000 total recording and alerting rules per workspace. Customers can also create multiple workspaces per account. This lets them store and analyze billions of Prometheus metrics across their organization. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a fully managed, Prometheus-compatible monitoring service. It helps you monitor and alert on operational metrics at scale. It scales ingestion and storage automatically for high-cardinality workloads across containerized, serverless and hybrid environments. To get started, create an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus workspace. To raise your active series or rules limits, file a service limit increase request in AWS Support Center or AWS Service Quotas. To learn more, see the Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus user guide and the product page.
title: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus supports 2B active metrics and 300K rules per workspace

summary: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) now extends Action Logs to include tasks, container instances, clusters, and capacity providers, so you can see why your tasks failed or why your clusters didn't scale as desired. Action Logs provide detailed, timestamped records of the actions Amazon ECS performs on your behalf, and until now covered service deployments and managed daemon updates. With the expanded coverage, you can diagnose task failures and scaling issues yourself, and resolve them faster than before, without contacting AWS support. If you use Action Logs already, you receive the new events automatically with no configuration changes. When a task fails to start, Action Logs show the reason. Examples include image pull failures, missing permissions for Amazon EBS volumes, or lack of available IP addresses in the subnet. When a running task stops, you can see the container exit code and the health check that triggered the stop. For cluster infrastructure, Action Logs record container instance registration and draining, Amazon EC2 instances that fail to register with a cluster, capacity provider changes, and managed scaling actions, including when an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group reaches its maximum size. Each log entry includes the event name, log level (INFO, WARN, or ERROR), relevant resource ARNs, and a status reason. Action Logs is available in AWS Regions, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions . You can opt in at the cluster level through the Amazon ECS co
title: Amazon ECS Action Logs now cover tasks, container instances, and capacity providers

summary: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) now supports Apache Kafka version 4.2 on Standard brokers. A key highlight of this release is Queues for Kafka, which is now production ready. With Queues, multiple consumers can process messages from the same topic partitions, which improves parallelism and throughput for workloads that need point-to-point message delivery. This release also includes Eligible Leader Replicas (ELR) enhancements that improve leader election correctness and strengthen availability. The new consumer rebalance protocol makes consumer group rebalances smoother and faster. The new Streams Rebalance Protocol extends broker-side coordination to Kafka Streams applications so tasks get assigned more efficiently. For the full list of improvements and bug fixes, see the Apache Kafka 4.2 release notes . To start using Apache Kafka 4.2 on Amazon MSK, select version 4.2.x when creating a new cluster with the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. You can also upgrade existing MSK provisioned clusters with an in-place rolling update. Amazon MSK orchestrates broker restarts to maintain availability and protect your data during the upgrade. Kafka version 4.2 support is available today in all AWS regions where Amazon MSK Standard brokers is offered. To learn how to get started, see the Amazon MSK Developer Guide .
title: Amazon MSK Standard Brokers adds support for Apache Kafka version 4.2

summary: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports up to 40 KB of filterable metadata per vector, up from 2 KB. You can attach and filter on more attributes per vector, such as category, permissions, timestamps, and descriptive tags, so your retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications can narrow results by more of the fields that matter to them. S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale. With this launch, indexes in new vector buckets support the higher limit by default, with no change to how you write vectors with PutVectors or run filtered queries with QueryVectors. To use the higher limit on an existing index, update it in place to enhanced index mode with the UpdateIndexMode API. The higher filterable metadata limit is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation .
title: Amazon S3 Vectors raises the filterable metadata limit to 40 KB per vector

summary: AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue event source mappings (ESMs) in provisioned mode , up from 10 messages previously. With larger batches, you can process high-volume, ordered workloads such as financial transactions, order processing, and inventory updates with fewer invocations and higher throughput. Lambda continues to preserve message ordering within each message group. Customers use SQS FIFO queues with Lambda to build event-driven applications that need strict message ordering and deduplication. With provisioned mode for SQS ESMs, you can use throughput controls to set a minimum and maximum number of event pollers to meet strict performance requirements. Previously, provisioned mode customers who needed higher throughput for SQS FIFO queues were limited by the maximum batch size of 10 messages. This required them to scale out invocations or add custom buffering logic, which added operational overhead and cost. With this launch, you can set a batch size of up to 10,000 messages and a batching window of up to 300 seconds for FIFO queues, so you can process large volumes of ordered messages in fewer invocations without re-architecting your applications. This feature is available for SQS FIFO ESMs in provisioned mode in all AWS commercial Regions. You can configure the batch size and the batching window when you create new ESMs or update existing ESMs by using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS
title: AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon SQS FIFO queues

summary: AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions in AWS Trusted Advisor . These recommendations identify on-demand functions where moving to Lambda Managed Instances (LMI) is estimated to reduce costs, and provide configuration guidance for running on LMI. With these recommendations, you can lower your Lambda costs by focusing your efforts on the functions with the greatest estimated savings. LMI lets you run Lambda functions on Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With LMI, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing options such as Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, without managing infrastructure. Previously, to determine whether a function was a good fit for LMI, you had to analyze its invocation patterns, estimate LMI costs, and select the right instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio yourself. This manual process added overhead and delayed savings. With this launch, Lambda automatically analyzes the invocation patterns, duration, and resource utilization of your high-volume Event Functions and recommends those where LMI is estimated to reduce costs. Estimates are based on a simulation of each function's invocation patterns, using public Lambda pricing and Amazon EC2 On-Demand pricing. Each recommendation includes the function ARN, the recommended EC2 instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio, the estimated current cost, the estimated LMI cost, and the
title: AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions

summary: Builders using the new AWS experience on the Paid plan can now receive spend limit alerts by text message (SMS), alongside existing email notifications. A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost for a project. Notifications are sent as a project approaches its limit, and when a project reaches its limit, AWS automatically pauses it. SMS gives builders a second way to stay informed about their project costs. Email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused. SMS alerts close this gap with a text message when a project's actual costs reach 90% of its spend limit, so builders have time to act, such as raising the limit or stopping resources they don't need. To turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits. Text alerts are only sent to verified numbers, and you can opt out at any time. SMS alerts for spend limits are available at no additional charge for US phone numbers, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa. To learn more, see Create a spend limit in AWS Settings , the AWS Account Management Reference Guide , or Get started with AWS .
title: Spend limits in the new AWS experience now support SMS alerts

summary: AWS Partner Central Agents now help AWS Partners create and manage AWS Partner Central and AWS Marketplace support cases in one place. The agents are available 24/7 and draw on Partner Central account details and authoritative, partner-specific knowledge from AWS to resolve most inquiries instantly. If a inquiry needs a support engineer, the agents will gather details and create a case. This reduces the time partners spend looking for help, and gives support teams the context they need to resolve cases faster. Partners can handle a case from start to finish in one chat, with the full record in AWS Support Center. To create a case, partners can start describing their issue to AWS Partner Central Agents or use the prompt "get support." The agents gather additional details necessary to resolve the case, set the category, and draft the description. Partners review and submit the case, and the agents route the case to the right support team. In the same chat, partners can view case communications, track progress, post replies, and add attachments. With this launch, Partner Central and AWS Marketplace cases also move to AWS Support Center. There, partners can view the full case history and translate support correspondence into Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. The new support experience is available today to all AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers in the AWS Partner Central console and through the AWS Partner Central Agents MCP server. With th
title: AWS Partner Central Agents now help partners create and manage Partner Central and Marketplace support cases

summary: Today, Amazon CloudWatch announces telemetry filtering for the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, so you can stop paying to ingest telemetry you don't use. You can now set cluster-wide include and exclude lists for namespaces, metric names, and pod and node labels. Exclude the non-production namespaces you don't monitor, drop high-cardinality metrics by name, and keep only the labels you group by rather than every label on every resource. Because ingestion is billed per GB, collecting less lowers what you pay, and you can adjust filters with a single add-on configuration update as your clusters change. Telemetry filtering is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry sent through the add-on is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing . To get started, see Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide .
title: Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on now supports telemetry filtering

summary: Amazon Transcribe now offers a synchronous transcription API, TranscribeAudio . Send a complete audio file in a single request and get the full transcript back in the same response. There is no job to start, no status to poll, no connection to manage. The transcripts are as accurate as Amazon Transcribe batch transcription, so you can add fast, accurate speech-to-text to interactive applications such as voice assistants, agent-assist tools and on-demand "transcribe this clip" features. The synchronous API supports the Amazon Transcribe features you already use, including: Word-level timestamps and smart formatting for numbers, dates, currency and phone numbers Automatic language identification Speaker diarization, and channel identification for up to two channels Custom vocabulary and vocabulary filtering, which you can provide directly in the request with no setup step PII redaction Send audio inline (up to 25 MB) or from Amazon S3 (up to 500 MB), 0.5 seconds to 1 hour long, in WAV, MP3, FLAC, M4A, MP4, Ogg, WebM or AMR format. The transcript comes back in the response, or Transcribe can write it to an S3 location you choose. Pricing is $0.0070 per minute of audio, billed per second, with speaker diarization, language identification, custom vocabulary and channel identification included. Two-channel audio is billed once on file duration. PII redaction is available as an add-on. Supports English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Korean and Chinese (Simp
title: Amazon Transcribe announces a synchronous transcription API

summary: Amazon DynamoDB vector search inline filters now support range comparisons, value lists, and logical operators in addition to the equality operator, so you can narrow a vector search to exactly the items you want. You can now filter on numeric ranges such as price, rating, or publish date, match an attribute against a list of values, check whether an attribute exists, and combine conditions with OR and NOT. Amazon DynamoDB vector indexes store vector embeddings alongside your operational data, and the SearchVectors API returns the items whose embeddings are most similar to your query vector. The search condition expression in a SearchVectors request now accepts the comparison operators <, <=, >, >=, and BETWEEN on Number attributes, the IN operator, the attribute_exists and attribute_not_exists functions, and the logical operators AND, OR, and NOT. DynamoDB applies the filter during the search, so every result it returns matches. For example, a retail application can return the products most similar to a shopper's query within a price range and a set of brands, and a retrieval-augmented generation application can limit results to selected document categories published after a given date. The new operators are available in all AWS Regions where DynamoDB vector search is available. To learn more, see vector search in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon DynamoDB page.
title: Amazon DynamoDB vector search now supports new inline filter operators

summary: Today, Amazon CloudWatch announces support for your own application telemetry in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on. The CloudWatch agent you already run now accepts metrics, traces, and logs from your applications, so you don't deploy and operate a separate collector to get them into CloudWatch. Applications instrumented with an OpenTelemetry SDK send to an OTLP endpoint that the agent serves on every node, on by default. Metrics arrive as CloudWatch metrics you query with PromQL, traces go to AWS X-Ray and Transaction Search, and logs go to CloudWatch Logs. For Prometheus metrics, the agent scrapes the targets described by standard ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor objects, with no Prometheus operator to run and no change to your scrape configuration. Each team defines its own targets alongside its application rather than in one central add-on configuration. Label selectors let you choose which monitors CloudWatch scrapes. Both sources carry the same Kubernetes, host, cloud, and service attributes the add-on applies to the pod they came from, so you can join application telemetry to your cluster metrics. Custom telemetry is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing . To get started, see Custom telemetry in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.
title: Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on now supports custom OpenTelemetry and Prometheus telemetry

summary: AWS Quick now includes enterprise guardrails, giving administrators configurable content safety and sensitive-information controls for user prompts. Administrators can apply guardrail policies to individual users or enterprise identity provider (IdP) groups or set a policy as the account default. User-level policies take precedence over group policies and account defaults. When multiple group policies apply, Quick combines their content restrictions, using the stricter setting when controls overlap. Administrators create guardrail policies in the Quick administration console using content filters, denied topics, blocked words and phrases, prompt-attack detection, and controls for selected types of personally identifiable information (PII). For example, an administrator can create a policy that blocks prompts containing confidential project names and assign it to an IdP group. Detect-only mode lets administrators test prompt-filtering rules against real production traffic before enforcing them. In this mode, Quick evaluates user prompts and logs policy matches without blocking requests, so administrators can assess the impact on business workflows and refine policies. When administrators enable enforcement, Quick blocks matching prompts and displays a message to the user. Administrators can review detected and blocked events in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Enterprise guardrails are available in preview for select Quick customers with Professional and Enterprise plans. For feature a
title: AWS Quick introduces enterprise guardrails (preview)

summary: Today, AWS announces the preview of Data Hub in AWS Billing and Cost Management, a managed data layer that enables AWS FinOps Agent to query cost and usage data with SQL. In preview, Data Hub is available to AWS FinOps Agent, so the agent can identify the individual resources behind a cost change, break down spend by team or cost allocation tag, and show how a resource's cost and usage change hour by hour. With AWS FinOps Agent and Data Hub, customers get these answers without setting up a data export or building and maintaining a cost data pipeline. Data Hub provides 13 months of hourly, resource-level cost and usage data in the published CUR 2.0 schema, including resource identifiers and cost allocation tags. AWS provisions the data, refreshes data daily, and maintains the schema as new services, commitments, and charge types are added. When set up from the management account, Data Hub covers cost and usage data across the accounts in your organization. Data Hub (preview) is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region and covers cost and usage data across regions. There is no charge for Data Hub during preview. To learn more about Data Hub, see the AWS Billing and Cost Management User Guide and the launch blog . You can get started from the Data Hub page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or from the AWS FinOps Agent console.
title: AWS announces Data Hub in AWS Billing and Cost Management (preview)

summary: AWS Quick now supports assignments for custom permissions and limit profiles to groups from your enterprise identity provider (IdP). Administrators can now apply feature restrictions and per-user resource limits to IdP groups, in addition to the existing user, role, and account assignments. Organizations can align governance with their enterprise identity structure without maintaining assignments for individual users. Administrators manage user, account or group assignments in the Quick administration console or through new policy assignment APIs. For example, an organization can assign its finance group a custom permissions profile that blocks members from creating agents, or apply Deny by Default so that, within selected feature categories, the group can use only capabilities an administrator explicitly allows. Administrators can also assign a limit profile to a group to set each member’s index capacity and agent hours. Quick enforces these limits automatically as users consume resources. When group-level assignments apply to a user who belongs to multiple groups, Quick resolves overlapping assignments as follows: for custom permissions, a capability denied by any group stays denied, and for limit profiles, the user receives the highest value for each limit type across those groups. Group assignments are available in Quick for Professional and Enterprise plans. For feature availability by AWS Region, see AWS Quick Regions . To learn more, see the custom permissions and limi
title: AWS Quick now supports group assignments for custom permissions and limit profiles

summary: Today, Amazon CloudWatch announces built-in monitoring for open source tools running on your Amazon EKS clusters, including Karpenter, KEDA, vLLM, KServe, SGLang, Ray and Knative Serving. You get dashboards for the tools you already use without running Prometheus or Grafana yourself. Monitoring starts automatically when you enable OTel Container Insights. For your AI inference workloads, you can see queued requests, time to first token, and KV cache usage for each model server. For autoscaling, you can see which scalers are failing and how long your scale loop takes. CloudWatch tags every metric with its pod, workload, and node, so you can trace a slow model server to the node it runs on. These EKS solutions are available in version 8.0.0 and later of the add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Metrics are charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing . To get started, see Solutions in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.
title: Amazon CloudWatch EKS Container Insights now offers built-in monitoring for open source Kubernetes tools

summary: AWS Partners can now organize enriched leads and plan outreach with lead groups and channel recommendations in AWS Partner Central. Enriched leads are automatically grouped by solution area and segmented into sales-ready, marketing-ready, and limited-potential groups, so you no longer have to segment leads by hand. Limited-potential leads help you avoid spending time and budget on leads unlikely to convert, lowering your cost of acquiring new customers. For each enriched lead, you also get guidance on whether phone or email may be more effective, along with AI-generated call scripts and email scripts to act on it. Marketing-ready lead groups can be sent to Demand Center to create assets and launch targeted campaigns. Sales-ready leads can be exported to the Partner's CRM for direct outreach. Lead groups and channel recommendations are available to ACE-eligible Partners on the Leads page in AWS Partner Central and through the AWS Partner Central Selling API. To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and go to the Leads page.
title: Lead groups and channel recommendations now available in AWS Partner Central

summary: AWS Partners can now map their target accounts against AWS records and find where to collaborate with AWS on joint go-to-market before an opportunity exists. Account Mapping and Planning in AWS Partner Central replaces manual, spreadsheet-based account mapping. Upload a target account list through CSV, API, or CRM integration, and accounts are matched automatically against AWS records, including accounts without an ACE opportunity and in any country. Partners can use Account Mapping and Planning to enrich matched accounts with AWS Marketplace propensity insights, solution-level purchase likelihood, and eligibility for programs such as the Partner Greenfield Program and the Partner-Led Sales Motion. This helps Partners prioritize high-propensity and program-eligible accounts for go-to-market activity. Eligible Partners can also request joint account planning with AWS sales on accounts marked Qualified, so AWS and Partner teams can align on an account strategy earlier. Account planning is available to Consulting Partners that are ACE-eligible, Premier tier and managed by an AWS Partner Development Manager (PDM), and to ISVs that are ACE-eligible, enrolled in the SaaS Co-sell Benefit program and PDM-managed. Account Mapping and Planning is available under the Sell tab in AWS Partner Central, and account matching and enrichment are open to all ACE-eligible Partners. Partners can work in the Partner Central console, through the API and SDK, through the Partner Central MCP server,
title: Account Mapping and Planning now available in AWS Partner Central

summary: AWS Partners can now plan, launch, fund, and measure demand generation campaigns in one AI-powered experience. Demand Center in AWS Partner Central succeeds Marketing Central and brings together Marketing Central and MDF capabilities, letting you work in Partner Central, in your CRM, or in your AI agents. Create hero and distribution assets in multiple languages in minutes with AI campaign creation. Generate content from reference materials, a URL, or a description, and launch it across email, social, and banner ads. Upload leads to get them enriched with propensity signals and recommended next actions. Choose from ready-to-run Partner Ready Campaign kits or connect with AWS-vetted agencies through Agency Connect. Generate case studies with AI from ACE closed-won opportunities, and tailor campaign content to the leads included in each campaign. Connect your CRM or marketing automation tool agent-to-agent, or use Demand Center inside agents such as AWS Quick through the Partner Central MCP server. Track campaign-to-revenue performance in Partner Analytics. To get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and select Demand Center.
title: Demand Center now available in AWS Partner Central

summary: Amazon CloudWatch now supports a 30-day query window for PromQL queries against OpenTelemetry metrics, up from 7 days. You can query a month of data in a single request, chart month-over-month and week-over-week trends on one dashboard, and alarm on a 30-day baseline. Teams typically define service level objectives (SLOs) over a 30-day rolling window, longer than a 7-day query can measure. You can now calculate availability and remaining error budget for a full SLO period in one query, and alarm when a service is on track to exhaust its budget. A month of history also makes capacity forecasts more reliable, because a 7-day baseline skews to a single busy weekend. This feature is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where PromQL queries against OpenTelemetry metrics in Amazon CloudWatch are available. To get started, see Query OpenTelemetry metrics with PromQL in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide .
title: Amazon CloudWatch extends the PromQL query window to 30 days

summary: Amazon Neptune Serverless now delivers up to 30% better performance at the same price per Neptune Capacity Unit, running on AWS Graviton4 processors. The new Graviton4-based platform also brings an improved scaling algorithm that adjusts Neptune Capacity Units (NCUs) more closely to your workload. This especially helps applications with many concurrent graph queries, such as real-time fraud detection, recommendation engines and generative AI applications that run graph lookups on every request. Neptune Serverless scales database capacity automatically as your application’s demand changes, so you can run graph applications with spiky or unpredictable traffic, such as fraud detection, recommendation engines, and generative AI applications, without provisioning for peak capacity. You pay only for the capacity you use. All newly created Neptune Serverless instances will be using AWS Graviton4 processors. You can create new Neptune Serverless instances using AWS Management Console or the AWS CLI . You can upgrade existing clusters to the latest version in the next release. For more information on pricing and regional availability, refer to the Amazon Neptune pricing page and Neptune Serverless documentation .
title: Amazon Neptune Serverless now delivers up to 30% better performance and smarter scaling

summary: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports Replica First Patching, which reduces downtime during minor version upgrades. Replica First Patching is available for Enterprise Edition DB instances. With Replica First Patching, you apply a minor version upgrade to a replica in the same AWS Region first while your primary DB instance continues to serve traffic, and then switch over to the replica when you're ready to complete the upgrade. If the replica is in read-only mode, you can validate the new minor engine version with your read traffic. Replica First Patching helps you keep mission-critical Oracle workloads current on minor versions with less disruption. You choose when to switch over within the switchover window, for example during a low-traffic period. If you don't switch over within the window, Amazon RDS rolls back the replica to its original minor engine version. After the switchover, Amazon RDS completes the upgrade on the new primary DB instance. Amazon RDS then upgrades your other replicas, including your former primary DB instance, to the same minor engine version. We recommend that you connect your applications through the Primary Endpoint when you use Replica First Patching. The Primary Endpoint is a DNS name that resolves to the current primary DB instance, so your applications reach the new primary DB instance after the switchover without connection string changes. Replica First Patching is available at no additional charge in all co
title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports Replica First Patching for reduced downtime

summary: Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication (MRR) now supports additional AWS Regions, extending the resilience benefits of MRR to more workloads. Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices in minutes, and MRR lets you synchronize user and machine identity data, including credentials, user pool configurations, and federation setups, to a secondary user pool in a standby Region you designate in near real-time. With user data in the standby Region, you can redirect traffic and keep authentication available if there is a disruption in your primary Region. Previously, MRR was available in 16 commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. You can now also use MRR to replicate your user data to Asia Pacific (Hyderabad, Hong Kong, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, New Zealand, Osaka, Taipei, Thailand), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan, Spain, Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Mexico (Central), Africa (Cape Town) Regions, helping you meet resilience, data residency, and compliance requirements in the Regions that best align with your needs. MRR is available as an add-on for user pools on the Essentials or Plus feature plans, and requires a multi-Region AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). For the full list of AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available, see AWS Capabilities by Region . To get started, visit the developer guide for instructions and the pricing page for pricing details.
title: Amazon Cognito extends multi-Region replication to additional AWS Regions

summary: AWS Network Firewall announces the public preview of automated Internet firewall, a new centralized control that allows you to configure Network Firewall, with native network address translation (NAT) capability, on the internet gateways of all the Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) in your environment. Using automated Internet firewall mode, you can centrally define your Network Firewall security rules and enforce them on all inbound and outbound traffic across the internet gateways of your VPCs. You are not required to make routing or architectural changes to deploy automated Internet firewall. You can deploy it across select VPCs or your entire account, organization or organization unit. AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC. Customers use it to inspect their traffic and secure AWS resources. Prior to this launch, customers would configure AWS Network Firewalls inside their VPCs in the traffic path of all internet communication to achieve thorough security coverage against the threats on the internet. They deployed Network Firewall endpoints in dedicated subnets and made route updates for every subnet that needed internet access across all their VPCs. In addition, they monitored the environment to ensure that no new internet network paths bypassed these security controls. Automated Internet firewall makes this deployment and management simpler. You just define and maintain filtering rules, and A
title: AWS Network Firewall introduces automated Internet firewall in public preview

summary: AWS Lambda now publishes Event Function state change events to Amazon EventBridge . Lambda emits an event each time an Event Function version changes state because of a customer action, such as creating, updating, publishing, or deleting a function. These events help platform and DevOps teams to trigger automation as soon as a function becomes ready to invoke, an update finishes, or an operation fails, without polling the GetFunction API. Customers use Lambda Event Functions to build APIs, event processing workloads, multi-step workflows, and data pipelines. As organizations grow to thousands of functions, platform teams need to know when a function changes state so they can take the next step. For example, a deployment pipeline can run integration tests and then shift alias traffic once a new version becomes active. Until now, these tools had to poll the GetFunction API to track state changes. Polling consumed API quota, slowed down pipelines, and required custom retry logic, which added operational overhead. With this launch, you can create EventBridge rules that match on fields such as the function ARN, detail type, or state, and route matched events to targets such as AWS Step Functions , AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS , or Amazon SQS . This helps you build reliable, event-driven deployment pipelines across all of your functions, without writing or maintaining custom polling logic. This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions . You can create rules by using the EventBr
title: AWS Lambda now publishes Event Function state change events to Amazon EventBridge

summary: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now provides a Primary Endpoint, a DNS name that always resolves to the current primary DB instance in a replica configuration. When you switch over to an Oracle replica, Amazon RDS points the Primary Endpoint to the new primary DB instance, so you don't need to change your application connection strings. Previously, after each switchover, you had to update connection strings or DNS records to point to the new primary DB instance, which often required change approvals and coordination across teams. With Primary Endpoint, you can run planned switchovers, such as disaster recovery drills, to replicas in the same AWS Region or to cross-Region replicas without changing your application configuration. If your applications connect through the Primary Endpoint, you don't need to update their connection strings after the switchover. Every RDS for Oracle Enterprise Edition DB instance has a Primary Endpoint at no additional charge, and you don't have to create it. The Primary Endpoint is provided in addition to the instance endpoint, so your existing applications aren't affected. Primary Endpoint is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. To learn more, see Using the Primary Endpoint for Amazon RDS for Oracle in the Amazon RDS User Guide.
title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports Primary Endpoint

summary: Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, the tool that grounds AI agents and applications in cited, current web information, now supports five new languages, plus non-US English, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock: Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Japanese. Agents serving users in these languages get results that draw on local-language sources. We are also introducing a new optional country field that biases results toward sources from a specific country - just pass an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, such as “JP” or “DE”. This is useful for agents that serve users in multiple countries, for questions whose answer depends on the user's actual or preferred location (e.g., local regulations, prices or public officials), and for surfacing regional sources. Both the expanded language support and the optional country field are available today in every Region where Web Search is offered: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland) for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and US Regions for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock. Queries are processed in the Region you call, helping organizations meet data residency requirements. Existing customers get the new language capabilities automatically, with no code changes, and pricing is the same in every language. To get started with Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, checkout the developer guide and the web search product page .
title: Web Search on Amazon Bedrock expands language support and country-aware search

summary: Amazon CloudWatch Omni now supports collecting Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network (VNet) flow logs, and traces from Application Insights. Teams that run workloads on both AWS and Azure no longer need separate monitoring tools or custom pipelines to see their whole environment. Central operations, DevOps, and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams can now view Azure telemetry alongside their AWS telemetry in one place. To get started, connect a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to your AWS account and Region. You can choose the telemetry types, subscriptions, Azure regions, resource types, and tags to collect. Azure telemetry lands in Amazon CloudWatch, and Omni spaces can monitor applications and infrastructure across cloud providers. For example, during an incident you can trace a slow request from an Azure-hosted service to its AWS dependencies without switching consoles. You can set up the connectors in the Amazon CloudWatch Omni console or with the AWS CLI. Azure telemetry collection is available in all Azure Public Regions and can be ingested to all regions where CloudWatch Omni is available. To get started, visit the CloudWatch Omni User Guide and for pricing visit pricing page.
title: Amazon CloudWatch Omni now supports Microsoft Azure platform logs, metrics and traces

summary: Today, AWS announces that AWS Quick, the AI workspace for business users, now supports Japanese, German, Vietnamese, and Chinese (Simplified and Traditional). AWS Quick now displays its interface in these languages and responds in the language each user chooses. Teams that work primarily in these languages can now use AWS Quick without switching to English. For example, a finance team in Japan can ask questions about their business data in Japanese and get answers in Japanese, and a marketing team in Germany can create research reports in German. Language support covers chat, research reports, and apps in the AWS Quick web app, the desktop app for macOS and Windows, and the mobile app for iOS and Android. Support for these languages is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Quick is available. To get started, open Settings in AWS Quick, choose Appearance and Language, and select your language. To learn more, see the AWS Quick product page .
title: AWS Quick now supports Japanese, German, Vietnamese, and Chinese

summary: Flows in AWS Quick now lets users build, run, and refine automations for themselves and their teams, all through conversation. Users describe a process in chat, and Quick builds the flow, with no coding needed. Flows can now orchestrate agents, skills, and tools, with access to structured data, knowledge, and apps. A flow can pull answers from the business data a team already reports on, produce ready-to-share documents, spreadsheets, and presentations, and save the results to a team space. Flows also support longer-running workflows and larger volumes of data. New deterministic steps help keep results consistent, and validations check each step's output against rules the user sets, such as requiring a summary table in a report, before the flow continues. For example, an accounts payable team can build a flow that uses agents to read invoices and match them to purchase orders, and deterministic steps to check totals and catch duplicates. Users can now run flows wherever they work, across desktop, web, and mobile. In the desktop app, flows can work with local files and complete tasks in the browser. In the mobile app, users can start flows and check on them on the go. These updates are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Quick is available. To learn more, see Flows in AWS Quick in the AWS Quick User Guide and the AWS Quick product page.
title: Build more capable automations through chat with Flows in AWS Quick

summary: The AWS Quick web app now brings the Quick desktop experience to your browser. Create, share, and use the same agents and skills as on desktop, with the same connectors. Start each day with a daily briefing and a prioritized feed of the email and messages that need your attention. Quick keeps your conversations, agents, and files synchronized across web, desktop, and mobile, so work you start on one surface carries over to the others. Your dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before. Additionally, agents you start or schedule from the web keep running after you close your browser. Schedule an agent in the morning, answer its questions from the mobile app between meetings, and review the results on your desktop. Mission Control shows what your agents have finished and where they need your input. The Quick browser extension and Microsoft 365 add-ins for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook are also updated. These updates are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and US East (N. Virginia). Existing Quick users can sign in to the web app to get started, or download the desktop app here . The Quick mobile app is available for free from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store . To learn more, see the AWS Quick User Guide .
title: AWS Quick launches a new web experience with updated browser extension and Microsoft 365 add-ins

summary: AWS Quick now supports plugins, agents, skills, connectors, and flows built for a specific task, role, or use case. Most work draws on several of these at once: connectors to reach your systems, skills for how your team works, agents to reason through tasks, and flows to orchestrate each process. Plugins package these capabilities together, so users can install everything a job needs in one step. To get started, users can browse and install official plugins from AWS, such as the Calendar and Meetings Assistant, which helps users plan time away and turn meeting notes into action items, or the Sales Development plugin, which takes a prospect from lead research to outreach and a proposal. More than 100 skills and plugins cover everyday productivity, roles such as finance, marketing and legal, industries, and popular business applications. Builders can also create their own custom plugins for their team, department, or organization. Just describe the job in chat, and Quick assembles the plugin. Then share it for teammates to discover. This is available in all Regions where AWS Quick is available. To learn more, see the AWS Quick User Guide . To get started with Quick, visit AWS Quick .
title: AWS Quick now supports plugins to bundle agents, skills, connectors and flows

summary: AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued. You can write IAM policies that allow or deny a certificate request based on its subject, subject alternative names (SANs), public key, signature algorithm, validity period, key usage, extended key usage, and basic constraints. You can share one private CA across teams and accounts, and each team can issue only the certificates your policies allow. Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains. To keep each team to its own domain names, customers ran a separate CA for each team or built their own authorization layer in front of AWS Private CA. Now, AWS Private CA evaluates your policies against the certificate as it would be issued, before anything is signed, and denies requests that don't comply. For example, you can limit each account to DNS names in its own subdomain, cap certificate lifetimes, require specified key algorithms and key sizes across your organization, and reserve CA certificates for your PKI team. You can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Each key takes its value from the final certificate, whether the attribute comes from the certificate signing r
title: AWS Private CA now supports X.509 IAM condition keys

summary: AWS DevOps Agent is now certified at the Federal Risk and Authorization Management (FedRAMP) Class D level in AWS GovCloud (US). AWS DevOps Agent is your always-available operations teammate that resolves and proactively prevents incidents, optimizes application reliability and performance, and handles on-demand SRE tasks across AWS, multicloud, and on-prem environments. Cloud Service Providers achieve and maintain FedRAMP Certification by meeting NIST 800-53 Rev 5 controls, undergoing annual independent assessment by a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service, performing continuous monitoring and vulnerability management, publishing quarterly Ongoing Certification Reports, and issuing Significant Change Notifications to agencies for material changes to any AWS cloud service offerings the agency uses. To learn more about AWS DevOps Agent, read the launch blog and see getting started . For information on FedRAMP Certification updates, including Significant Change Notifications, visit the FedRAMP Compliance FAQ .
title: AWS DevOps Agent achieves FedRAMP Class D Certification in AWS GovCloud (US-West)

summary: AWS Compute Optimizer automation rules can now target the organizational units (OUs) you manage with AWS Organizations, making it easier for large organizations to scale optimization across their accounts. Previously, management accounts could target up to 50 member accounts per rule. Now, a single rule can cover every account in an OU, including accounts added later. You also have the flexibility to exclude specific child OUs or member accounts as needed. Automation rules help you save cost and improve performance by applying recommended actions on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule when they match your criteria. These actions include cleaning up unattached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes and upgrading volumes to the latest-generation volume types. For example, from your management account, you can create an automation rule to clean up unattached volumes across your entire organization, while allowing resource owners to tag and exclude volumes they want to keep. To get started, turn on Automation for your selected OUs. Then, create rules that target them. Support for OUs is available in all AWS Regions where Compute Optimizer automation rules are available. To learn more, see Enabling Automation for your organization in the AWS Compute Optimizer User Guide , or visit the AWS Compute Optimizer product page.
title: AWS Compute Optimizer automation rules now support organizational units

summary: Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio now lets you save your PromQL and SQL metrics queries and reuse them. You no longer need to rewrite or search for queries you run often, such as a latency query you check during every incident. You can save a query under a name and use "/" in the name to organize queries into folders. In the Saved tab of the Queries panel, you can search, sort, and preview your saved queries. You can then apply one to replace what's in the studio, append it to your current queries, edit it, or delete it. Saved queries are stored in your account and Region, and you control who can create, view, and delete them by using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. You can also manage them programmatically with the new PutMetricDataQueryDefinition, GetMetricDataQueryDefinition, ListMetricDataQueryDefinitions, and DeleteMetricDataQueryDefinition APIs. You can use saved queries in Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Osaka), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney). To learn more, see Saving and reusing queries in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide . For product information, see Amazon CloudWatch .
title: Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio now supports saved queries

summary: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) now issues Amazon N2 certificates for mutual TLS (mTLS) and other authentication outside web browsers. ACM public certificates no longer include client authentication, in line with WebPKI requirements, so teams that needed client certificates had to define their own trust governance models and apply them to their private PKI. With Amazon N2 certificates, you can authenticate to partners and other organizations, such as a partner's client calling your API, without building and governing your own CA for them to rely on. Amazon N2 certificates come from the Amazon N2 certificate authorities (CAs), which are operated and governed by Amazon Trust Services, the same organization that operates the CAs issuing ACM public WebPKI certificates. Your peers add the Amazon N2 roots to their trust stores to verify your certificates. Certificates are valid for up to 395 days, and ACM renews them automatically: AWS integrated services use each renewed certificate, and you can also export them to your own clients and servers. You pay for each domain name in an ACM-issued Amazon N2 certificate, including when you use it with AWS integrated services. For details, see ACM pricing . Amazon N2 certificates are available in all commercial AWS Regions where ACM is available. To learn more, see Amazon N2 certificates in the AWS Certificate Manager User Guide .
title: AWS Certificate Manager now supports Amazon N2 certificates for mTLS

summary: You can now use Amazon S3 Access Points to copy or move data server-side between Amazon S3 general purpose buckets and Amazon FSx file systems within the same AWS Region, making it faster, lower-cost, and easier to move your data between S3 and FSx or across FSx file systems. An S3 Access Point for FSx is an S3 endpoint that allows you to access the data on your Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems via the S3 API and from S3-based services and applications. You can also use S3 Access Points to transfer data to and from your file system without the need to mount it—for example, to copy data into your file system from an S3 bucket owned by a partner or to export job results into another team's bucket. Previously, S3 Access Points for FSx didn't support server-side copies, so transferring your data meant downloading and then uploading each object from a server you run. Starting today, you can now transfer data server-side using S3's standard CopyObject and UploadPartCopy operations, reducing the time, cost, and effort needed to move data between S3 and FSx or between FSx file systems. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Access Points for FSx are available. You can copy data with the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or S3-compatible tools to move and copy data. To learn more, see the FSx for ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS user guides, and visit the Amazon S3 Access Points page .
title: You can now copy data server-side between Amazon S3 buckets and Amazon FSx file systems with S3 Access Points

summary: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP now lets you snapshot, clone, and replicate your data directly from the Amazon FSx Console and AWS CloudFormation. Today’s launch allows you to protect and copy your ONTAP data using the same AWS tools that you use across the rest of your AWS environments, with a few clicks in the AWS console or as part of your infrastructure-as-code workflows. FSx for ONTAP is the first and only storage service that allows you to launch and run fully managed, fully featured ONTAP file systems in the cloud. Previously, you could only set up and manage snapshots, volume clones, and SnapMirror replication via the ONTAP CLI or REST API. Starting today, you can also use the Amazon FSx Console, Amazon FSx API, and AWS CloudFormation, in addition to the ONTAP CLI and REST API, to manage these resources. AWS Console and CloudFormation support for these resources are available in all AWS Regions where FSx for ONTAP is available. To learn more, visit the FSx for NetApp ONTAP user guide and the Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP product page .
title: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP adds AWS CloudFormation and Console support for snapshots, clones, and data replication

summary: Automated API discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover every API behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF. Discovery is available through the new API Gateway API Portal, which identifies the APIs automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. The API Portal classifies the APIs it finds, identifies zombie and shadow APIs, evaluates each API's security posture, and reports findings, including the ones that are missing WAF protections. For unprotected APIs, customers can enable protection using WAF. Protection is available through the new AWS WAF API Security managed rule group, which protects your APIs against the most exploited API attack categories: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), where the attackers change record IDs in requests to read other users' data, Broken Authentication and Credential Stuffing, where the attackers forge tokens or try stolen passwords at scale, and API Reconnaissance and Enumeration, where the attackers map an API by guessing hidden routes and probing for exposed docs. The events detected by WAF are consolidated into the API Portal findings to provide a complete security picture of your APIs. You can use API Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications. Together, API Portal and API Security provi
title: AWS WAF announces automated discovery and protection for API endpoints

summary: AWS Device Farm , a service for testing mobile and web apps, now offers Device Connect. With Device Connect, you and AI agents can use remote Android devices from your local machine in an IDE, terminal, or development environment of your choice, as if it were plugged into your laptop. You can attach a debugger, profile performance, preview builds, run ADB (Android Debug Bridge) commands, and interact manually with the devices. You also get live video along with device and test logs. Tools and test frameworks that work with ADB locally now run on a real device that Device Farm manages for you. Previously, you used Device Farm devices manually in a web browser or for automated tests through APIs. You couldn't reach them from your local tools, such as Android Studio or a terminal. Device Connect closes that gap by connecting your local machine to a device hosted in AWS. Your existing ADB-based workflows run unchanged. To get started, install the Device Connect client from GitHub, create a remote access session on Device Farm, and attach to the session's device with the 'devicefarm-connect' command. Device Connect supports Android OS versions nine and later. The client runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows with no additional cost. Device usage is billed at standard Device Farm rates. Device Connect is available in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. To learn more, see the AWS Device Farm Developer Guide .
title: AWS Device Farm launches Device Connect for local access to remote Android devices

summary: Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML now lets customers search across multiple instance types and AWS Regions in a single search, making it easier to find and reserve the capacity their ML workloads need.
